Account Usage.name: Authentication Events
Account Usage.purpose: Identifies where authentication of credentials actually occurred, distinguishing local/workgroup account authentication (recorded on the workstation itself) from domain/Active Directory authentication (recorded on the domain controller), via NTLM and Kerberos protocol events.
key_fields: Event ID 4776 (NTLM) - the system attempted to validate credentials for an account, success or failure
Event ID 4768 (Kerberos) - a Ticket Granting Ticket was requested/granted, indicating a successful logon
Event ID 4769 (Kerberos) - a Service Ticket was requested, indicating access to a server resource
Event ID 4771 (Kerberos) - Kerberos pre-authentication failed, indicating a failed logon
Account Usage.normal_baseline: 4768/4769 activity concentrated on domain controllers, matching normal business-hours logon and resource-access patterns for known accounts; 4776 activity limited to expected local/workgroup authentication scenarios.
anomalies: A burst of 4771 (Kerberos pre-authentication failed) events against one or many accounts followed by a 4768 success, consistent with a password-spray or brute-force attack that ultimately succeeded
4769 Service Ticket requests for service accounts using weak/legacy ticket encryption at unusual hours, consistent with Kerberoasting
4776 NTLM authentication occurring where Kerberos would normally be expected for that account/resource, consistent with a forced protocol downgrade or a pass-the-hash style attempt

Authentication events recorded on a host other than where the analyst expects for that account type (e.g., a domain account appearing to authenticate locally rather than at a domain controller), consistent with cached-credential logon
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: These events are recorded only on the system that actually performed the authentication - a host showing no local 4776/4768/4769 activity for a given account has not necessarily seen no authentication, it may simply mean the authentication happened elsewhere (the domain controller for a domain account). Standard Security-log clearing and retention limits otherwise apply (see security-eventlog's Event ID 1102 note).
Account Usage.interpretation: Authentication events identify where authentication of credentials occurred, which is particularly useful when tracking local vs. domain account usage. They are recorded on the system that authenticated the credentials: Local Account/Workgroup authentication is recorded on the workstation itself, while Domain/Active Directory authentication is recorded on the domain controller.

Account Usage.name: Cloud Account Details
Account Usage.purpose: Identifies whether a local Windows account is actually a Microsoft cloud account by recording the email address tied to it, directly inside the SAM hive.
key_fields: InternetUserName value under the account's RID subkey: contains the email address tied to the Microsoft cloud account
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Accounts known to be signed in with a Microsoft account (personal or Azure AD-backed) show an InternetUserName value matching the expected corporate or personal email; accounts that are genuinely local-only have no InternetUserName value at all.
anomalies: An InternetUserName value present on an account that was assumed to be a local-only service or admin account, indicating undisclosed cloud-account linkage
InternetUserName email domain that doesn't match the organization's expected domain, suggesting a personal Microsoft account was used to sign into a corporate machine
A newly created account with an InternetUserName tied to an external, unfamiliar email address shortly before or during a suspected compromise
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The value only exists if the account was ever configured to sign in with a Microsoft cloud account; a purely local account will simply have no InternetUserName value, which is not itself suspicious. Converting a cloud-linked account back to local removes this value going forward, but historical evidence may still be recoverable from registry hive backups (RegBack) or Volume Shadow Copies.
Account Usage.interpretation: The presence of this value is what distinguishes a Microsoft cloud account from a purely local one at the SAM level. Check it whenever you need to know whether a given local username actually authenticates against a Microsoft identity rather than a locally-stored password. Cross-reference the email domain against known-good corporate domains to catch personal-account usage on managed hardware.

Account Usage.name: Last Login and Password Change
Account Usage.purpose: The SAM registry hive maintains a list of local accounts and associated configuration information, including last login time, last password change, and login counts.
key_fields: Accounts listed by their relative identifiers (RID)
Last login time
Last password change
Login counts
Group membership
Account creation time
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Last-login timestamps align with known usage patterns for the account owner; password-change dates align with the organization's rotation policy; login counts grow steadily rather than jumping abruptly.
anomalies: An account with a recent creation time but no login history, consistent with an account staged for later use
A password change immediately followed by first-time or unusual login activity, especially on a privileged account
Login count inconsistent with the account's expected usage frequency (e.g. a service account showing interactive-style login patterns)
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: SAM is unreadable in place while Windows is running except via SYSTEM-level access; an offline copy or a Volume Shadow Copy is typically needed for analysis without extracting the hive live via `reg save`.
Account Usage.interpretation: This is the same underlying data as the `sam-hive` artifact's F-value fields, called out here specifically because the SANS poster treats it as its own 'evidence of account usage' question distinct from the SAM hive's broader persistence/credential role. Cross-reference against `cloud-account-details` to determine whether the account authenticates locally or via a Microsoft cloud identity before interpreting login timestamps.

Account Usage.name: Logon Event Types
Account Usage.location: %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\logs\Security.evtx: the Logon Type field within Event ID 4624
Account Usage.purpose: Determines by exactly what means a logon was attempted, in addition to date, time, username, hostname, and success/failure status. The single field that separates a console logon from a network logon, RDP session, or scheduled-task logon.
key_fields: Logon Type 2: logon via console
Logon Type 3: network logon
Logon Type 4: batch logon
Logon Type 5: Windows service logon
Logon Type 7: credentials used to unlock screen, or an RDP session reconnect
Logon Type 8: network logon sending credentials in cleartext
Logon Type 9: different credentials used than the logged-on user
Logon Type 10: remote interactive logon (RDP)
Logon Type 11: cached credentials used to logon
Logon Type 12: cached remote interactive (similar to Type 10)
Logon Type 13: cached unlock (similar to Type 7)
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Logon Type 2 for regular console users during business hours; Type 3 for expected file-share/network access; Type 10 only from known admin or remote-work sources.
anomalies: Logon Type 10 (RDP) from an unexpected source at an odd hour
Logon Type 8 (cleartext network credentials) appearing at all on a modern, properly configured network
Logon Type 9 (different credentials than the logged-on user) on a host with no legitimate reason for credential switching, consistent with pass-the-hash or RunAs abuse
Logon Type 5 (service logon) tied to an account that isn't a known service account
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The Logon Type is only as trustworthy as the 4624 event itself, if Security-log auditing is disabled or the log is cleared, this classification is lost along with the rest of the logon record.
Account Usage.interpretation: Always read the Logon Type alongside the account name and source IP/workstation fields on the same 4624 event. The type alone tells you the *mechanism*, not whether the logon itself was legitimate. Use this table to disambiguate `successful-failed-logons` records and to interpret Type 10 correctly for `rdp-eventlogs` correlation.

Account Usage.name: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) Usage
Account Usage.purpose: Tracks RDP logons and session reconnections to a target machine, and identifies which accounts were used to do so, purely from the Security log's account-usage perspective.
key_fields: Event ID 4624: Logon Type 10 (remote interactive logon)
Event ID 4778: session connected/reconnected
Event ID 4779: session disconnected
Hostname and IP address of the remote machine making the connection, recorded on the 4624/4778/4779 events
Account Usage.normal_baseline: RDP account usage aligns with known admin jump-box or approved remote-work sources, at expected times and from expected source hosts.
anomalies: Logon Type 10 from an account with no legitimate remote-access business need
4778/4779 reconnect/disconnect pairs from a source IP that changes mid-session, suggesting session hijacking
RDP account usage outside normal business hours with no corresponding change ticket or on-call justification
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: This account-usage view is narrower than the full RDP session-lifecycle picture. It only sees what the Security log's 4624/4778/4779 triad records. For the fuller cross-channel session timeline (including the RemoteConnectionManager and LocalSessionManager Operational logs' 1149 and 21-25 events), see `rdp-eventlogs`, which is the more complete, multi-channel version of this same evidence.
Account Usage.interpretation: Use this entry when the question is specifically "which accounts used RDP and from where" (an account-usage/audit question); use `rdp-eventlogs` when the question is "reconstruct the full session timeline for this RDP connection" (a session-forensics question). The two overlap on 4624/4778/4779 but `rdp-eventlogs` adds the pre-auth and session-lifecycle channels this entry doesn't cover.

Account Usage.name: Service Events
Account Usage.os_min: Event ID 7045 requires Windows Server 2008 R2+; 4697 auditing requires Windows 10+
Account Usage.location: System.evtx (Win7+): Event IDs 7034/7035/7036/7040/7045; Security.evtx (Win10+, requires auditing enabled). Event ID 4697
Account Usage.purpose: Analyzes logs for suspicious Windows service creation, persistence, and services started or stopped around the time of a suspected compromise; service events also record account information.
key_fields: Event ID 7034 (System log): service crashed unexpectedly
Event ID 7035 (System log): service sent a Start/Stop control
Event ID 7036 (System log): service started or stopped
Event ID 7040 (System log): start type changed (Boot | On Request | Disabled)
Event ID 7045 (System log, Win2008R2+): a service was installed on the system
Event ID 4697 (Security log, Win10+): a service was installed on the system, requires auditing enabled
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Service creation/start/stop events correspond to known software installs, Windows updates, and expected maintenance windows.
anomalies: Event ID 7045 for a service with a suspicious ImagePath, an unsigned binary, or a name mimicking a legitimate Windows service
A service repeatedly crashing (7034) coinciding with a known attack technique that targets that specific service or process
7040 start-type change flipping a security-relevant service to Disabled shortly before or during an incident
4697 present with no corresponding 7045, or vice versa, when both logs should be capturing the same install and auditing is enabled for both. Suggests log tampering or a gap in visibility
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: A large amount of malware and worms in the wild use services for persistence and privilege; services started on boot illustrate persistence (desirable to malware), and services can also be intentionally crashed via attacks like process injection to disable defensive tooling. 4697 requires the Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory to be enabled, which many environments don't turn on by default, leaving 7045 as the only reliable source.
Account Usage.interpretation: Treat System.evtx as the baseline source for service lifecycle events (available without extra auditing) and Security.evtx's 4697 as a bonus corroborating source only where that audit policy is already enabled. Cross-reference the service name/ImagePath against the `services-persistence` artifact's registry-level view (CurrentControlSet\Services) to confirm what the service was actually configured to run.

Account Usage.name: Successful/Failed Logons
Account Usage.purpose: Profiles account creation, attempted logons, and account usage through the core Security-log authentication event IDs.
key_fields: Event ID 4624: successful logon
Event ID 4625: failed logon
Event ID 4634 / 4647: successful logoff
Event ID 4648: logon using explicit credentials (runas)
Event ID 4672: account logon with superuser (administrator) rights
Event ID 4720: an account was created
Account Usage.normal_baseline: 4624/4634 pairs align with expected work-hours usage for known accounts; 4625 failures are isolated and infrequent; 4672/superuser logons correspond to known administrative activity; 4720 account-creation events align with change-managed onboarding.
anomalies: A burst of 4625 failures against one or many accounts in a short window, consistent with password spraying or brute force
4648 (explicit credential logon / runas) using an account that shouldn't have a reason to authenticate from that host
4672 superuser logon for an account outside the expected administrator list
4720 account creation outside a documented change window, especially followed shortly by a 4672 admin-rights logon for the same account
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The Security log can be cleared (itself logged as Event ID 1102) or rotated out under high logon volume; correlate with a SIEM/forwarder for retention beyond local log rotation limits.
Account Usage.interpretation: Use 4624/4625 as the anchor pair for any account-usage timeline, then layer 4648 (explicit creds) and 4672 (elevated rights) on top to distinguish a routine logon from a privilege-escalation-relevant one. Cross-reference with `logon-event-types` for what each 4624 Logon Type code actually means (console vs network vs RDP vs service, etc.) before drawing conclusions from the raw event alone.

Account Usage.name: User Accounts
Account Usage.purpose: Identifies both local and domain accounts that have interactively logged on to the system, by enumerating one subkey per user SID with a pointer to that user's profile folder.
key_fields: Subkey name - the account's SID
ProfileImagePath value - the filesystem path to that account's profile folder
SID structure - the RID suffix identifies well-known accounts (e.g., -500 for the built-in Administrator) independent of any display-name rename
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Subkeys correspond only to expected local and domain accounts known to have legitimately logged onto the machine, with ProfileImagePath values pointing to standard C:\Users\<name> paths.
anomalies: A new SID/profile subkey appearing shortly before or during an incident for an account absent from the organization's identity system
ProfileImagePath pointing to a nonstandard location outside the normal C:\Users tree
A profile subkey present with no corresponding active local or Active Directory account, consistent with an account that has since been deleted while its ProfileList entry persisted
A domain SID mapped under ProfileList that doesn't correspond to the domain the asset records show this host as joined to
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting a local user account does not automatically remove its ProfileList subkey or profile folder, so a stale entry can remain as evidence of a since-deleted account; conversely, an attacker who manually deletes both the ProfileList subkey and the profile folder can attempt to hide that an account ever logged on locally, though this can still leave traces in the sam-hive or security-eventlog.
Account Usage.interpretation: ProfileList is useful for mapping a SID to its account name; each subkey is named for a user's SID and contains a ProfileImagePath value indicating that user's profile path. Well-known SID RID suffixes (e.g., -500 for the built-in Administrator) can help identify privileged accounts even after a display-name rename.

Account Usage.name: DPAPI Master Keys
Account Usage.os_min: Windows 2000+ (DPAPI itself introduced in Windows 2000; current per-user master key file format in use since Windows XP/2000 era, largely unchanged through modern Windows)
Account Usage.location: C:\Users\<Username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Protect\<User SID>\<MasterKey GUID> (per-user master keys); C:\Windows\System32\Microsoft\Protect\S-1-5-18\User\<GUID> (SYSTEM/machine master keys); CREDHIST file in the same Protect\<SID> folder; domain DPAPI backup key held on Domain Controllers
Account Usage.purpose: Stores the symmetric master keys the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) uses to derive encryption keys for user secrets — saved browser/Wi-Fi passwords, Credential Manager entries, private keys/certificates, and EFS keys — with each master key itself protected by a key derived from the user's logon password or a domain/local backup key.
key_fields: MasterKey GUID (filename)
Version
Salt
MasterKeyLen
BackupKeyLen
CredHistLen
DomainKeyLen
encrypted MasterKey blob
encrypted BackupKey blob
CredHist GUID reference (CREDHIST file)
DomainKey blob (RSA-encrypted with domain DPAPI backup key)
Account Usage.normal_baseline: One Protect\<SID> folder per local profile that has ever used DPAPI-backed protection (browsers, Wi-Fi profiles, EFS, Credential Manager, password managers); a small number of GUID-named master key files accumulate over time, generally one new key per password change or periodic rotation, alongside a CREDHIST file in the same folder.
anomalies: Master key files copied off-host (temp directory, removable media, exfil staging) without corresponding legitimate user activity
Access to another user's Protect\<SID> folder from a different user context or an unrelated SYSTEM/admin process
Master key files created/modified immediately following a suspicious password reset (can be used to force derivable new master keys)
Command-line/process evidence of dpapi::masterkey, dpapi::cred, or SharpDPAPI/dploot triage commands coinciding with master key file access
Theft of the domain DPAPI backup key (via LSASS or NTDS.dit access) followed by mass reads across many users' Protect folders, indicating domain-wide decryption capability
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: Master key files are opaque binary blobs with no plaintext indication of what they protect, so their presence alone reveals nothing without the user's password, the domain backup key, or the SYSTEM DPAPI_SYSTEM/DPAPI_USERS LSA secret; an attacker who obtains the domain backup key from a Domain Controller can decrypt any domain user's master keys indefinitely without ever touching the victim host again, leaving no artifact there to find.

Account Usage.name: Credential Manager Vault
Account Usage.os_min: Windows Vista+ (Credential Manager/Windows Vault introduced with Vista; backup/restore and modern locker split added in Windows 7)
Account Usage.location: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Vault\<GUID>\ (Web/Windows Vault: Policy.vpol, *.vcrd, *.vsch); %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials\ (Windows Credentials locker); %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Vault\ ; %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Vault\<GUID>\ (system-wide vault); C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault (SYSTEM profile vault)
Account Usage.purpose: Stores encrypted credentials — usernames/passwords and, for Web Credentials, website login data — that applications and Internet Explorer/legacy Edge save via the Windows Credential Manager APIs so users are not re-prompted for authentication.
key_fields: Vault Policy GUID (per-vault folder identifier)
Policy.vpol (DPAPI-protected vault encryption key, contains a GUID matching the vault folder)
*.vcrd (individual encrypted credential entry: target/resource name, username, encrypted secret, last-written timestamp)
*.vsch (schema file describing how to interpret a decrypted .vcrd entry)
Credentials locker blob files under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Credentials
Account Usage.normal_baseline: Vault and Credentials folders present per user profile with entries tied to legitimately saved RDP connections, mapped network drives, IIS/SQL, Microsoft 365, and browser (IE/legacy Edge) saved logins; .vcrd file counts stay low and grow only when a user opts to 'remember' credentials.
anomalies: vaultcmd.exe /listcreds or /list enumeration immediately followed by process access to the Vault/Credentials folders
rundll32.exe keymgr.dll KRShowKeyMgr execution (Stored User Names and Passwords backup/restore UI abuse)
CredEnumerateA/CredEnumerateW API calls invoked from non-standard or unsigned processes
New .vcrd/.vpol files copied to an unexpected path or exfil staging directory
Vault access by a process running as a different user than the vault owner without a prior privilege-escalation event
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: Vault secrets are DPAPI-protected with per-user master keys, so copying .vcrd/.vpol files alone yields nothing without the corresponding master key or domain backup key; attackers commonly stage DPAPI master key theft together with vault file theft, and native tools (vaultcmd.exe, keymgr.dll) generate minimal process telemetry distinguishable from legitimate credential-manager use unless command-line auditing is enabled.

Account Usage.name: LSA Secrets
Account Usage.os_min: Windows NT+ (Policy\Secrets store present in the SECURITY hive since early Windows NT; AES-based hashedBootKey encryption confirmed added with Windows Vista/Server 2008, replacing the RC4 scheme used on NT/2000/XP/2003)
Account Usage.location: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets (live registry, readable only by SYSTEM by default); on-disk backing file %SystemRoot%\System32\config\SECURITY
Account Usage.purpose: Stores sensitive secrets managed by the Local Security Authority — service account passwords, cached auto-logon credentials, the domain machine account password, DPAPI system-level key backup material, and other application-registered secrets — encrypted with a key derived from the SYSTEM boot key (SysKey).
key_fields: $MACHINE.ACC (CurrVal/OldVal subkeys — domain computer account password, current/previous)
NL$KM (cached domain logon / DCC hash encryption key)
DPAPI_SYSTEM (SYSTEM and per-user DPAPI master key backup material)
DefaultPassword (autologon password when configured, e.g. via Sysinternals Autologon)
_SC_<ServiceName> (logon password for services configured to run as a named account)
CurrVal / OldVal / CupdTime / OupdTime / SecDesc (per-secret subkey structure)
Account Usage.normal_baseline: $MACHINE.ACC present on any domain-joined machine; NL$KM present when domain cached logons are enabled; _SC_<ServiceName> entries only for services deliberately configured with a named service account (not LocalSystem/NetworkService); DefaultPassword absent unless autologon was intentionally configured.
anomalies: Remote or local access to the SECURITY hive/Policy\Secrets outside scheduled system maintenance (reg save, Volume Shadow Copy hive extraction, remote registry)
Presence of DefaultPassword indicating autologon was configured (a stored, recoverable cleartext credential)
New or unexpected _SC_ entries for services not normally run under a named account
Command-line indicators of lsadump::secrets (Mimikatz), secretsdump.py, or reg save on SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hives
Use of the REG_OPTION_BACKUP_RESTORE flag via custom tooling to read Policy\Secrets while bypassing normal ACL checks
parsing_tools: reg.exe (hive export, combined with offline decryption tooling)
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: Reading Policy\Secrets live requires SYSTEM privileges, so attackers typically pivot through a SYSTEM-level context (PsExec, WMI, scheduled task) or export the SECURITY and SYSTEM hives (reg save / Volume Shadow Copy) to decrypt offline, leaving little live-process trace against the hive itself; because decryption requires SysKey from the SYSTEM hive plus the LSA key from SECURITY, an exported SECURITY hive alone is useless — analysts should always correlate SECURITY and SYSTEM hive access/exfiltration together.

Account Usage.name: Windows Hello / NGC Container
Account Usage.os_min: Windows 10 (1507)+; Windows Hello for Business cloud/hybrid trust deployments require Windows 10 1511+
Account Usage.location: C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Ngc\ (per-credential NGC container subfolders, ACL-restricted to SYSTEM/LocalService); supporting key protector material also relies on the user's DPAPI master keys
Account Usage.purpose: Stores the Next Generation Credential (NGC) key containers backing Windows Hello and Windows Hello for Business — the private key material unlocked by a PIN or biometric (fingerprint/face) gesture that authenticates the user without a transmitted reusable password.
key_fields: Per-credential GUID subfolder name (one per enrolled sign-in method)
Protector key blobs (PIN-derived or TPM-sealed)
Key attestation / AIK certificate references (Windows Hello for Business)
DPAPI-wrapped private key blob requiring PIN-derived unlock
Account Usage.normal_baseline: One NGC container subfolder per enrolled Windows Hello credential (PIN and/or biometric) per user on the device; contents are unusable outside the originating TPM and outside the SYSTEM/LocalService security context; subfolder count increases only when a user enrolls an additional sign-in method.
anomalies: NGC folder contents copied off the device (the folder is never legitimately accessed or exported outside SYSTEM/LocalService)
New credential subfolder appearing with no corresponding Windows Hello enrollment event in the Security event log
PIN reset/repair activity (Ngc folder deletion and recreation) with no matching help-desk ticket or user-initiated reset
Evidence of NGC-targeting extraction tooling being staged or run (requires SYSTEM plus SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive access), indicating offline credential-cracking preparation
parsing_tools: WINHELLO2hashcat (Banaanhangwagen, GitHub) with dpapick3, for offline PIN hash extraction
DPAPI forensic tooling (Mimikatz DPAPI module, dpapick) for the supporting master-key material
Account Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The NGC container never holds a plaintext private key on disk — material is TPM-sealed or DPAPI-wrapped with the PIN — so deleting the folder (or performing a Windows Hello PIN/face/fingerprint reset) destroys the credential rather than concealing evidence of its use; an attacker with SYSTEM and access to the SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hives can still stage an offline PIN-cracking attempt without modifying the container itself, leaving no direct on-disk trace in the NGC folder.

Application Execution.name: Amcache.hve
Application Execution.os_min: Windows 8 (backported to Windows 7 SP1 via KB2952664)
Application Execution.location: C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve (standalone registry hive, plus Amcache.hve.LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs in the same folder)
Application Execution.purpose: A registry hive maintained by the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser / Inventory Collector that catalogs executables, installed applications, and loaded drivers seen on the system, recording each file's path, SHA-1 hash, and size. Because the entry is written independently of the file itself, it commonly survives after the underlying binary has been deleted, making it valuable evidence of program presence/first-run even post-deletion.
key_fields: LowerCaseLongPath: full file path of the executable
FileId: a 41-character value: literal prefix "0000" + the SHA-1 hex digest (hashed over roughly the first 31 MiB of the file)
KeyLastWriteTimestamp: registry last-write time of the entry; the closest available proxy for when the entry was first inventoried
LinkDate: PE header compile/link timestamp (attacker-controllable, not a filesystem time)
Size: file size in bytes
Publisher / Version / BinFileVersion: PE resource / code-signing metadata
ProgramId: links a file entry (InventoryApplicationFile) to its parent install record (InventoryApplication)
Application Execution.normal_baseline: On Windows 10 1607+ / Windows 11, entries live under Root\InventoryApplicationFile, Root\InventoryApplication, and Root\InventoryDriverBinary inside the hive (older Windows 7 SP1 / Windows 8.x builds instead use a legacy Root\File\{VolumeGUID}\{FileRef} and Root\Programs layout). A clean system accumulates entries for OS binaries, installed applications, and drivers over its lifetime, with plausible LinkDate values consistent with each vendor's known build/release dates and paths under Program Files, Windows, or System32.
anomalies: Executable path under Temp, Downloads, AppData\Local\Temp, ProgramData, or another user-writable/unusual directory with no corresponding InventoryApplication install record
FileId (SHA-1) matches a known-malicious hash, especially when the path is atypical for that hash's known-good usage

Amcache entry exists (proving the file was once present/executed) with no matching file on disk. Evidence of a deleted binary, especially valuable when the same timeframe shows corroborating Prefetch, Shimcache, or BAM entries
LinkDate that postdates KeyLastWriteTimestamp, or is otherwise inconsistent with the rest of the file's metadata. A sign the PE compile timestamp was forged
The same SHA-1 recorded across many hosts under different file names/paths, consistent with a single payload redeployed by an actor
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting the binary from disk does not remove its Amcache record: the inventory snapshot persists in the hive until the next Compatibility Appraiser scheduled-task run, and the prior entry is often still recoverable from the Amcache.hve.LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs even after that. An investigator who collects only the .hve file (not its .LOG1/.LOG2 companions) on a system that wasn't cleanly shut down can miss the most recent writes. Wiping or replacing Amcache.hve outright, or disabling the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser task, stops new entries from being recorded going forward but is itself an unusual, noteworthy action to find during triage.

Application Execution.name: BAM/DAM
Application Execution.location: Pre-Windows 10 1809: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\UserSettings\{SID} and HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\dam\UserSettings\{SID}. Windows 10 1809 and later: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\bam\State\UserSettings\{SID} and \dam\State\UserSettings\{SID} (a 'State' subkey was inserted into the path).
Application Execution.purpose: BAM is a Windows service that throttles background application activity to conserve battery/resources; as a side effect it records, per user SID, the full path of each executable that ran and the timestamp of its last execution. DAM is the equivalent mechanism for devices supporting Connected Standby (primarily mobile/tablet hardware). Both key their entries under the executing user's SID, giving analysts direct user attribution for a launched binary even though the data lives in the machine-wide SYSTEM hive.
key_fields: Value name: full path of the executable that was run
Value data: an 8-byte little-endian FILETIME embedded in the REG_BINARY value, representing the last execution time of that executable for that user
SID subkey: identifies which user account ran the executable
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Under each active user's SID subkey, a list of paths to applications that user has run recently (within roughly the last 7 days), covering normal OS components, shell integrations, and everyday applications launched from local disk.
anomalies: Executable path under Temp, Downloads, or another user-writable/unusual directory attributed to a SID for a user who wouldn't normally run such tools
A BAM/DAM entry for an executable whose file no longer exists on disk (deleted after execution). Corroborate against Amcache/Prefetch/Shimcache for the same binary
Execution attributed to a SID inconsistent with the expected interactive user (e.g. a service account or a rarely-used local account) at an unusual time of day

Entries missing entirely for a period where other execution artifacts (Prefetch, Shimcache) show activity, since BAM/DAM only covers roughly the trailing 7 days and purges on reboot, absence does not by itself prove non-execution and must be time-correlated
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: BAM/DAM entries are automatically purged roughly 7 days after the recorded activity, and an entry is removed once its associated executable no longer exists at its original location, and again on the next reboot, so this artifact has a naturally short retention window even with no attacker interference. It only records executables launched from local storage; programs run from removable media or network shares are not captured. Because the data lives in the live SYSTEM hive rather than a separate log, wiping it requires direct registry-key deletion (an unusual, detectable action) rather than simple file deletion.

Application Execution.name: CapabilityAccessManager
Application Execution.purpose: Records which applications accessed sensitive device capabilities, such as the microphone and camera, and when.
key_fields: Capability subkey name - e.g. microphone, webcam, location - identifies which sensitive capability was accessed
Application subkey - per-app entry named by package family name (Microsoft Store apps) or executable path
LastUsedTimeStart - FILETIME marking the beginning of the most recent access session
LastUsedTimeStop - FILETIME marking the end of the most recent access session
NonPackaged subkey - groups entries for traditional (non-Microsoft-Store) desktop applications separately from packaged UWP apps
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Microphone/camera entries limited to applications the user knowingly uses for calls or recording (Teams, Zoom, Skype, browser-based meeting tools), with LastUsedTimeStart/Stop windows matching known meeting or call times.
anomalies: A NonPackaged entry for an unfamiliar or unsigned executable with microphone or webcam LastUsedTimeStart/Stop activity, especially outside any known call or meeting
LastUsedTimeStart with no corresponding LastUsedTimeStop, suggesting the process terminated abnormally (e.g. killed) while still holding the device open
Access sessions for camera or microphone occurring while the user reports being away or the workstation was locked
An application capability entry appearing for the first time immediately following a phishing or execution event elsewhere in the timeline
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: ConsentStore only records that a capability was accessed and for how long - it does not capture the actual audio or video content, so it can corroborate but not prove data was captured or exfiltrated. An attacker with registry access can delete the specific application subkey to remove evidence of a single tool's access without disturbing entries for other applications, so a suspiciously sparse capability history on an otherwise active system is worth investigating.
Application Execution.interpretation: LastUsedTimeStart and LastUsedTimeStop bound only the most recent single access session for that application/capability pair - earlier sessions are overwritten and not retained as history, so this key reflects the latest use, not a full access log. The NonPackaged subkey is the one to check for conventional Win32 desktop malware, since packaged Microsoft Store apps are instead tracked directly under the capability subkey by package family name.

Application Execution.name: Commands Executed in the Run Dialog
Application Execution.purpose: Records the most-recently-used command strings typed into the Run dialog (Win+R), letting an analyst reconstruct commands, paths, or scripts a user (or an attacker operating in that user's context) manually invoked via Run.
key_fields: Value names - single lowercase letters (a, b, c, ...) each holding one typed command string, generally suffixed with '\1'
MRUList - REG_SZ string whose character order gives the recency order of the lettered values (leftmost = most recently used)
Key LastWrite time - approximates when the most recent command was executed via Run
Application Execution.normal_baseline: A short list of familiar administrative commands and paths (cmd, mstsc, \\server\share, control, appwiz.cpl, notepad, common file/folder paths the user navigates to via Run).
anomalies: PowerShell/cmd invocations with encoded, obfuscated, or unusually long argument strings
UNC paths to unfamiliar internal or external hosts, or to admin shares (\\host\C$)
References to script interpreters (wscript, cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32) with file paths in Temp, Downloads, or AppData
Commands referencing archive extraction tools or living-off-the-land binaries not normally used interactively by that user
RunMRU key or individual lettered values missing/reset while other evidence (Prefetch, EventLogs, UserAssist) shows Run-dialog-style activity in the same window, suggesting deliberate clearing
Only the letter values remain with no MRUList, or the MRUList does not reference all present letters, indicating partial/manual tampering rather than normal overwrite behavior
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Only the last ~26 distinct commands are retained (one per lowercase letter a-z; the oldest is evicted as new commands are added), so heavy Run-dialog use can push older evidence out through normal operation, not just tampering. An entry is only committed to the registry once the Run dialog is closed, so live/volatile use may not yet be on disk. Attackers who know about this artifact often delete specific values or the whole key, but doing so still requires closing the Run dialog to commit the change, and its absence alongside other execution evidence is itself suspicious.

Application Execution.name: Jump Lists
Application Execution.purpose: Tracks recently/frequently accessed files per application via embedded shell-link data, providing file-access evidence even for files later deleted.
key_fields: Target file path
AppID (identifies the application)
Access/pin count and recency (DestList MRU)
Up to ~2,000 recently/frequently accessed items tracked per application, per user account
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Entries correspond to files the user is known to have opened with the associated application.
anomalies: Entries referencing files on removable/network shares with no current device
Target file path pointing to a staging or exfiltration directory
parsing_tools: JLECmd (Eric Zimmerman): e.g. JLECmd.exe -d AutomaticDestinations --csv output-folder --csvf JumpLists.csv
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: The referenced file does not need to still exist for the Jump List entry to remain, aiding recovery after deletion; can be individually pruned via 'Remove from this list'.
Application Execution.interpretation: A Jump List entry is created the first time an application is used by that user account. It does NOT record whether an application is currently pinned to the taskbar, so it cannot be used to determine pinned-app status. Best used in combination with Prefetch, LNK files, RecentDocs, and Shellbags to strengthen an activity timeline rather than relied on alone.

Application Execution.name: Last Visited MRU
Application Execution.purpose: Tracks which applications the user has run through a standard Open/Save dialog and the last folder location each application interacted with.
key_fields: MRUListEx - binary DWORD-array giving the order entries were used, most recent first
Value data - the executable name of the application that opened the dialog, paired with a binary PIDL (Win7+) or plain path (XP) for the last-used folder
Key LastWrite time - approximates when the most recent entry was recorded
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Entries for common applications (Office, PDF readers, browsers) paired with everyday working folders (Documents, Desktop, project directories) the user regularly accesses.
anomalies: An application paired with a folder location the user has no business reason to access, including other users' profiles or administrative shares
A folder path referencing a hidden, obfuscated, or unusually named directory (dotted or random-character names) used as a working/staging location
Applications commonly used for malicious purposes (archive tools, scripting hosts) appearing paired with folder locations tied to sensitive data
Entries pointing to a removable/external drive letter not otherwise associated with that user's normal workflow
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Like other ComDlg32 MRU keys, entries are only written once the dialog interaction completes, so activity in a dialog left open (or a process killed before the dialog closes) may not be captured. Entries persist after the referenced folder is renamed or deleted, so the recorded path can outlive the location it names.
Application Execution.interpretation: This key yields two distinct pieces of evidence in one place: which applications the user actually ran through a file dialog, and the last filesystem location each application touched - not necessarily the same as where the current file resides. Because the PIDL/path often points at directories with no other UI presence, this is a common source for identifying hidden or otherwise-unadvertised directories the user (or a GUI-driven malicious application) has visited.

Application Execution.name: Prefetch
Application Execution.location: C:\Windows\Prefetch\{EXECUTABLENAME}-{HASH}.pf. Prefetching (and therefore .pf creation) is controlled by HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters\EnablePrefetcher, and is disabled by default on systems whose boot volume is an SSD.
Application Execution.purpose: Windows' prefetcher records which files and directories an executable references during its first ~10 seconds of launch, storing that data in a .pf file so future launches can be sped up by pre-loading those resources. Because a .pf file is created/updated only when the named executable actually runs, Prefetch is one of the strongest single-artifact indicators of program execution and its history (run count, run times).
key_fields: Executable name (limited to 29 characters in the filename)
Run count: total number of times the executable has been launched since the .pf file was created

Last-run timestamp, plus (format version 26 and later, i.e. Windows 8 and newer) up to 7 additional previous run timestamps for a maximum of 8 stored execution times; format version 23 (Vista/Windows 7) records only the single last-run timestamp with no run history array
Volume information: source volume path, serial number, and creation time
List of files and directories referenced during the executable's startup phase

Prefetch file format version number (17 = XP/2003, 23 = Vista/7/2008/2012, 26 = Windows 8/8.1, 30 = Windows 10). Identifies which decompression/parsing logic applies (Windows 10 .pf files are compressed and require Windows 8+ APIs to decompress)
Application Execution.normal_baseline: One .pf file per distinct executable path that has been run, up to a Microsoft-documented cap of 128 retained files on Windows XP/7 (oldest purged once the cap is reached) or up to 1,024 files on Windows 8 and later; run counts and run-time clusters that line up with normal user/application behavior (e.g. daily logon scripts, frequently used applications).
anomalies: A .pf file for an executable run from a Temp, Downloads, or other user-writable/unusual path, especially with a low run count consistent with a one-off tool execution
A high run count concentrated in a very short time window, consistent with automated/scripted repeated execution rather than normal interactive use
Referenced-files list inside the .pf naming unusual DLLs, staging directories, or files that no longer exist on disk. Useful for recovering paths of since-deleted malware components
A .pf file whose executable no longer exists at the referenced path (deleted post-execution) while the .pf itself remains. Direct evidence of a since-removed binary having run

Complete absence of expected Prefetch activity on a system that should have it enabled. Always confirm EnablePrefetcher's registry value and whether the boot volume is an SSD (which disables prefetching by default) before treating an empty/sparse Prefetch folder as suspicious
parsing_tools: PECmd (Eric Zimmerman): e.g. PECmd.exe -d "C:\Windows\Prefetch" --csv output-folder --csvf prefetch.csv
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Prefetch files are ordinary files on disk (not registry-embedded), so they can be deleted individually or in bulk with simple filesystem operations. A documented anti-forensic technique corresponding to ATT&CK T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion). Deletion of .pf files does not remove all trace, however: the NTFS Master File Table ($MFT) retains a record of the deleted file's name, size, and timestamps, and the $UsnJrnl records the deletion event itself. Because prefetching is off by default on SSD-booted systems and can be disabled entirely via EnablePrefetcher, a sparse or empty Prefetch folder is not inherently suspicious and must be evaluated against the system's actual configuration before being treated as evidence of tampering.
Application Execution.interpretation: Combine Prefetch with SRUM, BAM/DAM, and UserAssist for a fuller execution story. Each has different retention limits and blind spots, so the overlap is what makes the finding solid. The first-run time is only an approximation: it's derived from the .pf file's own creation time minus up to ~10 seconds, not a directly recorded field.

Application Execution.name: Shimcache
Application Execution.location: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache (Windows 2003 and later); HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatibility\AppCompatCache on Windows XP/2000. Values are held in memory and only periodically flushed to the registry, typically on shutdown.
Application Execution.purpose: Part of the Application Compatibility infrastructure: when Windows evaluates whether an executable needs a compatibility shim, it records the file's path, size, and last-modified time in a cache so it doesn't have to re-evaluate the file on every launch. Because the cache captures files the OS has looked at, it's used as evidence a given executable existed (and, on some versions, ran) on the system.
key_fields: File full path
$STANDARD_INFORMATION last-modified timestamp of the file (NOT a run time)
File size (present on some Windows versions)

Process Execution Flag: present on Windows Vista, 7, Server 2008, and Server 2012 only; TRUE indicates the entry reflects actual execution, FALSE indicates the file was merely referenced (e.g. via directory browsing by the Application Experience Lookup Service) without running
Cache entry position/order (reflects last-update order, exploited for approximate sequencing)
Application Execution.normal_baseline: A large list of legitimate OS and application binaries with last-modified timestamps matching their known install/patch dates, generally clustered around Windows Update and application install events; entry order roughly tracks last-referenced order rather than true execution order.
anomalies: Entry for an executable in a Temp, Downloads, or other user-writable path with a last-modified timestamp inconsistent with any known legitimate install
On Windows Vista/7/2008/2012, an entry with the Process Execution Flag set to TRUE for a binary in a suspicious location. A stronger indicator of actual execution than presence alone

A single-use or renamed binary appearing once with no corresponding Prefetch, Amcache, or event-log evidence of execution. Consistent with a tool that was staged/inspected but not run, or with an execution artifact that was separately cleared

Timestamp manipulation: because the cached time is the file's $STANDARD_INFORMATION last-modified value (attacker-controllable via timestomping), a suspiciously 'clean' or backdated last-modified time on a malicious binary should be cross-checked against $FILE_NAME timestamps or other artifacts
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Critical version-dependent caveat: Shimcache reliability as proof of execution has changed across Windows releases. On Windows XP/2003 there is no execution flag at all, so presence alone was historically treated as a rough proxy for execution. On Windows Vista, 7, Server 2008, and Server 2012 a Process Execution Flag was added that distinguishes actual execution (TRUE) from mere presence, e.g. directory browsing (FALSE), though Mandiant notes the flag's true internal semantics were never officially documented by Microsoft. On Windows 8 and later the execution-flag behavior changed again and is widely reported as unreliable/removed, meaning an entry can exist for a file that was never executed. Because of this, Shimcache should never be used alone to prove execution on modern Windows. Always corroborate with Prefetch, Amcache, or BAM/DAM. The cache itself lives in memory and is only flushed to the registry hive periodically (typically at shutdown), so a hard power-off can lose recent updates, and clearing/rebuilding it requires kernel-level access rather than a simple deletion.

Application Execution.name: System Resource Usage Monitor (SRUM)
Application Execution.purpose: Tracks application execution, CPU/network resource usage, and per-app network data volume over time, written hourly and at shutdown.
key_fields: ApplicationName (full path)
Timestamp
BytesSent/BytesRecvd
UserSID
Table name/identifier mappings stored in SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SRUM\Extensions. Needed to correlate SRUDB.dat's internal table GUIDs back to what they actually represent
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Reflects normal application and network usage; retention commonly cited as 30-60 days depending on configuration.
anomalies: Large BytesSent volume from an unexpected application, indicating possible exfiltration
Execution record for an application with no matching Prefetch/Amcache entry
parsing_tools: SRUM-DUMP (Mark Baggett): e.g. srum_dump.exe -i SRUDB.dat -o output-folder -r SOFTWARE -f xls
SRUMECmd (Eric Zimmerman): e.g. SrumECmd.exe -f SRUDB.dat -r SOFTWARE --csv output-folder
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: SRUDB.dat can be deleted directly and Windows will recreate an empty one at next write, so a suspiciously short-lived SRUM history around an incident is itself a signal.
Application Execution.interpretation: Entries are written into the database in periodic (roughly hourly) blocks rather than at the moment activity occurs, so the exact time an action happened cannot be pinned down from SRUM alone. Treat its timestamps as approximate. SRUDB.dat is also not guaranteed to be flushed to disk on every shutdown, so the most recent activity before a crash or abrupt power-off may be missing entirely. Parsing the SOFTWARE hive alongside SRUDB.dat (most tools accept both together) is required to resolve the raw table GUIDs into human-readable field names.

Application Execution.name: Task Bar Feature Usage
Application Execution.purpose: Logs how a signed-in user interacts with taskbar-pinned and running applications, distinguishing deliberately pinned apps from apps that merely received window focus.
key_fields: AppLaunch subkey - per-application counters incremented when a pinned app is launched from the taskbar
AppSwitched subkey - per-application counters incremented every time an app receives taskbar focus, pinned or not
Value name - the application's AUMID (Application User Model ID) or executable identifier
Value data - a running count, with no embedded timestamp
Application Execution.normal_baseline: AppLaunch counts concentrated on a small set of apps the user has intentionally pinned (browser, mail client, Office apps); AppSwitched counts spread more broadly across whatever windows the user alt-tabs or clicks between during the day.
anomalies: AppSwitched entry for an unfamiliar or unsigned executable receiving repeated focus, suggesting a GUI-based tool (e.g. a fake update window, RAT console) the user or attacker interacted with
AppLaunch entry for a pinned taskbar shortcut pointing at a script or LOLBin (powershell.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe) rather than a normal application
AppLaunch/AppSwitched counts present for an app with no corresponding Prefetch, Amcache, or UserAssist execution evidence, or vice versa - a gap worth reconciling
A sudden increment in either counter during a window when the legitimate user reports being away from the keyboard, suggesting an attacker interacting with the desktop over remote access
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: FeatureUsage stores only cumulative counters with no timestamps, so on its own it cannot place activity in time - it must be correlated with UserAssist, Prefetch, or event logs to build a timeline. Clearing the key removes historical counts entirely with no partial-deletion trace, and because it is a rarely-examined key, wholesale deletion is easy to miss unless explicitly checked for.
Application Execution.interpretation: AppLaunch and AppSwitched measure different things. AppLaunch only increments for applications the user has pinned to the taskbar, so it demonstrates the user's prior knowledge of and intent toward that application - the counter also persists after the app is later unpinned, so historical pinning survives removal from the visible taskbar. AppSwitched increments on any change of taskbar focus regardless of whether the app is pinned, reflecting general interaction/attention rather than deliberate pinning. Neither value carries a timestamp, so this artifact answers 'did the user know about and use this application' rather than 'when'.

Application Execution.name: UserAssist
Application Execution.purpose: Tracks GUI-launched programs and shortcuts per user, including how many times an item was run, how long it held focus, and when it was last executed. Populated by the Windows Explorer shell (explorer.exe/userassist.dll) when a user double-clicks an icon, shortcut, or Start Menu/Taskbar entry.
key_fields: GUID subkey {CEBFF5CD-ACE2-4F4F-9178-9926F41749EA} - executed .exe files
GUID subkey {F4E57C4B-2036-45F0-A9AB-443BCFE33D9F} - shortcut (.lnk) launches, e.g. Start Menu items
Value name - ROT13-encoded full path or shortcut name of the launched item
Binary value data (Windows 7+, 72 bytes): Run Count (offset 4), Focus Count (offset 8), Focus Time in milliseconds (offset 12), Last Execution Time as FILETIME (offset 60)
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Populated with common user-facing applications (browsers, Office, Explorer, Settings) and OS utilities the user launched via the shell. Run counts grow gradually over normal daily use; focus time is nonzero for applications the user actually interacted with.
anomalies: Entry for an executable in an unusual location (Temp, Downloads, AppData, ProgramData) with a high run count in a short time window

Run count present but focus time and focus count are zero or near-zero, suggesting the program launched and exited immediately (consistent with a dropper or one-shot loader) rather than genuine interactive use
Last-execution timestamp updated even though the underlying binary no longer exists on disk, indicating deleted post-execution malware
Entries for LOLBins (rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe, cmd.exe) launched via the shell (double-click/shortcut) rather than command line, which is unusual for these utilities
Complete absence of expected UserAssist entries for a period when other artifacts (Prefetch, EventLogs) show GUI activity, suggesting the key or its Count subkey was cleared
Session ID field indicating logons/sessions the analyst cannot otherwise account for
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Value names are ROT13-encoded, not encrypted, so this is trivially reversible and not a real obstacle to analysis. However, using 'Open file location' or similar shell actions from a search/menu can update a UserAssist entry's run count and timestamp without the target actually being executed, which can produce a false positive for execution if not corroborated with focus time/count or other execution artifacts (Prefetch, Amcache). The entire UserAssist key can be deleted or disabled by an attacker with registry access, and its absence where GUI activity is otherwise evidenced is itself a red flag.

Application Execution.name: Windows 10 Timeline
Application Execution.purpose: Stores a rolling history of applications and files the user interacted with, which Windows used to present as a chronological 'Timeline', including content viewed inside those applications.
key_fields: AppId / Activity table - full executable path of the application that generated the activity
StartTime / EndTime - when the recorded activity began and ended
Duration (derived) - EndTime minus StartTime
ContentInfo / AppActivityId - items opened within the application (document names, in-app content identifiers)
Uri / AdditionalProperties - URLs visited, when the activity originated from a browser
LastModifiedTime - when the database row itself was last updated
Application Execution.normal_baseline: A continuous, dense history of everyday application use (browser, Office, chat clients) with start/end times and durations that line up with the user's normal working hours and habits.
anomalies: Activity entries for an application run from an unusual path (Temp, Downloads, AppData) with a very short duration, consistent with a one-off malicious tool launch
URLs recorded for browsing sessions to malicious or unexpected domains, especially just before other compromise indicators
A gap in the timeline spanning the suspected incident window while surrounding periods are densely populated, suggesting the database or feature was tampered with
Activity for an application the user denies having run, with start/end times matching other suspicious artifacts (Prefetch, EventLogs)
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: ActivitiesCache.db is an ordinary SQLite file the current user account can delete or overwrite outright; Windows will simply recreate an empty database on next use, so a short-lived or newly-created file where a long history is expected is itself notable. Microsoft later deprecated the Timeline user interface, but the underlying ConnectedDevicesPlatform database and its population can continue running in the background on affected builds, so the absence of the visible Timeline UI does not mean the database stopped recording.
Application Execution.interpretation: Because the database captures full application paths, per-item content opened inside the application, and visited URLs together with start/end times, it is one of the few artifacts that ties 'what' (specific document or URL), 'how long' (session duration), and 'in what application' together in one place. Records populated by this feature persist in ActivitiesCache.db even on systems where the Timeline feature was later removed from the Windows 10 UI in a late-Win10 update, so absence of the visible feature does not mean absence of the underlying data - always check for the database file regardless of the build's UI state.

Application Execution.name: PowerShell ScriptBlock Logging & Transcripts
Application Execution.os_min: PowerShell v5.0+ (native on Windows 10 / Server 2016+; back-ported to Windows 7 SP1+ / Server 2008 R2 SP1+ via Windows Management Framework 5.0/5.1); Module/Transcription logging exist earlier but full Script Block Logging requires v5.0
Application Execution.location: Event channel: Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational (PowerShell 7: PowerShellCore/Operational); Transcript files: path set by HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription\OutputDirectory (Start-Transcript without policy configuration defaults to the user's Documents folder); Policy registry keys: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging, ...\ScriptBlockLogging, ...\Transcription
Application Execution.purpose: Captures the actual content of PowerShell activity — full de-obfuscated script text via Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104), invoked module/cmdlet parameters via Module Logging (Event ID 4103), and complete session input/output via Transcription files — reconstructing exactly what commands and scripts ran and in what order, beyond what the general powershell-operational log channel records on its own.
key_fields: EventID (4103 module logging / 4104 script block logging)
ScriptBlockText
ScriptBlockId
MessageNumber / MessageTotal (for scripts split across multiple 4104 events)
Path (source script file, if any)
ContextInfo: Host Application, User, Runspace ID
Transcript header: start time, username, machine name, PSVersion, command line
Transcript body: full command input/output text
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Routine admin/scripting activity: module imports, scheduled maintenance scripts, DSC/config management, signed internal automation; most 4104 events are Verbose/Information level and short; module logging fires for common modules (ActiveDirectory, Microsoft.PowerShell.*) during normal admin tasks.
anomalies: 4104 events flagged Warning (Level 3) containing suspicious keywords (-enc, DownloadString, Invoke-Expression/IEX, Net.WebClient, EncodedCommand, mimikatz)
Large base64-encoded or heavily obfuscated script blocks split across many MessageNumber parts
Script block content with no corresponding on-disk script file (fileless/in-memory execution)
Invocation with -Version 2 forcing the legacy PowerShell v2 engine to evade Script Block Logging
Transcript files missing despite policy being enabled, or appearing outside the configured OutputDirectory
Gaps or abrupt termination in transcript sequence/session continuity
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Adversaries can disable capture by clearing the EnableScriptBlockLogging, EnableModuleLogging, or EnableTranscripting registry values, run wevtutil cl to purge the Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational log, or force a PowerShell v2-engine downgrade (predates AMSI and Script Block Logging support) to bypass content capture entirely.

Application Execution.name: Windows Error Reporting (WER) Crash Dumps
Application Execution.os_min: Windows XP+ / Windows Server 2003+ (WER introduced); LocalDumps registry-configured user-mode dump collection requires Windows Vista SP1+ / Server 2008+
Application Execution.location: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportArchive; %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportQueue; %PROGRAMDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportArchive; %PROGRAMDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\WER\ReportQueue; per-crash Report.wer files and optional minidump (.dmp) files inside each report subfolder; configurable dump output under HKLM/HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps (default %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps); Application event log, source "Windows Error Reporting"
Application Execution.purpose: Records process crash, hang, and kernel-fault events with process metadata and, when configured, memory dump files — useful for reconstructing exploitation attempts, malware crashes, and post-crash behavior even after the offending binary is gone.
key_fields: Report.wer: EventType (APPCRASH/AppHang/BEX/Kernel), AppPath, AppName, OriginalFilename
Sig[0-9] fault signature fields (faulting module, offset, exception code)
EventTime (FILETIME)
OsInfo / OS version
LoadedModule list
ReportIdentifier (GUID)
Associated minidump (.dmp) filename
Application log Event ID 1001 (WER_EL_BUCKET_LOG) with P1-P10 problem-signature fields
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Occasional Report.wer folders in ReportArchive for common application crashes (Office, browsers, Explorer); ReportQueue is normally near-empty except transiently while a report awaits upload; LocalDumps folder is typically absent unless explicitly configured by an admin or developer.
anomalies: Report.wer entries for unsigned, unusual, or short-lived processes, or for security tooling/lsass.exe
WerFault.exe invoked against lsass.exe, consistent with the silent-process-exit ('LSASS shtinkering') credential-dumping technique
Minidump created for a process with no plausible legitimate crash cause
Repeated crashes of the same process/module immediately preceding successful code execution (exploitation attempt pattern)
WER artifact timestamps clustering around known exploitation or malware execution windows
Disabled=1 under the WER registry key, indicating deliberate suppression
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: WER can be disabled entirely via Disabled=1 under HKLM/HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting, or suppressed per-application via ExcludedApplications, preventing crash artifacts from ever being written; existing ReportArchive/ReportQueue folders and LocalDumps files can also simply be deleted post-incident.

Application Execution.name: Print Spooler Artifacts
Application Execution.os_min: Windows 2000+ (spool file structure); PrintService Admin/Operational Event Log channels require Windows Vista / Server 2008+ (Windows Event Log architecture)
Application Execution.location: %SystemRoot%\System32\spool\PRINTERS\ (*.SPL spool data, *.SHD shadow/job-settings files, *.EMF per-page graphics); %SystemRoot%\System32\spool\drivers\ (installed print driver DLLs, e.g. x64\3\); Event log channels: Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin (enabled by default) and Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational (disabled by default); print processor persistence key: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\<architecture>\Print Processors\<name>
Application Execution.purpose: Captures print job submission metadata and, transiently, spooled document data, plus print-driver installation/load events — enabling reconstruction of what was printed and by whom, and detection of print-driver-based execution or persistence such as PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) exploitation.
key_fields: SHD file: document name (only if ShowJobTitleInEventLogs is enabled), submitting user, printer name, submission time, port, data type
SPL file: raw or EMF-formatted spooled print data
PrintService/Operational Event ID 307 (document printed): user, printer, page count, byte size, job ID
PrintService/Admin Event ID 808 (driver load failure) and 316 (driver installation)
Print Processors registry value: Driver (DLL name loaded by spoolsv.exe)
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Transient .SPL/.SHD/.EMF files that exist only for the duration of an active print job before automatic deletion on completion; PrintService/Admin log shows routine driver installs from trusted, signed sources; PrintService/Operational log is disabled by default and empty unless explicitly enabled via wevtutil or GPO.
anomalies: Unexpected DLLs appearing under %SystemRoot%\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\ shortly before a spoolsv.exe crash or a new SYSTEM-level process
spoolsv.exe spawning rundll32.exe or another unexpected child process
New or modified Print Processors registry key pointing to a non-standard DLL
PrintService/Admin Event ID 808 (driver load failure) or 316 (driver install) immediately preceding suspicious activity
Carved/orphaned .SPL or .SHD files recovered from unallocated space referencing unexpected document names or users
Remote RpcAddPrinterDriverEx calls to spoolsv.exe from unauthenticated or unexpected accounts, consistent with CVE-2021-34527 exploitation
parsing_tools: EnCase 'Print Spool - SHD & SPL Parser' EnScript
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: SPL, SHD, and EMF files are deleted automatically by the spooler once a job completes, so they normally must be recovered via file carving from unallocated space; the PrintService/Operational log is disabled by default (must be manually enabled), so print-job history is frequently unavailable unless proactively configured, and document names are withheld from Event ID 307 unless ShowJobTitleInEventLogs is explicitly set.

Application Execution.name: Windows Recall (AI Explorer)
Application Execution.os_min: Windows 11 24H2 (build 26100.3915+), Copilot+ PC only (40+ TOPS NPU, Secured-core standard)
Application Execution.location: %LOCALAPPDATA%\CoreAIPlatform.00\UKP\{GUID}\ukg.db (SQLite database); %LOCALAPPDATA%\CoreAIPlatform.00\UKP\{GUID}\ImageStore\* (JPEG screenshot files, one per snapshot); SemanticTextStore.sidb / SemanticImageStore.sidb (vector index files) in the same UKP folder
Application Execution.purpose: Periodically screenshots the user's active display, runs local OCR and semantic indexing on the images, and stores the results as searchable timeline 'snapshots' so the user can retrieve anything previously seen on screen using natural-language search.
key_fields: WindowCapture table: WindowCreatedEvent/WindowChangedEvent/WindowCaptureEvent/WindowDestroyedEvent rows with timestamps
WindowCaptureTextIndex_content (OCR-extracted text from each snapshot)
App / AppDwellTime (process path, launch time, window dwell duration)
Web / WebDomainDwellTime (captured URLs and domains from supported browsers)
ImageToken linking a WindowCapture row to its JPEG in ImageStore
Exif.Photo.MakerNote tag (0x927c) inside each JPEG: window title, window bounds, capture timestamp, full path of the process that owned the window
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Present only where the user opted in on a Copilot+ PC and completed Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security enrollment; ukg.db and ImageStore grow continuously during active use, bounded by the configured storage cap (default allocation scales with disk size, e.g. 25 GB on a 256 GB device) or the configured max retention duration (30/60/90/180 days on managed devices); oldest snapshots are purged first once a limit is hit.
anomalies: ukg.db/ImageStore populated on a device where org policy (AllowRecallEnablement) should have removed the feature entirely
Snapshot OCR text containing credentials, secrets, or full documents that sensitive-information filtering should have excluded
Evidence of a parsing tool (e.g., TotalRecall) having been run against the store by someone other than the profile owner
WindowCapture gaps inconsistent with the configured retention/storage policy, suggesting selective deletion
Recall data surviving after the user believes they disabled/reset the feature
parsing_tools: DB Browser for SQLite (manual ukg.db inspection)
Recall Timeline (open-source EXIF-based timeline reconstruction tool)
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: Turning off 'Save snapshots' or disabling the AllowRecallEnablement policy deletes all previously saved snapshots; Settings > Recall & Snapshots > Advanced Settings > Reset Recall purges ukg.db and ImageStore; running Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Recall -Remove removes the on-disk store entirely; app/website deny-list policies can pre-emptively prevent capture of chosen processes or sites so no artifact is ever created for them.

Application Execution.name: PSReadLine Console History
Application Execution.os_min: Windows PowerShell 5.0+ (PSReadLine bundled and loaded by default); also applies to PowerShell 7+
Application Execution.location: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt (default for Windows PowerShell/powershell.exe host; a different interactive host writes $($Host.Name)_history.txt in the same folder)
Application Execution.purpose: Persists the literal text of commands a user typed interactively at a PowerShell console prompt, across session restarts, independent of any audit/logging policy — distinct from Script Block Logging or Transcription which are policy-gated and capture executed script content rather than raw keystrokes.
key_fields: One line per full raw command-line string as typed (no built-in timestamp)
Chronological ordering (oldest at top, newest appended at bottom)
No user, session ID, or exit-code metadata recorded
Application Execution.normal_baseline: Grows incrementally with routine interactive commands (navigation, module imports, admin cmdlets); capped at PSReadLine's MaximumHistoryCount (module default 4096 entries, oldest trimmed first); HistoryNoDuplicates (default True) suppresses only recall/search duplicates, not file writes; HistorySaveStyle defaults to SaveIncrementally, so entries are written as each command runs.
anomalies: Plaintext credentials, API keys, or ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText strings recorded
Encoded/obfuscated invocations (-EncodedCommand, base64 blobs, IEX/Invoke-Expression download cradles)
Living-off-the-land or offensive tooling commands (credential dumping, Defender tampering, lateral-movement cmdlets)
File missing or empty on a system with clear evidence of recent interactive PowerShell use elsewhere
File Modified timestamp far newer than expected activity, with truncated/short content — consistent with delete-then-recreate
Application Execution.anti_forensic_notes: An adversary can delete the file directly (Remove-Item $env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt), set -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing to stop further writes for the session, or use an -AddToHistoryHandler script block to silently exclude specific commands (e.g., those matching a pattern) from ever being written, leaving no gap to notice; deleting mid-session causes PowerShell to silently recreate an empty file on the next command, producing a Created/Modified timestamp mismatch.

Browser Activity.name: Auto-Complete Data
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: places.sqlite, formhistory.sqlite ; Chrome/Edge: History (keyword_search_terms table), Web Data (autofill table), Shortcuts, Network Action Predictor, Login Data
Browser Activity.purpose: Aggregates data a user has typed into the browser across several distinct databases. Search-engine queries, web form entries, Omnibox/address-bar input, letter-by-letter typed predictions, and typed credentials.
key_fields: keyword_search_terms table (History): items typed into search engines
autofill table (Web Data): items typed into web forms
Shortcuts table: items typed in the Omnibox URL bar
Network Action Predictor: records what was typed letter by letter
Login Data: inputted user credentials
moz_formhistory (Firefox formhistory.sqlite)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Typed terms and form entries reflect routine work tasks and known account usage for the profile owner.
anomalies: Search terms or typed URLs referencing hacking tools, exploit frameworks, or data-exfiltration services
Network Action Predictor entries showing a fully-typed sensitive term never submitted through the visible History, suggesting the user aborted before completion
Autofill/form entries containing credentials, tokens, or PII for accounts that do not belong to the profile owner
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Typed-data evidence is spread across five-plus independent databases, so clearing one (e.g., autofill) often leaves corroborating entries in another (e.g., Network Action Predictor or Shortcuts), making full suppression of typed history difficult without wiping the entire profile.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Includes both the typed-in data itself and metadata about the data type (search term vs. form field vs. URL vs. credential). Cross-referencing the separate tables connects typed content to a timeline and, combined with profile ownership, ties the typing activity to a specific user account rather than just "the browser."

Browser Activity.name: Bookmarks
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: places.sqlite, bookmarkbackups\bookmarks-<date>.jsonlz4 ; Chrome/Edge: Bookmarks (JSON), Bookmarks.bak (Chrome) / Bookmarks.msbak (Edge)
Browser Activity.purpose: Records default browser items as well as sites a user chose to save for future reference.
key_fields: moz_bookmarks table (Firefox places.sqlite)
bookmarkbackups\bookmarks-<date>.jsonlz4 (Firefox dated backups)
Bookmarks JSON: name, url, date_added (Chrome/Edge)
Bookmarks.bak / Bookmarks.msbak (prior-save backup copy)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Bookmark set matches the user's known interests/workflow, added at a reasonable, spaced-out cadence.
anomalies: A bookmark for a known malicious, C2, or paste-site URL that does not otherwise appear in browsing history, indicating a reference was saved without (yet) being visited
A burst of bookmarks added in a short window inconsistent with normal usage, suggesting bulk import or scripted activity
A Bookmarks.bak/backup copy showing entries later deleted from the live Bookmarks file
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Firefox retains multiple dated backups in bookmarkbackups\, and Chrome/Edge keep a .bak/.msbak copy of the prior save, so deleting a single live bookmark file does not remove these backup copies. Recently-deleted bookmarks are frequently recoverable.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Firefox's bookmarkbackups folder can hold multiple backup copies of the entire bookmark set in JSON format inside a compressed jsonlz4 container, letting an analyst diff bookmark state across dates. Chromium Bookmark files are plain JSON. Not all bookmarks are user-generated intent to visit. A URL can be bookmarked and never actually visited, so a bookmark alone is not proof of a visit.

Browser Activity.name: Browser Downloads
Browser Activity.location: Chrome/Edge: History.downloads table in the profile folder; Firefox: downloads recorded via moz_annos in places.sqlite (or separate downloads.sqlite on older versions)
Browser Activity.purpose: Modern browsers include a built-in download manager capable of keeping a history of every file downloaded by the user, providing information about websites visited and corresponding items retrieved.
key_fields: Filename, size, and type
Source website and referring page
Download start and end times
File system save location
State information: success or failure
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Downloads correspond to work-related documents/installers from known sources.
anomalies: Download from a known malicious-tool distribution site or file-sharing service immediately preceding execution evidence for the same file
A download recorded as failed/incomplete that nonetheless has execution evidence, suggesting the file was retrieved through another channel and the browser record was only partial
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Downloads table entries can be cleared alongside general history clearing; the downloaded file itself, if kept, will separately carry Zone.Identifier MOTW evidence of its origin.
Browser Activity.interpretation: This entry is downloads specifically; the browser's separate crash-recovery tab/window state is its own dedicated `session-restore` artifact, not part of this one. The two used to be combined here but were split to match the poster's own separate boxes.

Browser Activity.name: Browser Preferences
