Browser Activity.location: Firefox: prefs.js (profile root) ; Chrome/Edge: Preferences (JSON, profile root)
Browser Activity.purpose: Configuration data associated with the browser application, including privacy settings and synchronization preferences.
key_fields: Firefox: sync status, last sync time, artifacts selected to sync
Chrome: per_host_zoom_levels
Chrome: media_engagement
Chrome: site_engagement
Edge: account_info
Edge: clear_data_on_exit
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Sync tied to a single known account; privacy and clear-on-exit settings consistent with organizational policy or the user's established habits.
anomalies: Sync account_info referencing a personal or unauthorized account on a corporate device, indicating possible data exfiltration via browser sync
clear_data_on_exit or an equivalent privacy setting enabled shortly before or during an incident window, suggesting deliberate anti-forensic staging
site_engagement/media_engagement scores showing heavy interaction with a domain otherwise absent or sparse in History
parsing_tools: Manual JSON review (text editor / JSON viewer)
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Preferences/prefs.js is a live file rewritten frequently during normal use, so it reflects only the current/recent configuration; prior settings changes are not versioned unless captured through other means (backups, Volume Shadow Copies).
Browser Activity.interpretation: Firefox's prefs.js exposes sync status, last sync time, and which artifact categories (history, passwords, bookmarks, etc.) are configured to sync. Useful for tracing data that may have propagated to another device. Chrome's per_host_zoom_levels, media_engagement, and site_engagement values are indirect but useful proxies for how much a user actually interacted with a given site, beyond a simple visit count. Edge preferences additionally carry account_info and clear_data_on_exit/sync settings.

Browser Activity.name: Cache
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: Cache (older) / cache2 (Firefox 32+) folder under the profile ; Chrome/Edge: Cache\ folder under the profile (data_# index files and f_###### content files)
Browser Activity.purpose: Local storage of web page components (images, scripts, stylesheets, media) retained to speed up subsequent visits to the same site.
key_fields: Cached object URL
First-saved timestamp
Last-accessed timestamp
Content-Type / MIME type
Cached file content (data_#/f_###### or cache2 entries)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Cache contains component files from routinely visited, work-appropriate sites, refreshed on a normal schedule as pages are revisited.
anomalies: Cached page content or images matching known phishing kits, C2 panels, or malicious payload delivery pages
Cache entries for a site with no corresponding History record, indicating History was cleared while Cache was left intact
Cached executable or script content served from an otherwise benign-looking domain
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Cache is typically cleared separately from History in browser "clear data" dialogs unless a user explicitly selects it, so an emptied History with an intact Cache (or vice versa) is common. Each should be checked independently.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Cache provides a genuine snapshot in time of what a user was looking at, including the literal files rendered (images, scripts) rather than just a URL reference. Useful for confirming exactly what content a page displayed at a given moment. It is tied to the specific local user account whose profile holds it, and its two timestamps (first-saved vs. last-viewed) can separate a one-time visit from repeated return visits.

Browser Activity.name: Chrome / Edge (Chromium) Browser Artifacts
Browser Activity.location: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default (Chrome) or \Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default (Edge); History, Login Data, Web Data, Cookies (under Network\), Bookmarks, Preferences
Browser Activity.purpose: SQLite databases and JSON files recording browsing history, downloads, saved logins, autofill, and cookies.
key_fields: History.urls / History.downloads tables
Login Data.logins table
Web Data.autofill table
Cookies (Network\Cookies) table
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: History reflects normal work-related browsing; Login Data contains credentials for known, approved services.
anomalies: History entries for known malicious-tool download sites or paste sites shortly before an incident
Downloads entry for a payload matching a known hash
Unexpected extension IDs not present in the organization's approved list
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Clearing browsing history removes rows from the SQLite tables but does not necessarily overwrite the underlying file pages, so carving deleted SQLite records can sometimes recover cleared history.

Browser Activity.name: Cookies
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: cookies.sqlite ; Chrome/Edge (newer): Network\Cookies ; Chrome/Edge (older, pre-network-isolation): Cookies
Browser Activity.purpose: Site-set tokens that provide insight into what websites have been visited and, for authentication cookies, what activities might have taken place there.
key_fields: Origin/host
Cookie name/value
Creation time
Last-accessed time
Expiration time
Secure flag
HttpOnly flag
moz_cookies table (Firefox)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Cookies correspond to sites regularly visited by the user, with expiration/session lifetimes consistent with normal session behavior.
anomalies: A session/authentication cookie for a sensitive application present on a host that never independently authenticated, consistent with cookie theft/replay (pass-the-cookie)
Cookie last-accessed time occurring after the associated user's account was reported compromised or after the user's last known logon
Cookies for a domain with no corresponding History entry, suggesting the cookie was set via a background/tracking request rather than a direct visit
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Clearing cookies through browser settings removes the underlying SQLite rows, but a stolen/exported session cookie used elsewhere (pass-the-cookie) leaves no trace in the victim's own cookie store, so local absence does not rule out prior capture and reuse.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Cookies establish that a site was visited and, via their secure/httponly flags and expiration, how the site intended the cookie to be used (session-only vs. persistent, script-accessible vs. not) along with origin site and last-access time. Session/authentication cookies are the direct target of session-hijacking attacks. An adversary holding a valid, unexpired session cookie can access an account without ever touching the stored password.

Browser Activity.name: Extensions
Browser Activity.location: Chrome/Edge: User Data\Default\Extensions\<extension-id>\<version>\manifest.json; Preferences JSON also lists installed extension IDs
Browser Activity.purpose: Identifies browser extensions installed for a profile, including sideloaded/unpacked extensions not from an official store.
key_fields: Extension ID
manifest.json (name, permissions, version)
Install source (webstore vs. unpacked)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Extension list matches the organization's approved/allow-listed set.
anomalies: Unpacked/developer-mode extension with broad host permissions (e.g. <all_urls>)
Extension ID not present in the official store, suggesting sideloading for credential theft or session hijacking
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Removing an extension deletes its folder; the Preferences JSON's extension history or sync data may retain remnants briefly after removal.

Browser Activity.name: Firefox Browser Artifacts
Browser Activity.location: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\<profile>\ ; places.sqlite (history/bookmarks), cookies.sqlite, formhistory.sqlite, logins.json + key4.db (saved passwords)
Browser Activity.purpose: Stores browsing history, bookmarks, cookies, form autofill history, and encrypted saved logins in per-profile SQLite/JSON files.
key_fields: moz_places / moz_historyvisits tables (URL, visit_date, visit_count)
moz_bookmarks
logins.json encrypted credential entries
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: History reflects normal work-related browsing patterns for the profile owner.
anomalies: History entries for malicious-tool or paste-site domains
A profile folder present with no corresponding profiles.ini entry, suggesting a portable/hidden profile
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting the whole profile folder removes all Firefox artifacts at once; profile folder can be copied off intact even after the browser is closed, as recommended by Mozilla for backups.

Browser Activity.name: History and Download History
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\<randomtext>.default\places.sqlite (Win7+; XP: %USERPROFILE%\Application Data\...) ; Chrome/Edge: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\History and \Microsoft\Edge\User Data\<Profile>\History (Win7+; XP under Local Settings\Application Data)
Browser Activity.purpose: Records websites visited by date and time, forming the primary source for reconstructing a user's browsing activity.
key_fields: Visit URL and page title
Visit timestamp
Visit count / frequency of visits
Profile identifier: look for multiple Chromium profiles ("Default", "Profile 1", etc.)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: History entries correspond to expected work-related or personal browsing consistent with the user's role, spread across normal business hours.
anomalies: History entries for known malicious-tool distribution sites, paste sites, or C2 infrastructure
A second, unexpected Chromium profile directory (e.g. "Profile 1") with its own separate history, suggesting an attempt to segregate activity from the primary profile
A visit-count spike to a single external domain immediately preceding a security incident
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Web browser artifacts are stored per local user account, so history for one account tells you nothing about another; clearing history removes rows from the SQLite tables but does not necessarily overwrite the underlying database pages, so carving deleted records can sometimes recover cleared history.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Always check for multiple profiles in Chromium-based browsers before concluding history is complete. A single "History" file query against the wrong profile folder silently misses activity in another profile. This is the general browsing-history counterpart to the more specific `browser-downloads` (download manager metadata) and `media-history` (audio/video playback) entries.

Browser Activity.name: HTML5 FileSystem
Browser Activity.location: Chrome: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\File System ; Edge: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\<Profile>\File System (Chromium browsers only; not implemented by Firefox)
Browser Activity.purpose: Implements the HTML5 local storage FileSystem API, letting web applications store larger binary data locally than the 10MB text-only limit of HTML5 Web Storage allows.
key_fields: LevelDB index database (maps visited URLs to assigned subfolders)
Temporary storage subfolders ("t")
Persistent storage subfolders ("p")
Origin/domain identifier
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Populated by web apps the user actively uses for offline functionality (webmail attachment caches, offline-capable SaaS tools, progressive web apps).
anomalies: File System storage tied to a domain absent from browsing History
Binary content in a "p" (permanent) subfolder resembling executables, scripts, or archives rather than typical web app cache data
Recently modified File System data timestamped within a known compromise window
parsing_tools: ccl_chrome_indexeddb (CCL / obsidianforensics: includes a FileSystem API module)
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Clearing "site data" in browser settings removes File System storage for that origin; because it is a lesser-known storage mechanism, it is less commonly targeted for anti-forensic cleanup than history or cookies and can retain data longer as a result.
Browser Activity.interpretation: A LevelDB database within the File System folder maps visited URLs/origins to the numbered subfolders that actually hold the stored files. Data splits between "t" (temporary, browser-managed, evictable) and "p" (permanent, explicitly requested by the site) storage. Content in permanent storage reflects a more deliberate site action and is generally more forensically interesting.

Browser Activity.name: HTML5 Web Storage
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\<randomtext>.default\webappstore.sqlite ; Chrome: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Local Storage ; Edge: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\<Profile>\Local Storage
Browser Activity.purpose: Per-domain, text-based persistent storage (up to 10MB per domain) that websites use for state and tracking data. Functionally a "super cookie" that outlives typical cookie settings.
key_fields: Domain/origin key
Stored key-value text data
LevelDB .ldb/.log files (Chrome/Edge)
webappstore.sqlite records (Firefox)
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Storage entries correspond to sites the user actively uses (web apps, SaaS logins, e-commerce carts) with reasonable per-domain data volume.
anomalies: Local Storage data present for a domain never visited according to browsing History, suggesting cross-site tracking, a compromised ad/tracking script, or staged payload data
A per-domain storage blob approaching the 10MB cap, well beyond typical application state
Storage entries encoding obfuscated, base64, or otherwise encoded script content rather than typical application state
parsing_tools: ccl_chrome_indexeddb (CCL / obsidianforensics: LevelDB Local Storage parser)
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Web Storage is cleared only when a user clears "site data" (not just cookies/history) or removes the profile, so it survives many routine cleanup actions and is less commonly targeted precisely because it is less well known than cookies.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Chrome and Edge store Local Storage as LevelDB databases: a binary key-value store requiring a LevelDB-aware parser rather than a text editor, since keys can remain in unflushed .log files. Firefox uses SQLite (webappstore.sqlite). Legacy IE/EdgeHTML stored the equivalent data in XML files.

Browser Activity.name: Media History
Browser Activity.location: Chrome: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\<Profile>\Media History ; Edge: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\<Profile>\Media History (Chromium browsers only; no Firefox equivalent)
Browser Activity.purpose: SQLite database tracking audio and video playback on visited websites, recorded separately from the general browsing History file.
key_fields: playbackSession table
origin table
playback table
URL
last play time
watch time duration
last video position
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Entries correspond to legitimate streaming or media sites (video platforms, corporate training portals, etc.) consistent with the user's known media consumption.
anomalies: Media History entries with no corresponding record in the general History table, indicating history was selectively cleared while Media History survived
Playback sessions tied to unfamiliar or suspicious domains not otherwise seen in browsing activity
Watch-time/position data patterns suggesting automated or scripted playback rather than human interaction
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Clearing browsing data through the standard browser history-clearing UI does not clear Media History, so surviving media playback records can corroborate or contradict a claim that all browsing history was wiped.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Three primary tables link together: playbackSession (session-level playback events), origin (site-level aggregation), and playback (individual playback records). Join on their session/origin identifiers to reconstruct which site was played, when, and for how long. Because Media History is not cleared by normal history-clearing actions, its presence alongside an empty History file is itself significant.

Browser Activity.name: Session Restore
Browser Activity.location: Firefox (older): sessionstore.js ; Firefox (newer): sessionstore.jsonlz4, sessionstore-backups\ ; Chrome/Edge (older): Current Session, Current Tabs, Last Session, Last Tabs files in the profile root ; Chrome/Edge (newer): Sessions\ folder with Session_<timestamp> / Tabs_<timestamp> files
Browser Activity.purpose: Automatic crash-recovery feature that lets the browser restore open tabs and windows after a crash or restart.
key_fields: Historical websites viewed in each tab
Referring website
Time session started/ended
HTML/JavaScript/XML/form data from the page
Transition type
Browser window size
Pinned tabs
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Session-restore data reflects the user's active tabs at the time of the last close or crash, consistent with their known work context.
anomalies: Restored tabs referencing a C2 panel, exfiltration endpoint, or attacker infrastructure open at the time of a crash or shutdown
Session data with form/JavaScript state indicating an in-progress data-exfiltration upload or credential-harvesting page
A Last Session/Last Tabs file present with no matching Current Session, suggesting an abrupt or deliberate browser termination
parsing_tools: Manual JSON review (after jsonlz4/mozLz4 decompression, Firefox)
Manual/hex review of Session_*/Tabs_* files (Chrome/Edge: no universal open-source parser)
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: Because these files exist specifically to survive crashes, even a normal, clean browser shutdown can leave the prior session's data in "Last Session"/backup files; fully suppressing this evidence requires clearing both the live session files and profile-level backups (e.g., sessionstore-backups\).
Browser Activity.interpretation: Session restore can retain far more than URLs: the actual HTML/JavaScript/XML/form data present on a page, the referring site, transition type (typed, link, reload), window size, and which tabs were pinned. A richer point-in-time capture of browsing state than history alone, useful for reconstructing exactly what was on-screen at shutdown or crash time.

Browser Activity.name: Stored Credentials
Browser Activity.location: Firefox: logins.json (+ key4.db) ; Chrome/Edge: Login Data
Browser Activity.purpose: Browser-based password-manager storage holding site credentials a user chose to save, typically protected with Windows DPAPI encryption.
key_fields: Firefox logins.json: hostname, formSubmitURL, encryptedUsername/encryptedPassword, timeCreated, timeLastUsed, timesUsed, timePasswordChanged
Chrome/Edge Login Data (logins table): origin_url, action_url, username_value, password_value (DPAPI-encrypted), date_created, date_last_used
Browser Activity.normal_baseline: Stored credentials correspond to known, approved organizational or personal services consistent with the user's role.
anomalies: Stored credentials for services outside the organization's approved application list, especially file-sharing or paste sites
date_last_used timestamps for a credential occurring while the associated account was reported unavailable/offline, suggesting reuse by another party
Credential metadata present but tied to a DPAPI master key or user profile that has been altered, itself worth flagging as possible evasion
Browser Activity.anti_forensic_notes: DPAPI ties decryption to the Windows user account, and, for Microsoft cloud accounts on Windows 10/11, to a 44-character randomly generated password rather than the account's actual password, so decrypting real credential values is far easier on a live, logged-in system than from an offline disk image. Metadata (URLs, timestamps, usage counts) remains readable regardless of whether the credential value itself can be decrypted offline.
Browser Activity.interpretation: Firefox stores hostname, URL, creation time, last-used time, times-used count, and last-password-change time in JSON even when the credential value itself is encrypted. Chromium browsers store the equivalent in SQLite with origin URL, action URL, username, and created/last-used dates. In both cases, credential metadata is forensically useful even when the encrypted credential value cannot be recovered offline.

Cloud Storage.name: Box Drive
Cloud Storage.location: Default reparse point to virtual filesystem: %USERPROFILE%\Box. Default local file cache: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Box\Box\cache. File metadata and configuration data: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Box\Box\logs\ (Box_Streem logs); %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Box\Box\data\ (sync.db and streemsfs.db = file metadata, metrics.db = user account info).
Cloud Storage.purpose: Box Drive presents its synced content as a virtual filesystem implemented through an NTFS reparse point rather than a real local copy, and it logs unusually detailed metadata for both locally cached and cloud-only files.
key_fields: sync.db - file sync metadata database
streemsfs.db - virtual filesystem metadata database, including file hashes
metrics.db - user account information
Box_Streem logs - detailed operational logs under logs\; searchable for the value "logDriveInformation" to locate the virtual filesystem folder if its path is not otherwise apparent
Cloud Storage.normal_baseline: A single %USERPROFILE%\Box reparse point tied to one authenticated Box account, with sync.db/streemsfs.db metadata and cache growth tracking routine file access, and Box_Streem logs showing regular, unremarkable sync activity during working hours.
anomalies: streemsfs.db recording SHA1 hashes for a large batch of cloud-only files accessed or downloaded in a short window shortly before resignation or termination, consistent with data staging for exfiltration (T1567.002)
A Box Drive installation with no corresponding business justification or IT-issued account on a corporate endpoint
Box_Streem logs showing the virtual filesystem folder relocated away from the default %USERPROFILE%\Box path with no administrative change record
metrics.db reflecting an account identity that does not match the endpoint's assigned user, suggesting shared or unauthorized credential use
Gaps or truncation in Box_Streem logs beyond the normal several-week retention window that coincide with a known incident timeframe, limiting available detail
parsing_tools: Generic SQLite browser (e.g. DB Browser for SQLite) for sync.db, streemsfs.db, and metrics.db
Generic text/log viewer for Box_Streem logs
Cloud Storage.anti_forensic_notes: Because Box Drive implements its virtual filesystem as an NTFS reparse point rather than storing full file content locally by default, a directory listing of %USERPROFILE%\Box does not by itself prove file content was ever present on disk - streemsfs.db and sync.db must be examined to establish what was actually cached versus cloud-only. Box_Streem log retention is typically limited to a few weeks, so older activity may not be recoverable from logs alone even though the metadata databases can retain longer history.
Cloud Storage.interpretation: streemsfs.db and sync.db together cover metadata for both locally cached and cloud-only files, including SHA1 hashes useful for confirming file identity independent of filename. If the virtual filesystem folder location is not obvious from the reparse point, search Box_Streem logs for the string "logDriveInformation" to recover it. Detailed usage logging is available but generally only spans a few weeks, so timely collection matters more here than with some other cloud-sync clients.

Cloud Storage.name: Dropbox
Cloud Storage.location: Default local file storage: %USERPROFILE%\Dropbox; %USERPROFILE%\Dropbox\.dropbox.cache (up to 3 days of cached data). File storage folder location: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\SyncRootManager\Dropbox!<SID>!Personal\UserSyncRoots. File metadata and configuration data: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Dropbox\ (nucleus.sqlite3, sync_history.db, aggregation.dbx = usage and file metadata; older versions: filecache.dbx, config.dbx, both DPAPI-encrypted; info.json = app configuration data).
Cloud Storage.purpose: Dropbox synchronizes a local folder with the user's cloud account; older client versions encrypt most metadata with Windows DPAPI making it host- and user-bound, while recent versions expose substantially more metadata in plain SQLite databases.
key_fields: nucleus.sqlite3 - current-version usage and file metadata database
sync_history.db - record of sync events
aggregation.dbx - usage and file metadata
filecache.dbx / config.dbx - older-version databases, DPAPI-encrypted
info.json - application configuration data
SyncRootManager\Dropbox!<SID>!Personal\UserSyncRoots - registry confirmation of the configured sync folder path per user SID
Cloud Storage.normal_baseline: A single Dropbox account tied to the user's SID under SyncRootManager, local folder activity and nucleus.sqlite3/sync_history.db entries consistent with routine file use, and .dropbox.cache holding only the last few days of transient sync data.
anomalies: sync_history.db or aggregation.dbx showing a large, concentrated batch of uploads shortly before resignation or termination, consistent with data staging for exfiltration (T1567.002)
A Dropbox Personal account configured under SyncRootManager on a corporate-managed endpoint with no business justification
DPAPI-encrypted filecache.dbx/config.dbx present with no way to decrypt outside the original user/host context, potentially masking older activity from investigation
info.json or nucleus.sqlite3 reflecting an account identity inconsistent with the endpoint's assigned user
Evidence of files present in .dropbox.cache with no corresponding entry in nucleus.sqlite3 or sync_history.db, suggesting deletion or tampering with the primary metadata store
parsing_tools: Generic SQLite browser (e.g. DB Browser for SQLite) for nucleus.sqlite3, sync_history.db, aggregation.dbx
DPAPI decryption tooling (requires the original user context/master key) for legacy filecache.dbx and config.dbx
Cloud Storage.anti_forensic_notes: Older Dropbox client versions encrypt filecache.dbx and config.dbx with Windows DPAPI, which is tied to the user account and host - without that context, this metadata cannot be decrypted, effectively limiting recovery to whatever the newer plaintext databases retain. .dropbox.cache only retains up to three days of cached data, so transient evidence there is short-lived. Consumer Dropbox exposes only a limited "Events" activity page rather than full audit logging, constraining what can be corroborated outside local artifacts.
Cloud Storage.interpretation: Because encryption scope changed across Dropbox client versions, always identify the installed version before assuming metadata is readable - recent clients (nucleus.sqlite3, sync_history.db, aggregation.dbx) are far more forensically useful than older DPAPI-encrypted ones. Metadata can be recovered for local, cloud, and deleted files alike. Deleted files may exist in both local and online recycle bins; online recycle bin retention is 30 days for Personal accounts and 120 days for Business. Dropbox Business "Advanced" tier provides detailed audit logging, while consumer Dropbox is limited to the basic Events page.

Cloud Storage.name: Google Drive for Desktop
Cloud Storage.location: Local drive letter and account ID: NTUSER\Software\Google\DriveFS\Share\. Default local file cache: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\DriveFS\<account identifier>\content_cache. File metadata: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\DriveFS\<account identifier>\metadata_sqlite_db.
Cloud Storage.purpose: Google Drive for Desktop is the merged successor to Google Backup and Sync and Drive File Stream; it presents a virtual FAT32 volume named "My Drive" that is only mounted and accessible while the associated Google account is logged in.
key_fields: metadata_sqlite_db - SQLite database of file/folder metadata, with many important fields stored in protobuf format rather than plain columns
content_cache - local cache of file content under the per-account folder
NTUSER\Software\Google\DriveFS\Share\ - records the assigned virtual drive letter and account identifier tying the mount to a specific Google account
Cloud Storage.normal_baseline: One virtual drive letter mounted per active Google account session, consistently assigned across logins, with metadata_sqlite_db growth and content_cache activity tracking the user's routine file access during normal working hours.
anomalies: A second, unexpected account identifier appearing under DriveFS with its own content_cache and virtual drive letter, indicating a personal or unauthorized Google account mounted alongside (or instead of) the corporate one
Large or rapid growth in content_cache volume immediately preceding a resignation or termination date, consistent with bulk staging of files for exfiltration via T1567.002

Virtual drive letter access recorded in shell/LNK/jump-list artifacts with no corresponding DriveFS registry entry, suggesting the mount was removed or the account switched after the activity occurred
metadata_sqlite_db present with no matching Drive process in execution artifacts, suggesting prior use that was later uninstalled without full cache cleanup
parsing_tools: Generic SQLite browser (e.g. DB Browser for SQLite) for metadata_sqlite_db table structure

No verified dedicated public parser for the protobuf-encoded fields inside metadata_sqlite_db - manual protobuf decoding or a purpose-built parser is typically required to fully interpret those columns
Cloud Storage.anti_forensic_notes: The "My Drive" volume only exists while the user is authenticated - it is not persistent storage, so a live-response or memory-only view of mounted drives will miss it once the session ends and Drive is signed out. Uninstalling Google Drive for Desktop does not necessarily remove the AppData\Local\Google\DriveFS cache directory, so metadata and cached content can outlive the visible application.
Cloud Storage.interpretation: The assigned virtual drive letter recorded under NTUSER\Software\Google\DriveFS\Share\ is the key pivot for tying other artifacts (LNK files, jump lists, shellbags, recent-docs) that reference that drive letter back to Google Drive activity. metadata_sqlite_db stores many fields in protobuf format rather than readable text/columns, so raw SQLite inspection alone will not surface everything - protobuf-aware parsing is needed for full field recovery. Google Workspace Admin Reports provide up to 180 days of user activity logging and should be cross-checked against local cache evidence.

Cloud Storage.name: OneDrive
Cloud Storage.location: Default local file storage: %USERPROFILE%\OneDrive (Personal) or %USERPROFILE%\OneDrive - <CompanyName> (Business). File storage folder location: NTUSER\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive\Accounts\<Personal|Business1>. File metadata: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive\logs\<Personal|Business1>\ (SyncDiagnostics.log, SyncEngine "odl" logs). Settings/account data: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive\settings\<Personal|Business1>\ (<UserCid>.dat).
Cloud Storage.purpose: OneDrive ships by default on Windows 8 and later but stays inactive until a user authenticates to a Microsoft cloud account, after which it silently maintains a two-way sync between a local folder and the associated Personal or Business OneDrive tenant.
key_fields: SyncDiagnostics.log - sync engine diagnostics, sometimes contains file metadata
odl (SyncEngine) logs - low-level sync engine trace logs under logs\<Personal|Business1>\
<UserCid>.dat - account/settings identifier file under settings\<Personal|Business1>\
NTUSER\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive\Accounts\<Personal|Business1> - confirms which account type is configured and the local sync folder path
Cloud Storage.normal_baseline: A single Personal or Business OneDrive account (occasionally both) configured under one NTUSER hive, with a local sync folder matching the registry-recorded path, log volume proportional to routine file activity, and sync activity confined to the user's normal working hours and known devices.
anomalies: A Business OneDrive account newly configured on a machine shortly before resignation or termination, with a spike in file additions to the local sync folder consistent with staging data for exfiltration (T1567.002)
A Personal OneDrive account signed in and syncing on a corporate-managed endpoint with no business justification, suggesting use of an unsanctioned account to move data outside corporate visibility
Local sync folder path in the registry pointing to a location that does not match the visible %USERPROFILE%\OneDrive folder, indicating a relocated or hidden sync root
SyncDiagnostics.log or odl logs showing large batches of file uploads immediately preceding account deletion, log deletion, or OneDrive uninstall - evidence tampering or cleanup
Metadata directories present under AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive with no corresponding OneDrive process history, suggesting a prior enablement that was later hidden or partially removed
parsing_tools: Generic text/log viewer for SyncDiagnostics.log and odl trace logs (plain-text/structured log format)
Registry viewer (e.g. Registry Explorer) for NTUSER OneDrive Accounts keys
Cloud Storage.anti_forensic_notes: Metadata files (logs, settings) only exist if OneDrive was actually enabled by user sign-in - a system with OneDrive installed but never authenticated will show no metadata trail at all, which can mask prior use if an account is later removed and logs are cleared. Some files are cloud-only and never touch local disk, so the local folder and its metadata are not a complete record of what the user stored in the tenant. Deleted items land in an online recycle bin (30 days Personal, 93 days Business) - past that window, recovery depends entirely on Microsoft 365 retention/audit rather than local artifacts.
Cloud Storage.interpretation: Always confirm the local sync folder location via the registry rather than assuming the default path - it can be relocated by the user or by policy. SyncDiagnostics.log is a diagnostics log, not a guaranteed metadata source, but can incidentally contain file-level detail worth checking. Because cloud-only files never sync to disk, local artifacts alone cannot prove the full contents of a user's OneDrive at a point in time. For OneDrive for Business, Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Logs supply up to 90 days of user activity (uploads, downloads, sharing) that should be cross-referenced against local sync evidence.

Communication.name: MSG/EML File Metadata
Communication.location: No fixed location - individual .msg (Outlook drag-and-save, or 'Save As' from a message) and .eml (saved by most other mail clients, and by Outlook when exporting/forwarding as RFC 822) files can appear anywhere on disk: user Documents/Desktop, Downloads folder, email attachments, removable media, or extracted attachments from an OST/PST.
Communication.purpose: Individual saved-email files that carry a full self-contained copy of one message, independent of any mailbox store. .msg is Microsoft's OLE/Compound File Binary Format (CFBF) container preserving Outlook-specific MAPI properties; .eml is a plain-text file following the RFC 822/MIME structure used by virtually every other mail client, making it the more portable but MAPI-metadata-poor of the two.
key_fields: MSG: OLE Compound File Binary Format container - each MAPI property (subject, sender, recipients, body, flags, categories, follow-up dates) lives in its own named stream; recipients and attachments each get their own storage, extractable independent of Outlook

MSG: PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS (0x007D) property - the original raw internet headers (including the full Received chain) preserved even though the message is now stored in Outlook's proprietary format
EML: plain-text RFC 822/MIME header block at the top of the file - From, To, Cc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, and the Received header chain, human-readable without any special parser

Received headers (both formats) form a stack, each relay prepending its own line; read bottom-up to trace the hop-by-hop path from originating server to final delivery, per RFC 5321 section 4.4 timestamp/host semantics
Authentication-Results header (EML, and preserved in MSG's transport headers) - SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification outcomes, which are far harder to forge than the From/Reply-To fields themselves

MIME boundary-delimited attachment sections (EML) vs. discrete attachment storages (MSG) - both preserve original attachment filenames and content, independent of whether the parent mailbox still contains the item
Filesystem metadata of the saved file itself (created/modified/accessed timestamps) - reflects when the message was exported to disk, not when it was originally sent/received
Communication.normal_baseline: Saved .msg/.eml files correspond to messages the user can explain (an attachment they saved, an email exported for a ticket/case), with filesystem save-timestamps that align with a plausible reason to export that specific message, and internal headers consistent with the claimed sender.
anomalies: A saved .msg/.eml file whose internal Date/Received headers place the original message well before the user account or mailbox existed, or whose Message-ID domain doesn't match any header's claimed sending server - suggesting a fabricated or edited file
Missing or truncated Received header chain on an EML that should have passed through multiple hops, consistent with hand-crafted phishing lures rather than genuine delivered mail

A .msg file's PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS stream absent or empty despite the message showing standard sender/recipient properties, which is atypical for genuinely-delivered mail and can indicate the item was manually constructed in Outlook rather than received
SPF/DKIM/DMARC results in Authentication-Results showing fail/none on a message purporting to be from an internal or trusted domain

Saved-file location or naming inconsistent with normal user workflow (e.g., staged in a temp directory with sequential generic names), suggesting bulk export for exfiltration rather than individual message handling

Discrepancy between the file's filesystem timestamps and the internal message Date header far exceeding what a simple save/forward would produce, suggesting the file was copied from another system or backdated
parsing_tools: MFCMAPI (Microsoft, open-source - browses MSG MAPI properties, converts MSG to/from EML)
extract-msg (open-source Python library for reading MSG/CFBF structure and MAPI properties)
Any text editor (EML is plain text; headers are human-readable without a parser)
Communication.anti_forensic_notes: Because EML is plain text and MSG headers are user-editable through MAPI property editors like MFCMAPI, both formats can be hand-crafted or altered to fabricate a convincing-looking message - unlike a message still resident in a live mailbox store or mail server log, a standalone saved file has no independent chain of custody proving it was actually delivered. Cross-referencing the file's internal Received chain and Message-ID against the corresponding OST/PST store or mail server logs (where available) is the primary way to validate authenticity; absence of any corroborating server-side record for a claimed-received message is itself a red flag.

Communication.name: Outlook OST/PST Files
Communication.location: Classic Outlook cached-mode OST: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\ (default since Outlook 2013/2016). PST: %USERPROFILE%\Documents\Outlook Files\ (Outlook 2013+ default) or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook\ (legacy/upgraded profiles, hidden folder). Exact per-store paths are recorded in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\Outlook\Profiles\<profile>\9375CFF0413111d3B88A00104B2A6676\<service>\001f6700 (or similarly-named binary values) and in the legacy HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles\<profile> key. Note: the current "New Outlook" / Outlook for Windows (Monarch) client does not use the classic Cached Exchange Mode/OST model for Exchange/M365 mailboxes - Microsoft does not document an equivalent user-accessible cache file path for it, so do not assume a New-Outlook mailbox has a parseable local OST.
Communication.purpose: OST (Offline Storage Table) is a local, encrypted cache of an Exchange/IMAP mailbox used for offline access and cached mode sync; PST (Personal Storage Table) is a self-contained archive/local-delivery store an analyst can open independently of any server. Both are structured containers (folders, messages, contacts, calendar) and are frequently the single richest local source of a user's email history, including items the user believes were deleted from the server.
key_fields: File header 'magic' bytes: PST files begin with the ASCII signature '!BDN'; both formats follow the Microsoft [MS-PST] structured-storage layout (B-tree-on-heap, node database) even though OST is not itself covered by a public Microsoft spec

PST content type flag distinguishes ANSI (pre-Outlook 2003, 2 GB practical size limit) from Unicode (Outlook 2003+, much larger limit) format variants, which affects which parsing tool/library version is required

Per-message MAPI properties, e.g. PR_SUBJECT, PR_SENDER_EMAIL_ADDRESS, PR_MESSAGE_DELIVERY_TIME, PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS (0x007D) - the raw internet header block including the Received chain, preserved even when the item is viewed only through Outlook's rendered UI
Folder hierarchy and per-folder message counts, including Deleted Items and Recoverable Items/Dumpster-equivalent folders inside the store itself

OST encryption cookie tying the file to the specific mailbox/profile that created it (a 'compressible encryption' or 'high encryption' substitution cipher per [MS-PST]), which is why an orphaned OST cannot be opened by Outlook without its originating profile
Attachment objects stored as embedded MAPI attachment streams, extractable independent of whether the parent message is still 'live' in the active view
Communication.normal_baseline: A single OST per configured Exchange/IMAP account under the current user's profile, actively growing/syncing, paired with a matching Outlook profile in the registry; any PSTs present correspond to user-created archives or explicitly imported/exported data files the user can account for.
anomalies: An orphaned OST (no matching Outlook profile in the registry, or the referencing profile was recently deleted) - for forensic purposes this is often more valuable than a live one, since it is a frozen snapshot of mailbox state as of the last sync, including server-side items the user has since deleted

A PST located outside the standard Documents\Outlook Files or AppData paths, especially on a removable drive, in a temp/download folder, or with a name suggesting exfiltration staging (e.g., generic or misleading filenames) rather than a normal archive name
PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS present on a message but showing a Received chain inconsistent with the claimed sender domain, or missing entirely on a message type that should carry one
A PST/OST file with a modification time far newer than any Outlook process activity on the host, suggesting the file was copied in from elsewhere rather than generated locally

Registry profile entries (Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles or Outlook\Profiles) referencing a PST/OST path that no longer exists on disk - indicates deletion or relocation of a data file after the profile was configured

PST file password-protection (CRC32-based, not strong encryption per historical Outlook implementations) present on a file otherwise inconsistent with the user's normal workflow, suggesting deliberate access restriction
parsing_tools: libpff / pffexport (libyal, open-source, implements the OST/PST structured-storage format)
MFCMAPI (Microsoft, open-source on GitHub - low-level MAPI property browser, can convert between MSG/EML and inspect PR_TRANSPORT_MESSAGE_HEADERS)
Kernel/Aid4Mail-class commercial e-discovery viewers for bulk PST/OST processing
Communication.anti_forensic_notes: OST files cannot be opened outside their originating Outlook profile because the encryption cookie is bound to the mailbox's unique ID validated against the profile/server - this is a legitimate access control, not tampering, but it means an examiner must either restore the original profile context or use a format-aware parser (libpff) that bypasses the MAPI layer entirely. Deleting a PST/OST removes the local copy, but for an OST this is low-impact anti-forensics since the data still exists server-side and Outlook will simply resync; deleting a PST used for local-only archiving or POP3 delivery is high-impact since no server copy exists. Registry profile remnants (Windows Messaging Subsystem\Profiles, Outlook\Profiles) can survive deletion of the data file itself and are useful for proving a store once existed at a specific path.

Communication.name: Teams/Slack Local Cache (LevelDB)
Communication.location: Teams 2.x (current, Electron-based): %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\MSTeams_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalCache\Microsoft\MSTeams\ containing an IndexedDB directory whose LevelDB files hold cached messages/posts/contacts. Legacy classic Teams 1.x: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Teams\IndexedDB\. Slack desktop: %APPDATA%\Slack\Local Storage\leveldb\ for LevelDB key-value data, with a separate Cache_data folder holding cached attachments/media (Chromium disk-cache format). Exact subfolder names can shift between client versions - confirm the live path on the target build before relying on it.
Communication.purpose: Modern Teams and Slack desktop clients are Electron/Chromium apps that persist recent conversation state client-side using LevelDB (Chromium's key-value storage engine, backing IndexedDB and Local Storage) rather than a conventional flat file, so a forensic copy of these directories can yield message text, contact/channel metadata, and cached attachments even without server-side access.
key_fields: LevelDB directory structure: .ldb (sorted table) files holding the actual key-value records, a MANIFEST file describing the current set of SST files, a CURRENT file pointing to the active manifest, and a LOG/LOCK file - all must be collected together, not just one .ldb file, or the store may not parse

IndexedDB object store records (JSON-like serialized values) containing message text, sender ID, channel/conversation ID, and timestamp for Teams; equivalent Local Storage key-value pairs for Slack workspace/session state
Chromium-format disk cache (Cache / Cache_data folder) holding cached images, files, and other attachment blobs referenced by conversation records, parseable with standard Chrome-cache tooling

Tombstone entries: LevelDB does not overwrite deleted records in place - a delete is appended as a new entry with an empty value and a higher sequence number, so the original key (and sometimes prior value fragments) can remain recoverable in the .ldb file until the database is compacted
Workspace/tenant and user-account identifiers embedded in the store path or records, useful for confirming which of several Teams/Slack identities the cache belongs to on a shared machine
Communication.normal_baseline: A single active LevelDB store per installed client tied to the logged-on user's profile, growing incrementally with normal conversation use, whose message timestamps align with the user's known working hours and known chat/channel memberships.
anomalies: Presence of a Teams/Slack LevelDB cache directory persisting after the application was uninstalled - deletion of the app does not remove the cache, so recovered messages can predate or postdate the visible install by longer than expected

Recovered tombstone/deleted-record remnants in .ldb files containing message content the user claims was never sent or was deleted, indicating deleted messages are still forensically recoverable pre-compaction
Cache data belonging to a workspace/tenant or account the user is not authorized to access on that host, suggesting credential reuse or unauthorized account access

Message timestamps in the cache with no corresponding entry in server-side/admin-exportable chat logs (where cross-checkable), suggesting local tampering or a client-side spoofing tool rather than genuine app-generated data
Unusually large or unexplained growth in Cache_data volume shortly before a suspected exfiltration window, consistent with bulk attachment download and caching
parsing_tools: forensicsim (open-source Autopsy module/parser for Microsoft Teams IndexedDB LevelDB data)
leveldb-dump / ccl_chrome_indexeddb (open-source LevelDB and Chromium IndexedDB record parsers)
ChromeCacheViewer (Nirsoft, for the Chromium-format Cache_data attachment cache)
Communication.anti_forensic_notes: LevelDB's append-only, log-structured design means deleted messages are not immediately purged - they persist as recoverable tombstones in .ldb files until the database runs compaction, so a user 'deleting' a message in the Teams/Slack UI does not reliably remove it from the local cache at the time of collection. Conversely, waiting too long before imaging a system, or the client running a compaction pass, can permanently remove that recoverable content - LevelDB evidence is time-sensitive in a way flat-file artifacts are not. Uninstalling the client does not delete the AppData cache directory, so absence of the parent application does not mean absence of message history.

Communication.name: Windows Notification Database
Communication.os_min: Windows 10 (Windows Push Notification service / Action Center)
Communication.location: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications\wpndatabase.db (per-user, SQLite) and its wpndatabase.db-wal write-ahead log; system-wide copy at C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Notifications\wpndatabase.db; associated image cache folder wpnidm
Communication.purpose: SQLite database storing toast notification metadata and payload content generated by installed apps (mail, chat, security software, etc.), often retaining evidence of user-facing alerts and message previews no longer present in the originating application.
key_fields: Notification table: arrival time, expiry time, payload (toast content, may include message previews)
NotificationHandler table: app/AUMID that generated the notification
Primary/foreign keys linking handler to notification entries
Communication.normal_baseline: Continuous accumulation of routine toast entries from mail clients, calendar reminders, Windows Security/Defender alerts, and chat apps, expiring and being pruned on a rolling basis by the Windows Push Notification service.
anomalies: Notification payloads referencing security-tool alerts that no longer have a corresponding surviving log entry in the tool itself, indicating the source log was deleted post-alert
Chat/email message content preserved in notification payloads that has since been deleted from the source application
Gaps in the notification timeline coinciding with other anti-forensic activity
parsing_tools: SQLite browser/CLI (DB Browser for SQLite, sqlite3)
Communication.anti_forensic_notes: Because notification content is cached independently of the originating application, deleting an alert or message in the source app does not remove the already-recorded entry in wpndatabase.db; entries do eventually expire/get pruned, and the database (including its WAL file) can be carved for deleted rows using tools such as bring2lite or fqlite.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: Recycle Bin
Deleted Items and File Existence.os_min: Windows Vista ($Recycle.Bin / $I / $R format; the earlier centralized INFO2 format is used on Windows 2000/XP/Server 2003 at C:\RECYCLER\<SID>\INFO2)
Deleted Items and File Existence.location: C:\$Recycle.Bin\<user SID>\ containing paired $I<random>.<ext> (metadata) and $R<random>.<ext> (content) files for each deleted item
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Records files a user deleted through Explorer or another Recycle-Bin-aware path, preserving both the deleted content and metadata about the item's original path, size, and deletion time - allowing recovery of the file and reconstruction of what was deleted, when, and by which account.
key_fields: $I file - header with version, original file size, deletion timestamp (FILETIME), and the original full path of the deleted item
$R file - the deleted item's actual bytes (a renamed copy of the original file, or a full copy of a deleted folder's contents)
Shared random identifier - the 6-character suffix common to an $I/$R pair, linking metadata to content
Per-user SID subdirectory under $Recycle.Bin - attributes the deletion to a specific local or domain account
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: A small, rotating set of recently user-deleted files whose original paths, sizes, and deletion times match plausible user activity, such as deleting items from Downloads, Desktop, or Documents.
anomalies: An $I file present with no matching $R file (or vice versa) - the content was permanently removed after being sent to the Recycle Bin (e.g., 'Empty Recycle Bin' or direct deletion of the $R file), while the metadata trace survives

The original path recorded in an $I file points to a security-relevant location (an EDR/AV install directory, a Startup folder, System32) - consistent with an attacker deleting evidence or disabling defenses
A burst of deletions across many $I/$R pairs in a short window, consistent with an attacker or wiper clearing a staging directory
The deletion timestamp in an $I file falls outside the SID subdirectory owner's known logon sessions, suggesting the deletion was performed under someone else's profile/context
The entire $Recycle.Bin\<SID> folder emptied of $I/$R pairs immediately following other evidence of malicious activity, inconsistent with routine user cleanup
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting a file directly (Shift+Delete, `del` from a command shell, or most malware self-deletion routines) bypasses the Recycle Bin entirely and leaves no $I/$R pair - the absence of an expected Recycle Bin entry for a known deletion is itself a signal that a non-Explorer deletion path was used. An attacker can also delete just the $R content file while leaving the $I metadata behind, or clear the whole $Recycle.Bin folder, so a lone surviving $I record should still be treated as valuable evidence of the deletion event even without recoverable content.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: Search – WordWheelQuery
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Maintains an ordered history of the search terms a user has typed into the File Explorer search box.
key_fields: Numbered values - each holding one Unicode search term string
MRUListEx - binary DWORD-array giving the order terms were entered, most recent first
Key LastWrite time - approximates when the most recent search term was entered
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: A handful of everyday search terms (partial filenames, project names, common file extensions) consistent with the user routinely locating their own files.
anomalies: Search terms for file extensions or keywords associated with sensitive data categories (passwords, finance, HR, credentials, wallet, config) shortly before a data-access or exfiltration incident
Search terms naming security tools, log files, or forensic artifacts (event log names, AV product names) suggesting reconnaissance or anti-forensic intent
Search terms for another user's name or profile-specific paths, suggesting lateral browsing of another account's data
A burst of many distinct search queries in a very short window, inconsistent with normal manual typing
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: WordWheelQuery is not touched by mainstream browser-focused privacy cleaners, so its survival alongside cleared browser history can point an analyst toward local file-system searching that other tools missed. The key can still be cleared directly via registry edit, and its complete absence on an otherwise active profile is itself worth noting.
Deleted Items and File Existence.interpretation: Search terms are stored in Unicode and ordered purely by the MRUListEx sequence, not by embedded timestamps within each value - only the key's overall LastWrite time anchors the list in time, so establishing when an earlier (non-most-recent) search term was entered is not possible from this artifact alone.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: Thumbcache
Deleted Items and File Existence.location: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer (per-user; one database per thumbnail size, e.g. thumbcache_256.db)
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Centralizes thumbnail images for pictures, documents, and folders into a per-user set of databases, one per thumbnail size (small/medium/large/extra large), replacing the per-folder Thumbs.db model used on Windows XP. Like Thumbs.db, it can retain evidence of a folder's prior contents after the source files are deleted.
key_fields: Thumbnail image data - an extractable copy of the original picture, document icon, or folder preview
Thumbnail Cache ID - cross-referenceable against Windows Search Database records to recover filename, path, and metadata
Database file per size tier (e.g., thumbcache_32.db, _96, _256, _1024)
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: Thumbcache databases populated with thumbnails matching pictures, documents, and folders the user has browsed in Explorer at the view sizes actually used (e.g., large icons vs. list view).
anomalies: Thumbnail images of sensitive documents or screenshots with no corresponding source file remaining anywhere on disk
Thumbnail Cache IDs with no matching record in the Windows Search Database, suggesting the source file or its index entry was deliberately removed after the thumbnail was cached
Thumbnails present for a user account whose role gives no reason to browse the folder or content type represented

A thumbcache database unusually small or missing expected entries relative to the user's known file activity, suggesting the cache was cleared (e.g., via Disk Cleanup's 'Thumbnails' option) to remove this evidence
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: Thumbcache databases can be cleared through Disk Cleanup's 'Thumbnails' option or third-party privacy cleaners, but because thumbnails are generated lazily on first view rather than proactively for every file, a clean or sparse database is also the expected state on a system where thumbnail view was rarely used-so absence alone is not proof of clearing. The source picture or document does not need to still exist for its thumbnail to remain.
Deleted Items and File Existence.interpretation: Database files are named by pixel dimension (e.g., thumbcache_256.db), with each file holding thumbnails generated for that display size; a given source file's thumbnail can appear in more than one size database if it was viewed at multiple Explorer view settings. Each cached thumbnail carries a Thumbnail Cache ID that can be looked up in the Windows Search Database to recover the original filename, path, and metadata the Thumbcache database itself does not store, since it retains only the rendered image.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: Thumbs.db
Deleted Items and File Existence.location: Hidden Thumbs.db file created inside each folder viewed in Explorer's thumbnail view (one per folder, colocated with the images it catalogs); creation behavior is OS-version dependent and most consistent on Windows XP
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Explorer's thumbnail-view feature writes a hidden Thumbs.db cache file into any folder whose contents were viewed as thumbnails. Because cached thumbnails and filenames remain in the file after the source pictures are deleted or moved, it functions as a historical record of a folder's prior contents.
key_fields: Embedded thumbnail image of the original picture
Original filename of the source image (Windows XP only)
Last modification time of the source file (Windows XP only)
Implicit folder path - one Thumbs.db per folder, so its location identifies the catalogued directory
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: Thumbs.db present in ordinary picture or media folders (My Pictures, Downloads, camera-import folders) on Windows XP systems, with thumbnails consistent with the images currently or previously stored there.
anomalies: Thumbnail images of sensitive documents, credentials, or screenshots inside a Thumbs.db located in a folder the user's role gives no reason to browse
Thumbnails proving a folder once held files that have since been deleted, with no corresponding files remaining on disk
Thumbs.db present in a folder accessed only via a UNC network path on a modern (post-XP) system-an unusual circumstance the source material flags explicitly
Thumbnails consistent with exfiltration staging (screenshots of internal systems, scanned documents) in a location with no legitimate business use for image viewing
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: Thumbs.db is not commonly targeted by mainstream privacy cleaners, so it often survives well after the pictures it catalogs are deleted. Since Windows Vista, thumbnail caching moved by default to the centralized per-user Thumbcache database, so the absence of Thumbs.db on a modern system is expected and not itself suspicious-but its presence there (e.g., via a UNC-accessed folder) is worth explaining.
Deleted Items and File Existence.interpretation: Thumbs.db is most relevant to Windows XP investigations, where each viewed folder gets its own file carrying the original filename and last-modified timestamp alongside the thumbnail image. On Vista and later, Windows shifted to the centralized Thumbcache database (see thumbcache), so a lone Thumbs.db on a modern OS usually indicates the folder was viewed through an unusual path, such as a UNC network share, rather than ordinary local thumbnail caching.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: User Typed Paths
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Records paths a user manually typed or pasted into the File Explorer address/path bar, including local paths and remote UNC paths to network shares. Proves deliberate navigation to a specific location rather than passive browsing.
key_fields: Value names - url1, url2, url3, ... sequential
Value data - the literal path or UNC string the user typed (e.g. C:\Users\jdoe\Desktop\staging, \\fileserver\hr$)
Key LastWrite time - when the most recent typed path was committed
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: A handful of familiar local folders and known network shares the user regularly navigates to by typing rather than clicking through folder hierarchies.
anomalies: UNC paths to unfamiliar internal hosts or admin shares (\\host\C$, \\host\ADMIN$) typed by a user with no administrative reason to browse them
Paths into other users' profile directories
Typed paths to removable/external drive letters or mount points not otherwise associated with that user
Typed paths referencing staging or exfiltration-style folder names shortly before large file transfers or archive creation evidenced elsewhere
Key entries present with a LastWrite time inconsistent with the newest url# value, suggesting manual edits to the underlying hive
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: An entry is only written to the registry once the File Explorer window is closed, so a typed path used and abandoned mid-session in a still-open window will not appear in an acquired hive. TypedPaths is not cleared by mainstream privacy/cleanup tools (CCleaner, BleachBit, Windows Disk Cleanup), so its presence is comparatively reliable, but the key's LastWrite time reflects when Explorer was closed, not the moment the path was typed.

Deleted Items and File Existence.name: Windows Search Database
Deleted Items and File Existence.location: Windows XP: C:\Documents and Settings\All Users\Application Data\Microsoft\Search\Data\Applications\Windows\Windows.edb; Windows 7+: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Search\Data\Applications\Windows\Windows.edb, plus the GatherLogs\SystemIndex subfolder under the same Applications\Windows path
Deleted Items and File Existence.purpose: Windows Search maintains an Extensible Storage Engine (ESE) database indexing metadata-and in many cases partial content-from over 900 file types, plus email, so users can search by keyword. Because it indexes a file's metadata and content independent of the file's current location, it can preserve evidence of files later moved, renamed, or deleted.
key_fields: Indexed file/email metadata (path, filename, author, timestamps, properties)
Partial or full indexed content for supported file types
GatherLogs\SystemIndex candidate list - files queued for indexing over a rolling 24-hour window
Record identifiers usable to cross-reference against Thumbnail Cache IDs from Thumbcache
Deleted Items and File Existence.normal_baseline: Index reflects ordinary documents, email, and media the user's account has created, received, or stored in indexed locations (profile folders, Outlook data files, Desktop, Documents).
anomalies: Indexed metadata or content for sensitive files no longer present anywhere else on disk, indicating deletion after the fact
GatherLogs\SystemIndex candidate entries referencing files in staging or archive-tool output directories shortly before a data-loss event
Indexed keyword content matching known-sensitive or exfiltrated document names/text the user's role gives no reason to possess
Index entries for files on removable or network volumes no longer connected to the system
Deleted Items and File Existence.anti_forensic_notes: Windows.edb is a live ESE database typically locked while the Windows Search service is running, so acquisition generally requires a tool capable of reading locked files or stopping the service first. Deleting or corrupting the .edb forces Windows to rebuild the index from scratch, destroying historical entries for files no longer present on disk. Indexing can also be disabled entirely or scoped away from specific folders through Indexing Options, which would explain an unexpectedly sparse index.
Deleted Items and File Existence.interpretation: The database is stored in Microsoft's Extensible Storage Engine (ESE) format-the same format used by WebCacheV*.dat and Exchange/AD databases-so ESE-aware tools are required to parse it. GatherLogs\SystemIndex tracks a separate rolling 24-hour candidate list of files the indexer intends to process next, which can surface file activity slightly ahead of what has made it into the finished Windows.edb index. Because indexed content can include partial file text, this database can evidence not just that a file existed but some of what it contained.

Event Logs.name: Application.evtx
Event Logs.purpose: Records application-generated events including crashes, installer errors, and some AV/EDR product logging.
key_fields: Event ID (application-specific)
Source application
Error/warning description
Event Logs.normal_baseline: Occasional application crash/error entries consistent with normal software instability.
anomalies: Crash entries for a security product coinciding with an incident timeframe
Installer entries for unrecognized software
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Lower signal-to-noise than Security/System logs for security investigations; useful mainly to corroborate AV/EDR crash-based defense evasion.

Event Logs.name: Windows Defender Operational Log
Event Logs.purpose: Records Defender detections, remediation actions, and Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule activity.
key_fields: Event ID 1116 (detection), 1117 (action taken)
Threat/signature name
File path
ASR rule Event IDs 1121-1134
Event Logs.normal_baseline: Occasional benign PUA detections consistent with normal software use; ASR audit events for known, tuned exceptions.
anomalies: 1116/1117 detection for a known offensive tool followed by no corresponding removal confirmation
ASR block (112x series) for a LOLBin invocation
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: A detected-and-quarantined threat still generates a 1116/1117 record even if the file itself is gone, making this log valuable when malware self-deletes; excluded paths configured via GPO produce no detection at all.

Event Logs.name: PowerShell Operational Log
Event Logs.os_min: Windows PowerShell 5.0 / Windows 10 (Module Logging available since PowerShell 3.0; Script Block Logging introduced with PowerShell 5.0)
Event Logs.purpose: Records detailed PowerShell engine activity when Script Block Logging and/or Module Logging are enabled via Group Policy, capturing the actual code executed - including code assembled or decoded at runtime - rather than just the invoking command line.
key_fields: Event ID 4103 - Module Logging: records pipeline execution details (parameters, variables) for the PowerShell modules configured for logging

Event ID 4104 - Script Block Logging: records the full text of an executed script block, including inline one-liners, downloaded scripts, and code reconstructed after de-obfuscation (e.g., after Base64 decoding or string concatenation)
Event ID 4105/4106 - optional start/completion events for each script block invocation (high volume; disabled by default even when script block logging is on)
ScriptBlockText - the field within 4104 containing the actual script content
ScriptBlockId - a GUID correlating a script block's start/stop/content events together
Event Logs.normal_baseline: A background level of 4103/4104 events generated by normal administrative scripting, scheduled tasks, and management tooling (e.g., DSC, module auto-loading), with script content matching known, benign automation.
anomalies: 4104 script block content containing obfuscation patterns: heavy Base64 encoding, string concatenation/reversal, or char-code array reconstruction used to hide the true command
4104 content showing download-and-execute patterns (e.g., Net.WebClient, Invoke-WebRequest piped into Invoke-Expression) or in-memory/reflective loading of .NET assemblies
4104 content invoking known offensive tooling or frameworks (e.g., credential-dumping or lateral-movement cmdlets) not part of normal admin workflows

A 4103/4104 event with no corresponding 4688 process-creation event for powershell.exe around the same time, suggesting execution via a hosted PowerShell engine (e.g., through another process's embedded runspace) rather than the standalone console
Script block logging or module logging disabled (missing 4103/4104 events entirely) on a host where the organizational GPO baseline requires it enabled
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Script Block Logging is specifically designed to defeat obfuscation: it records the fully deobfuscated script content immediately before execution regardless of how many layers of encoding, concatenation, or variable substitution were applied, so a Base64-encoded or string-split command still appears in plaintext in the 4104 event. However, both Script Block Logging and Module Logging are off by default and must be enabled via 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' / 'Turn on Module Logging' Group Policy - an attacker with sufficient privileges can also disable these settings or the EventLog service before executing, and their absence on a host expected to have them enabled is itself a signal worth investigating.

Event Logs.name: RDP / TerminalServices Event Logs
Event Logs.os_min: Windows Vista / Server 2008 (channel structure); RDP itself much older
Event Logs.purpose: Records the network-connection, authentication, and session-lifecycle stages of RDP activity across three separate log channels.
key_fields: Event ID 1149 (network authentication succeeded, RemoteConnectionManager)
Event ID 21/22/23/24/25 (session logon/shell start/disconnect/reconnect, LocalSessionManager)
Event ID 4624/4625 with Logon Type 10 or 7 (Security)
Event ID 4778 (session connected/reconnected, Security)
Event ID 4779 (session disconnected, Security)
Event Logs.normal_baseline: RDP sessions correspond to known admin jump-box or remote-work sources at expected times.
anomalies: 1149 events from unfamiliar source IPs
Session Event ID 25 (reconnect) shortly after an unexplained disconnect
4625 failures preceding a successful 4624/1149 pair (possible brute force then success)
A 4778 reconnect from a different source IP than the original 4624/1149 session establishment, suggesting session hijacking or credential reuse from a second host
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: 1149's description ('User authentication succeeded') is misleading, it reflects successful network-level authentication, not a completed interactive logon; correlating across all three channels (within about 1 minute tolerance) is needed for a complete session timeline.
Event Logs.interpretation: 4778/4779 track the session-lifecycle at the Security-log level (connect/reconnect vs. disconnect), complementing 1149's network-authentication signal and the LocalSessionManager channel's 21-25 events. All four sources should agree on the shape of a session; a mismatch between them (e.g. a 4778 reconnect with no matching LocalSessionManager Event ID 25) is worth investigating on its own.

Event Logs.name: Security Event Log
Event Logs.os_min: Windows 2000 (the event IDs and field names below reflect Windows Vista / Server 2008 and later)
Event Logs.purpose: The central Windows audit trail for authentication, authorization, and object-access activity, generated by the Local Security Authority. It is typically the first log an analyst pulls for logon/logoff activity, privilege use, process creation (when enabled), and account/group management.
key_fields: Event ID - identifies the audited action
Subject / Creator Subject - SID, account name, and domain of the principal that performed the action
Target / New Logon - SID and account name the action was performed against, or the identity of a newly created logon session

Logon Type (events 4624/4625) - numeric code for how the logon occurred: 2=Interactive, 3=Network, 4=Batch, 5=Service, 7=Unlock, 8=NetworkCleartext, 9=NewCredentials, 10=RemoteInteractive, 11=CachedInteractive
Logon ID - hexadecimal correlation value linking a logon session across 4624, 4634, 4672, 4688, and other events
4624/4625 - an account successfully/unsuccessfully logged on
4634 - an account was logged off
4648 - a logon was attempted using explicit credentials (commonly seen with runas / lateral movement)
4672 - special privileges assigned to a new logon (admin-equivalent token)
4688 - a new process has been created (Process Command Line is only populated if 'Include command line in process creation events' is enabled via GPO)
4720/4722/4725/4726 - a user account was created / enabled / disabled / deleted
4724 - an attempt was made to reset an account's password
4732 - a member was added to a security-enabled local group
4738 - a user account was changed
4740 - a user account was locked out
4768/4769 - a Kerberos TGT / service ticket was requested
4776 - the domain controller attempted to validate credentials for an account (NTLM)
1102 - the audit log was cleared
Event Logs.normal_baseline: A steady mix of paired 4624/4634 events for known accounts and their expected logon types, 4688 process creation consistent with approved software, and account-management events (4720, 4732, etc.) occurring only during known provisioning activity by authorized IT/HR staff.
anomalies: A rapid cluster of 4625 failures against one or many accounts (password spraying or brute force), especially followed by a 4624 success for the same account
4672 (special privileges assigned) immediately following a 4624 for an account not normally expected to hold administrative rights
4648 (explicit credentials) from a workstation to a server outside a normal admin workflow - a classic lateral movement / credential reuse indicator
4720 (account created) followed shortly by 4732 (added to a privileged local group) for the same account outside a known change-management window - a backdoor-account pattern
1102 (audit log cleared) with no corresponding scheduled maintenance activity - a high-confidence anti-forensic indicator
4688 New Process Name or Process Command Line showing encoded PowerShell, an unusual LOLBin invocation, or a process spawned from an unexpected parent (e.g., winword.exe spawning cmd.exe)
4768/4769 Kerberos ticket requests for service accounts using weak encryption types or occurring at unusual hours, consistent with Kerberoasting
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Clearing the Security log (via Event Viewer, `wevtutil cl Security`, or PowerShell) itself generates Event ID 1102 recording the account that performed the clear - an attacker cannot suppress this event without disabling the EventLog service or tampering with the .evtx file directly, both of which leave their own trace. Command-line auditing on 4688 is off by default and must be explicitly enabled via the 'Include command line in process creation events' GPO; its absence on an otherwise well-audited host silently blinds process-creation forensics to attacker command lines and is worth flagging on its own.

Event Logs.name: Sysmon (System Monitor)
Event Logs.os_min: Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2 and later (Sysmon is a Sysinternals tool, not a default Windows component, and must be separately installed and configured)
Event Logs.purpose: A Microsoft Sysinternals kernel-mode driver and service that logs detailed system activity - process creation with full command lines, network connections, file creation, registry changes, and more - to the Windows event log, extremely rarely present by default but very commonly deployed for DFIR and detection engineering.
key_fields: Event ID 1 - Process Create: full command line, hashes (SHA1 default, or MD5/SHA256/IMPHASH), ProcessGuid, parent process info
Event ID 3 - Network Connection: source process, source/destination IP and port, hostnames (disabled by default)
Event ID 5 - Process Terminate
Event ID 7 - Image Loaded: DLL/module load into a process, with hash and signature info (disabled by default, high volume)
Event ID 8 - CreateRemoteThread: source and target process, thread start address/module/function - a common process injection indicator
Event ID 10 - ProcessAccess: one process opening a handle to another (e.g., access to lsass.exe for credential theft)
Event ID 11 - FileCreate: a file was created or overwritten, useful for monitoring autostart and staging locations
Event ID 12/13/14 - RegistryEvent: key/value create-delete, value set, and key/value rename respectively
Event ID 22 - DNSEvent: a process performed a DNS query (Windows 8.1+ only)
ProcessGuid / LogonGuid - unique correlation identifiers that survive PID reuse, used to stitch related events together
Event Logs.normal_baseline: Event volume and content dependent entirely on the deployed Sysmon configuration file; on a well-tuned config, Event ID 1 (process creation) reflects known software launching from expected paths with plausible parent-child relationships, and configured network/file/registry events match approved application behavior.
