anomalies: Event ID 1 process creation with a suspicious parent-child relationship (e.g., an Office application spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe) or a command line containing encoded/obfuscated content
Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) targeting a sensitive process such as lsass.exe or a browser process, indicating likely code injection
Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) showing a non-standard process opening a handle to lsass.exe with access rights consistent with memory-reading tools (a classic credential-dumping indicator)
Event ID 1 showing process creation events abruptly stop while other logs (Security, System) continue - possible Sysmon tampering or filter-rule abuse rather than expected quiet
Event ID 11 (FileCreate) writing an executable into an unusual autostart location (Startup folder, Run key target directory) shortly before a corresponding Event ID 1 executing it
Registry events (12/13/14) creating or modifying known persistence keys (e.g., Run/RunOnce) from an unexpected parent process
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Sysmon explicitly does not attempt to hide itself or its driver from attackers, and its own documentation notes it provides no self-protection beyond running as a protected process; an attacker with sufficient privileges can uninstall it (sysmon -u), stop its service, or tamper with the 'Start'/'Enable' values under its EventLog-Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon-Operational Autologger registry key to silently suppress future logging without necessarily generating an obvious Sysmon-specific alert. Because Sysmon coverage and event volume depend entirely on the deployed configuration file, a gap in expected event types (e.g., no Event ID 3 network connections at all) may simply mean that event type was never enabled, not that it was tampered with - the configuration in place must be checked before drawing conclusions from absence.

Event Logs.name: System Event Log
Event Logs.os_min: Windows 2000 (the Service Control Manager event IDs below reflect Windows Vista / Server 2008 and later)
Event Logs.purpose: Records operating-system and driver/service-level activity, primarily generated by the Service Control Manager. For a DFIR analyst it is most valuable as the record of service installation, start/stop state changes, and startup-type changes - all common persistence and defense-evasion indicators.
key_fields: Event ID - identifies the SCM/system action
Service Name (param1) - the internal name of the affected service
Service state / new state (param2) - e.g. 'running' or 'stopped' for 7036; the new start type for 7040
Service File Name / binary path - the executable path recorded when a service is installed (7045)
Account context - the account a new service is configured to run as (7045)
7045 - a new service was installed on the system, including its name, binary path, service type, start type, and running account
7036 - a service entered the running or stopped state
7040 - a service's start type was changed
7034 - a service terminated unexpectedly (crashed, rather than stopping cleanly)
104 - the event log was cleared
Event Logs.normal_baseline: 7045 entries correspond to known, typically vendor-signed software or OS component installs; 7036 running/stopped transitions track expected boot, shutdown, and update cycles for known services; 7040 start-type changes are rare and tied to known administrative or update activity.
anomalies: 7045 for a service whose binary path sits in Temp, AppData, ProgramData, or another user-writable location, or whose name mimics a legitimate OS service (e.g., 'WindowsUpdate', 'SvcHost') without matching any real Microsoft service

7040 changing a security product's service start type away from Automatic (or to Disabled), especially shortly before a 7036 'stopped' event for that same service - a common pattern for disabling security tooling
7034 (unexpected termination) for a security product's service rather than a clean 7036 stop, suggesting the process was forcibly killed rather than stopped through its normal control path

7045 events with the same unusual service name, binary path, or hash appearing across multiple hosts in a short window, consistent with lateral movement via remote service creation (e.g., PsExec-style execution)
104 (log cleared) with no corresponding scheduled maintenance activity
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Attackers frequently favor stopping or reconfiguring a security service through the normal SCM control path (sc.exe stop, Stop-Service, or the SCM API) because it produces only a routine-looking 7036 'stopped' event rather than the more conspicuous 7034 crash event - so a 7036 stop for a security product is not automatically benign and should be checked against who/what triggered it. Clearing the System log to remove 7045/7036/7040 evidence itself generates Event ID 104, which an attacker must separately suppress or accept as a trace.

Event Logs.name: AppLocker / WDAC Event Logs
Event Logs.location: Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\AppLocker\EXE and DLL; \AppLocker\MSI and Script; \AppLocker\Packaged app-Deployment; \AppLocker\Packaged app-Execution; Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\CodeIntegrity\Operational
Event Logs.purpose: Records allow/block decisions made by AppLocker and Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) when executables, scripts, MSIs, packaged apps, DLLs, drivers, and COM objects are evaluated against application-control policy, in both audit and enforced modes.
key_fields: Event ID
File name / full path
Policy name (e.g., EXE, DLL, MANAGEDINSTALLER)
Rule type (path/hash/publisher) and rule name
User/group SID
Enforcement mode (audit vs enforce)
Correlation ActivityID (links a block event to its signature event)
TotalSignatureCount / signature index
Event Logs.normal_baseline: Event 8001 (policy applied successfully) at each policy refresh/boot; 8002/8005 (allowed) or 3099 (policy loaded) entries matching known, whitelisted line-of-business and system binaries; low, predictable event volume tied to logons and software installs.
anomalies: Bursts of 8003/8004 (EXE/DLL audit or enforced block) or 8006/8007 (script/MSI block) for files under %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, Downloads, or C:\Users\Public
3076/3077 (WDAC audit/enforced block) for unsigned or unexpected drivers and binaries
8036 (COM object blocked) indicating an attempted COM-based application-control bypass
Clustered 8000/8029/8040 error events on a single host suggesting active policy-evasion attempts
Gaps or truncation in the AppLocker or CodeIntegrity channels suggesting log clearing to hide blocked execution attempts
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: App Control does not log successful allowed executions by default (only blocks and would-be blocks), so an attacker who stays within policy generates no record; disabling the Application Identity service (AppIDSvc) or clearing the AppLocker/CodeIntegrity event channels removes both future and historical evidence of blocked execution attempts.

Event Logs.name: Windows Defender ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) Events
Event Logs.os_min: Windows 10 version 1709 (Fall Creators Update) or later for the ASR framework and most rules; specific rules require newer builds (e.g., version 1803 for the LSASS credential-theft rule, version 1903 for the WMI persistence rule); Windows Server 2016 (1803 Semi-Annual Channel) or later; requires Microsoft Defender Antivirus as the real-time engine
Event Logs.location: Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Windows Defender > Operational (channel: Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational), plus the companion Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/WHC channel
Event Logs.purpose: Records when an individual Attack Surface Reduction rule evaluated and acted on an event, distinct from Windows Defender's general malware-detection log, capturing rule-level block/audit/warn-override/config-change activity for behaviors such as Office child-process creation, LSASS credential theft, and executable content delivered via email or webmail.
key_fields: Event ID 1121 (rule fired in Block mode)
Event ID 1122 (rule fired in Audit mode)
Event ID 1129 (user overrode a Warn-mode block)
Event ID 5007 (ASR configuration/setting changed)
Rule GUID d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a = Block all Office applications from creating child processes
Rule GUID 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2 = Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (LSASS)
Rule GUID be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550 = Block executable content from email client and webmail
Advanced Hunting ActionType (e.g., AsrOfficeChildProcessBlocked, AsrLsassCredentialTheftBlocked, AsrExecutableEmailContentBlocked)
Target process image path acted on by the rule
Event Logs.normal_baseline: In environments running rules in Audit mode, 1122 events are expected in volume, especially for the LSASS credential-theft rule, which is noisy by design and frequently fires on benign processes (e.g., browser update checks) without indicating compromise. In Block mode, sparse 1121 events tied to sanctioned admin tooling (PsExec, WMI) are typical in managed environments.
anomalies: 1121/1122 events against the LSASS-credential-theft rule (GUID 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2) triggered by an unrecognized or unsigned process
Office child-process or code-injection rule firing immediately after a macro-enabled document was opened
1129 user-override events clustering on one host/user, indicating deliberate bypass of a Warn-mode block
5007 configuration-change events showing ASR rules disabled or downgraded from Block to Audit shortly before other suspicious activity
Executable-content-from-email rule blocking a payload immediately following a phishing email delivery
parsing_tools: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint advanced hunting (DeviceEvents table, Asr* ActionTypes)
Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) for centralized collection
Event Logs.anti_forensic_notes: Configuration changes to ASR rules generate their own 5007 event in the same Operational log, so an attacker who weakens or disables a rule leaves a corresponding tamper record alongside the rule-trigger history. Clearing or disabling the Windows Defender Operational log (or the AV engine entirely) removes both the trigger events and this tamper evidence together, which is itself a detectable event-log-clearing action.

External Device/USB Usage.name: Connection Timestamps
External Device/USB Usage.os_min: First Install/Last Connected/Last Removal properties require Windows 7+ (0064) / Windows 8+ (0066, 0067)
External Device/USB Usage.location: Plug and Play log: XP: C:\Windows\setupapi.log ; Win7+: C:\Windows\inf\setupapi.dev.log. Registry. Win7+: SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR\Disk&Ven_&Prod_\<USBSerial#>\Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a19231573b29}\####(0064=First Install, 0066=Last Connected, 0067=Last Removal); mirrored under \Enum\SCSI\... . Also Win10+: Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic.evtx Event ID 1006 per device connect/disconnect.
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Determines the temporal usage of specific USB devices connected to a Windows machine by combining the plug-and-play log file (first-ever install) with the registry's Properties GUID subkeys (first install, last connected, last removed) and the Partition/Diagnostic event log (every connect/disconnect).
key_fields: setupapi.dev.log entries: search for the device's serial number; log timestamps are in local time zone
Properties {83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a19231573b29}\0064: First Install (Win7+)
Properties {83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a19231573b29}\0066: Last Connected (Win8+)
Properties {83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a19231573b29}\0067: Last Removal (Win8+)
Timestamps stored in Windows 64-bit FILETIME format
Partition/Diagnostic Event ID 1006: recorded for each device connect/disconnect (log cleared during major OS updates)
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: Connection timestamps for known, approved removable media align with expected work usage windows and match the device inventory the user is authorized to use.
anomalies: A First Install timestamp for a USB device with no corresponding approval/inventory record, especially shortly before a data-loss incident
A Last Connected/Last Removal pair spanning a very short window immediately followed by evidence of large file transfers, consistent with rapid exfiltration to removable media
setupapi.dev.log entries for a device that has no matching USBSTOR registry key, or vice versa, suggesting partial artifact cleanup
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The Partition/Diagnostic event log is cleared during major Windows OS updates, so its coverage window can be shorter than the registry Properties subkeys, which persist across updates unless the device is fully removed from the registry.
External Device/USB Usage.interpretation: This is the correlation layer across three separate data sources: the plug-and-play log gives the very first time a device's driver was ever installed, the Properties GUID subkeys refine that into first/last-connected/last-removed, and Partition/Diagnostic gives a per-event connect/disconnect timeline (when not yet rolled off by an OS update). Use all three together rather than relying on one, since each has a different retention/coverage limitation. See `usb-device-identification` for the broader device-identity fields and `setupapi-devlog` for the log file format itself.

External Device/USB Usage.name: Drive Letter and Volume Name
External Device/USB Usage.location: Windows XP: SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR (find the device's ParentIdPrefix), then correlate that value against SYSTEM\MountedDevices to find the last mount point. Windows 7+: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Portable Devices\Devices; SYSTEM\MountedDevices (examine \DosDevices\<letter> values for a matching device serial number); SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Search\VolumeInfoCache.
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Discovers the last drive letter and volume name assigned to a specific USB device the last time it was connected to the system.
key_fields: USBSTOR ParentIdPrefix (Windows XP) - links a USBSTOR device entry to its MountedDevices record
MountedDevices \DosDevices\<letter> values - binary data containing a device serial number or volume GUID to match against a known device
SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Portable Devices\Devices subkeys (Windows 7+) - named for the device, storing the last friendly volume/device label
VolumeInfoCache entries (Windows 7+) - cached volume label and related metadata keyed by volume
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: A stable, small set of drive-letter assignments for known recurring devices, with volume names matching each device's manufacturer default or a user-assigned label the analyst can independently confirm.
anomalies: A drive letter reassigned between clearly unrelated devices in a short window, breaking the expected one-device-per-letter continuity an analyst would otherwise expect
A volume name that doesn't match a device's previously documented label, suggesting the media was relabeled/reformatted to blend in or to impersonate another known device
MountedDevices \DosDevices value manually deleted or edited, breaking the letter-to-serial-number correlation for a device otherwise evidenced elsewhere (usb-device-history, setupapi-devlog)
VolumeInfoCache or Windows Portable Devices entries present with no corresponding USBSTOR/MountedDevices record, indicating partial artifact deletion
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: These keys are overwritten on each new mount, so only the LAST drive-letter/volume-name mapping for a device is recoverable here - deleting or editing the relevant MountedDevices value removes that mapping with no lower-level history retained in these locations; connection history itself must come from usb-device-history's registry timestamps or setupapi-devlog.
External Device/USB Usage.interpretation: Only the last USB device mapped to a specific drive letter can be identified from these keys - historical drive-letter assignments over time are not retained here. Cross-reference the recovered volume name and letter against shell-item data in LNK files and shellbags to place the device in a broader activity timeline.

External Device/USB Usage.name: SetupAPI Device Install Log (setupapi.dev.log)
External Device/USB Usage.location: %SystemRoot%\inf\setupapi.dev.log (Windows Vista and later). On Windows XP/2000/Server 2003 the equivalent file is %SystemRoot%\setupapi.log (note: no 'inf' subfolder, different filename). ANSI plain-text file; when it grows large it is not simply truncated - a related setupapi.upgrade.log is created during OS upgrades to record driver migration for previously-installed devices.
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: System-wide, chronological plain-text log written by the Plug and Play (PnP) manager and SetupAPI recording every device/driver installation operation on the host, including the exact local-time timestamp a device's driver was first installed. For removable media this is the highest-confidence source for establishing precisely when a USB device was FIRST connected to a system, complementing (and independently corroborating) the registry-based USBSTOR 'last connected/removed' property timestamps.
key_fields: Text log header - operating system version and computer architecture, written once at the top of the file

Text log section header - format '[timestamp process-id.instance description]', e.g. a 'Device Install' section opening with a line like '>>> [Device Install (Hardware initiated) - USB\VID_xxxx&PID_xxxx\<serial>]' followed by a 'Section start YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS.sss' line
time_stamp field format: yyyy/mm/dd hh:mm:ss.sss, recorded in the local system time zone at the time of installation (not UTC, unlike most registry timestamps)

Device instance ID string embedded in the section header/body - contains device class, VID (vendor ID), PID (product ID), and the device's reported serial number, present for every Plug-and-Play device, not just USB mass storage

Driver installation outcome lines within the section (e.g., driver package search, selection, and install success/failure), useful for confirming whether a device install actually completed versus was only attempted
Section end marker with final status code, indicating whether SetupAPI considered the installation successful
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: A single append-only log file growing over the life of the OS install, containing device-install sections for expected hardware (docking stations, printers, and the same recurring set of user storage devices) with first-install timestamps that align with when the user says they first used each device, and no sections for unfamiliar device classes.
anomalies: A USBSTOR registry entry exists for a device with no corresponding Device Install section in setupapi.dev.log (or vice versa) - the two sources should agree on first-connection time, so a mismatch suggests log tampering, registry manipulation, or that the connection happened under a different/rolled-back log
A Device Install section timestamp inconsistent with the surrounding log entries (out of chronological order), suggesting the log file was edited or entries were spliced in after the fact

The active setupapi.dev.log missing historical entries the analyst expects based on other evidence (e.g., USBSTOR first-install property data older than the earliest entry in the current log), consistent with deliberate deletion/replacement of the log or a Windows Setup/upgrade event that reset it - check for a setupapi.upgrade.log, which can retain migration records for previously-connected devices even after the main log is cleared
A burst of many distinct, unfamiliar VID/PID device installs in a short window, especially immediately before or after a suspected data-exfiltration or intrusion timeframe
A gap in section timestamps spanning a period the host was known to be powered on and in use, suggesting the log was cleared or truncated during that window
parsing_tools: Any text editor / findstr/grep (plain ANSI text format, no proprietary parser required)
USB Detective (commercial - parses setupapi.dev.log alongside registry USB artifacts into a unified device timeline)
KAPE (Eric Zimmerman - collects setupapi.dev.log via built-in USB-related collection targets for offline review)
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: setupapi.dev.log only records the FIRST installation of a given device/driver combination system-wide - it does not log every subsequent reconnect, so later connect/disconnect timing must still come from registry property timestamps (USBSTOR Properties 0x0066/0x0067) or MountPoints2. Because it is a plain-text, non-protected file under %SystemRoot%\inf, it is straightforward to delete or edit and is explicitly called out in anti-forensic guidance as a file to remove to obscure USB history; deletion removes the earliest-connection evidence but does not affect the registry-based artifacts, so the two sources should always be checked together. A Windows Feature Update/in-place upgrade can also effectively reset this log, though a setupapi.upgrade.log may retain some historical migration records for devices that existed before the upgrade.

External Device/USB Usage.name: USB Device Identification
External Device/USB Usage.location: SYSTEM hive: CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR and CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB; per-device Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a1923f573b29} subkey (Windows 7+); NTUSER.DAT: Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\MountPoints2; C:\Windows\inf\setupapi.dev.log
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Reconstructs the history of USB devices (primarily mass storage) connected to a system: which device, when it was first installed, when it was last connected/removed, and which user account was logged on at the time.
key_fields: USBSTOR device subkey name - encodes device class, vendor (Ven_), product (Prod_), and revision (Rev_), e.g. Disk&Ven_SanDisk&Prod_Extreme&Rev_0001
USBSTOR instance ID subkey - contains the device's reported serial number (or a system-generated identifier)
Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a1923f573b29}\0064 - first install/plug-in timestamp (Windows 7+)
Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a1923f573b29}\0066 - last connected/arrival timestamp (Windows 8+)
Properties\{83da6326-97a6-4088-9453-a1923f573b29}\0067 - last removal timestamp (Windows 8+)
MountPoints2 - per-user record (with LastWrite time) linking a volume GUID to the user account that mounted it, showing who was logged on when a device was connected

setupapi.dev.log - system-wide, chronological plain-text log of device installation events, including the first-connection timestamp, VID/PID, and serial number, for every plug-and-play device including non-storage USB devices
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: A small, stable set of known storage devices (personal drives, approved corporate-issued media) with connection timestamps aligned to expected business use, and MountPoints2 attribution matching the device owner's account.
anomalies: A device with no corresponding setupapi.dev.log first-install entry despite a USBSTOR record, or vice versa, suggesting registry or log tampering (they should normally agree on first-connection time)
Devices connecting outside business hours or immediately before/after a suspected data-exfiltration window
A large number of distinct unfamiliar devices connected in a short time, or the same device connecting across many different user accounts/hosts
MountPoints2 entry attributing a device to an account other than the one an analyst expects, based on other evidence

First-install (0064) and last-connected (0066) timestamps far apart with no intervening evidence of removal, or a last-removal (0067) timestamp that precedes the last-connected time, indicating inconsistent or edited property data

USBSTOR serial number values that look system-generated (their second character is '&') mixed among otherwise consistent hardware serials-treat any single serial value as provisional rather than a guaranteed unique hardware identifier
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: The commonly cited rule that a serial number with '&' as its second character is always system-generated (i.e., the device itself has no hardware serial) has been shown to be unreliable in practice-Windows-reported values can be inconsistent across enclosures/adapters even for the same physical drive, so serial numbers should be treated as identifiers to correlate rather than as trustworthy hardware fingerprints. setupapi.dev.log only records the first installation of a given device/driver combination system-wide (not per subsequent reconnect), so later connect/disconnect timing must come from the registry property timestamps or MountPoints2, and deleting or rolling back that log removes the earliest-connection evidence.

External Device/USB Usage.name: Event Logs (Removable Device)
External Device/USB Usage.os_min: Windows 7 (Security.evtx / System.evtx events); Windows 10 (Partition/Diagnostic.evtx Event ID 1006)
External Device/USB Usage.location: System.evtx - Event IDs 20001, 20003 (Plug and Play driver install attempted). Security.evtx - Event IDs 4663 (attempt to access a removable storage object), 4656 (failure to access a removable storage object), 6416 (a new external device was recognized by the system) - these depend on system audit-policy settings. Windows 10+: Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic.evtx - Event ID 1006, recorded for each device connect/disconnect.
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Removable device connect/disconnect and access activity audited across multiple Windows event logs, giving an independent, timestamped, log-based record of USB activity that complements the registry-based USB artifacts.
key_fields: System.evtx Event ID 20001 - Plug and Play driver install attempted for a device
System.evtx Event ID 20003 - Plug and Play driver install attempted (companion event)
Security.evtx Event ID 4663 - an attempt was made to access a removable storage object
Security.evtx Event ID 4656 - a failure to access a removable storage object
Security.evtx Event ID 6416 - a new external device was recognized by the system
Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic.evtx Event ID 1006 (Windows 10+) - recorded for each device connect and disconnect
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: 20001/20003 and 6416 events limited to a small, known set of recurring storage devices, with no 4656 access failures outside expected permission changes; 1006 connect/disconnect pairs on Windows 10+ align with the registry-based first/last-connect timestamps for the same device.
anomalies: 6416/20001 events for a device with no corresponding record in usb-device-history or setupapi-devlog, or vice versa - the sources should agree on when a device first appeared
A cluster of 4656 access-failure events against removable storage objects, suggesting a blocked exfiltration attempt or a device-control policy being tested/probed
1006 connect/disconnect pairs occurring in rapid repeated succession for the same device, consistent with scripted/automated enumeration rather than normal human use
A gap in expected 20001/6416 events during a period other evidence shows a device was physically connected, suggesting audit settings were disabled or the log was cleared for that window
4663/4656 activity present with no matching audit-policy change history, when the org's baseline has removable-storage object-access auditing disabled by default
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: Security.evtx events (4663, 4656, 6416) are only generated if Object Access auditing for removable storage has been explicitly enabled via audit policy/GPO - their absence proves nothing about whether removable-device activity occurred, only that this auditing was not turned on. System.evtx PnP events (20001/20003) and the Windows 10+ Partition/Diagnostic 1006 event do not depend on that audit setting, making them a more reliable fallback when Security auditing is off; as with any .evtx, wholesale log clearing generates its own Security-log Event ID 1102 record.
External Device/USB Usage.interpretation: Security log events for removable storage are dependent on system audit settings being enabled - treat a lack of 4663/4656/6416 entries as inconclusive rather than as proof no device access occurred, and cross-check against the audit-independent System.evtx and Partition/Diagnostic.evtx channels.

External Device/USB Usage.name: User Information
External Device/USB Usage.location: SYSTEM\MountedDevices (document the device's Volume GUID) correlated against each user's NTUSER.DAT\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\MountPoints2 (per-user subkeys, one per mounted volume GUID).
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Identifies which user account(s) were logged on when a specific USB device was connected, by matching the device's Volume GUID between the system-wide MountedDevices key and individual users' per-profile MountPoints2 key.
key_fields: MountedDevices Volume GUID value - system-wide record of a mounted volume's unique identifier
MountPoints2 subkey name - a Volume GUID, present under a specific user's NTUSER.DAT when that user's Explorer process mounted the device
MountPoints2 subkey LastWrite time - approximates when that user's profile last interacted with the mount
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: A device's Volume GUID appears in MountPoints2 only under the profile of its expected/known owner, with LastWrite times consistent with that user's documented usage windows.
anomalies: A device's Volume GUID found in the MountPoints2 key of an account other than its expected owner

The same Volume GUID appearing across multiple unrelated user profiles on a shared workstation in a short time span, suggesting the device was passed between users or the workstation was used by multiple people around the same event

A MountedDevices record for a device with no corresponding MountPoints2 entry in any loaded user hive, despite other evidence (usb-device-history, usb-event-logs) indicating the device was used interactively - consistent with a deleted MountPoints2 subkey
MountPoints2 LastWrite time inconsistent with the device's connect/disconnect timestamps recorded elsewhere, suggesting registry tampering or an unloaded/incomplete user hive
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: MountPoints2 lives inside each individual user's NTUSER.DAT, so this attribution path disappears entirely if that user's hive is not collected/loaded, or if the specific MountPoints2 subkey is deleted - deletion removes only that user's linkage without affecting the system-wide MountedDevices record, so a GUID with no MountPoints2 match anywhere is itself worth flagging rather than dismissing.
External Device/USB Usage.interpretation: A Volume GUID match between MountedDevices and a user's MountPoints2 key indicates that user's profile was logged on (loaded) while that specific device was present on the system - it establishes presence/opportunity, not proof that the user actively interacted with the device's file contents.

External Device/USB Usage.name: Volume Serial Number (VSN)
External Device/USB Usage.location: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\WindowsNT\CurrentVersion\EMDMgmt - find the key matching the device's Volume Name and USB Unique Serial Number, then take the last integer in the matching line and convert it from decimal to hex to get the VSN; this key is often missing entirely on modern systems using SSD-based removable devices. Windows 10+: Microsoft-Windows-Partition/Diagnostic.evtx Event ID 1006 may include VBR data containing the VSN - 4 bytes located at offset 0x43 (FAT), 0x64 (exFAT), or 0x48 (NTFS) within each Volume Boot Record; this log is cleared during major OS feature updates.
External Device/USB Usage.purpose: Discovers the Volume Serial Number assigned to the file-system partition on a USB device - this is NOT the USB Unique Serial Number hardcoded into the device's firmware, nor any external label serial number - for correlating the device to files or shell items it produced elsewhere on the system.
key_fields: EMDMgmt key/value name - encodes the device's Volume Name and USB Unique Serial Number together with a trailing decimal integer that is the VSN once converted to hex
Partition/Diagnostic.evtx Event ID 1006 VBR payload - fixed-offset 4-byte VSN field, offset depends on the partition's file system (FAT 0x43, exFAT 0x64, NTFS 0x48)
External Device/USB Usage.normal_baseline: A consistent VSN recoverable across all available sources (EMDMgmt, VBR data in Event ID 1006, and any shell-item metadata in LNK files/shellbags/jump lists) for the same physical device over its lifetime on the system.
anomalies: A VSN recovered from shell-item metadata (LNK, shellbags, jump lists) with no matching EMDMgmt entry - on modern/SSD-based devices this can simply reflect the key's frequent absence rather than tampering, so weigh it alongside other USB artifacts before treating it as suspicious

Two connection events attributed to what is claimed to be the same physical device yielding different VSNs, consistent with the device having been reformatted or with two different devices being presented as one

A device's VSN appearing in LNK/shellbags shell-item data on a host with no corresponding usb-device-history or usb-event-logs record for that device, suggesting deleted or missing upstream USB artifacts
Partition/Diagnostic.evtx showing a gap spanning a known device-connection window, consistent with the log having been reset by a major OS feature update rather than by user action
External Device/USB Usage.anti_forensic_notes: EMDMgmt is frequently absent entirely on modern systems and SSD-based removable media, so its absence alone carries little weight; the Partition/Diagnostic.evtx channel is cleared during major Windows feature updates, meaning a VSN capture opportunity from that source can be lost across an OS-upgrade boundary independent of any deliberate anti-forensic action.
External Device/USB Usage.interpretation: The VSN is not the USB Unique Serial Number hardcoded into the device's firmware, nor any printed external label serial - it belongs to the file-system partition and changes if the device is reformatted. The VSN together with the device's Volume Name is what allows correlation of a specific USB device to files it touched elsewhere on the system, via shell items embedded in LNK files and other registry locations such as shellbags.

File and Folder Opening.name: Internet Explorer file:///
File and Folder Opening.location: IE6-7: %USERPROFILE%\Local Settings\History\History.IE5; IE8-9: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\History\History.IE5; IE10-11 and Windows 10+: %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\WebCache\WebCacheV*.dat
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Internet Explorer's history databases record local and remote (network share) file-path access per user, logged as file:/// URL entries. Because the underlying database formats persist across OS versions, some of this evidence can still be recovered even on Windows 11+ systems that no longer ship Internet Explorer.
key_fields: file:/// URL entries (format: file:///C:/<directory>/<filename>.<ext>)
Per-user History.IE5 / WebCacheV*.dat container, isolating evidence by profile
Access timestamp associated with each history entry
Container/partition table inside WebCacheV*.dat (IE10+) separating history, cache, and cookies within the single ESE file
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: file:/// entries pointing to local documents, downloads, or mapped/UNC network shares the user has legitimately opened through Explorer or an application's 'Recent Files' list, consistent with the account's normal file-access pattern.
anomalies: file:/// entries for sensitive network shares (finance, HR, executive) outside the user's documented job function
A burst of file:/// entries covering many distinct file paths in a short window, consistent with bulk browsing or staging ahead of exfiltration
file:/// entries referencing servers or shares the user has no legitimate business reason to access

Entries present despite Internet Explorer being uninstalled or never used on the account, indicating the access occurred through another shell component (e.g., Explorer, Office) that also writes to this database
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: History.IE5/WebCacheV*.dat can be cleared through Internet Explorer's 'Clear browsing data' or a general privacy cleaner, and WebCacheV*.dat also self-purges older records as a fixed-size ESE database fills. Because file:/// entries are generated regardless of whether Internet Explorer is installed or used, a missing or unusually sparse database on a system with clear evidence of local or network file activity can itself point to targeted clearing of this artifact rather than genuine non-use.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: Entries are recorded as file:///C:/<directory>/<filename>.<ext>. A file:/// entry does not mean the file was opened in a web browser-Explorer, Office's 'Recent Files', and other shell components generate the same records when a local or network file is accessed, so this artifact is general file-access evidence rather than proof of browser activity.

File and Folder Opening.name: MS Word Reading Locations
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Records the last cursor/scroll position a user reached within a specific Word document, along with when that reading session ended, so Word can resume the document at the same spot next time it's opened.
key_fields: Position subkey values - per-document entries keyed by file path/identifier
Date - the last-closed timestamp for that reading session
Position - the stored location (page/character offset) within the document at close
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Entries for documents the user has recently read or edited, with Date values reasonably close to other evidence of Word being open, and positions scattered throughout each document consistent with normal reading/editing.
anomalies: A Reading Locations entry for a document with no corresponding File MRU or Trust Records entry, or vice versa, suggesting one artifact was cleared while the other was missed
A recorded closing position at or near the very start of a large document, inconsistent with a claim that the user reviewed its full contents
An entry for a document the user denies having opened, with a Date value falling inside a suspected incident window
A Reading Locations entry referencing a document path under a Temp, Downloads, or email-attachment cache directory rather than a normal working location
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: This key only tracks documents opened long or interactively enough for Word to record a reading position, so a document opened only briefly may leave no entry here even though it does elsewhere (File MRU, Trust Records). Deleting the key removes reading-position history without affecting the separate File MRU list, so the two should be checked independently rather than assumed to rise and fall together.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: Cross-referencing the Date (last-closed) value here against the last-opened time recorded in the corresponding Office File MRU entry for the same document lets an analyst calculate an approximate session duration - how long the user actually had the document open - which neither artifact provides on its own.

File and Folder Opening.name: Office OAlerts
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Captures the alert dialogs MS Office applications show users during risky or unsaved-work actions, such as attempting to close a document without saving.
key_fields: Event ID 300 - used by all Office applications for these alerts
Program name - which Office application generated the alert
Dialog message text - the specific alert text shown to the user
TimeCreated - when the alert fired
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Occasional Event ID 300 entries tied to routine unsaved-changes or file-format warnings during normal Office use, at a low, steady rate.
anomalies: A cluster of alerts around the time a document was closed or corrupted immediately following a suspected malicious macro execution
Alert text referencing a document type or feature (e.g. a compatibility or repair warning) inconsistent with the file the user claims to have been working on
Complete absence of any OAlerts entries on a system with heavy Office usage evidenced elsewhere in the timeline, suggesting the log was cleared
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: As a standard Windows Event Log, OAlerts.evtx can be cleared wholesale via wevtutil or the Event Viewer UI, which itself generates a Security log clear-event (Event ID 1102) - correlating the two logs can reveal deliberate clearing. Because every Office application shares the single Event ID 300, the dialog message text is required to distinguish alert types; the ID alone is not diagnostic.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: All Office alert types share the same generic Event ID 300, so filtering on ID alone returns every kind of Office warning - the program name and message fields must be read together to determine what specific action (unsaved close, format warning, etc.) triggered a given entry.

File and Folder Opening.name: Office Recent Files
File and Folder Opening.location: NTUSER.DAT: Software\Microsoft\Office\<Version>\<AppName>\File MRU (Version: 10.0=OfficeXP, 11.0=Office2003, 12.0=Office2007, 14.0=Office2010, 15.0=Office2013, 16.0=Office2016/2019/M365) ; Microsoft 365 also under \User MRU\LiveId_####\File MRU (Microsoft account sign-in) and \User MRU\AD_####\File MRU (Azure AD sign-in)
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Each Office application maintains its own recently-opened-files list, separate from the OS-level RecentDocs registry key and the Windows Recent Items shell folder.
key_fields: Item # value names - numbered entries, most recent typically Item 1
Value data - full file path of the opened document plus a last-opened timestamp encoded in the string
LiveId_#### / AD_#### subkeys - separate per-account File MRU lists on Microsoft 365 installs signed in with a Microsoft account or Azure AD identity
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Entries matching documents the user has genuinely worked on recently, with full paths in expected profile/project locations and last-opened times consistent with the user's normal working pattern.
anomalies: Full path referencing a Temp, Downloads, or email-attachment-cache directory rather than a normal document location
A document opened via a specific Office application per this key with no corresponding Trust Records or Reading Locations entry where one would be expected
File MRU entries under a LiveId_#### or AD_#### subkey for an account the primary user does not recognize signing into that Office installation
A last-opened timestamp for a file that no longer exists anywhere on disk with no other legitimate explanation for its deletion
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Because full path and a last-opened time are recorded directly in the value data (unlike the OS RecentDocs key, which requires MRUListEx ordering to establish sequence), this list is comparatively easy to read but just as easy to clear wholesale by deleting the File MRU subkey - removing the entire per-application history at once rather than one entry at a time.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: Unlike the general RecentDocs registry key, each Office application's File MRU stores the complete file path and an explicit last-opened time per entry rather than relying on binary MRUListEx ordering, making it a more directly readable and often more precise source for reconstructing when a specific document was opened in a specific Office application. On Microsoft 365 installs, checking the correct account-specific subkey (LiveId_#### vs AD_####) matters, since separate signed-in identities keep independent lists.

File and Folder Opening.name: Office Trust Records
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Remembers a user's decision to trust a document that triggered a security warning, such as a Protected View or macro warning, so Office does not re-prompt the next time the same file is opened.
key_fields: Value name - full path of the trusted document
Value data - a binary structure encoding the time the document was trusted plus which trust grant was applied (e.g. enabling active content/macros vs. exiting Protected View)
Trust type flags - distinguish a plain trust decision from one that also enabled macro/active-content execution
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: A small number of trusted entries corresponding to internal templates, forms, or macro-enabled workbooks the user knowingly and repeatedly uses, trusted once and then opened without further warnings.
anomalies: A macro-enabled document trusted immediately before other compromise indicators, especially one received as an email attachment or downloaded from an external/unexpected sender

A trust decision timestamp only seconds after the document's creation or download time, consistent with a user immediately enabling content on an unfamiliar file rather than a document they habitually use
A trusted document path under Temp, Downloads, or an email-attachment cache directory rather than a normal working location
Multiple documents from the same unfamiliar source or naming pattern trusted in quick succession, suggesting a mass-mailed macro campaign
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: A TrustRecords entry is only created after the user actively grants trust - a document opened and then closed without enabling content (or blocked by Protected View and never trusted) leaves no entry here even though it may appear elsewhere (File MRU, Reading Locations). Because trust is granted per full file path, renaming or moving a previously-trusted malicious document forces a fresh trust decision and therefore a fresh, checkable record.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: This key exists specifically to avoid re-prompting the user, so its presence is direct evidence of an affirmative user action to bypass a security warning, not merely that the file was opened. The stored data includes both the time trust was granted and which specific permission was extended, which for a macro-enabled document is typically the single most important pivot point in reconstructing a phishing-to-execution chain.

File and Folder Opening.name: Open/Save MRU
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Tracks individual files opened or saved through any application's standard Windows shell Open/Save dialog, spanning Office, browsers, chat clients, and most other common desktop software.
key_fields: "*" subkey - a combined MRU of the most recent files of any extension used in an Open/Save dialog
.<ext> subkeys - one per specific file extension (e.g. .docx, .pdf, .zip), each with its own MRUListEx-ordered entries
MRUListEx - binary DWORD-array recording access order, most recent first, at both the "*" and per-extension level
Value data - filename plus (Win7+) a binary PIDL encoding the folder path the file was opened or saved from
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Extension subkeys matching file types the user regularly works with, populated with filenames and folder paths consistent with normal document, media, and download workflows.
anomalies: A new extension subkey appearing for file types the user never normally handles (.ps1, .vbs, .hta, .scr, .iso, .lnk) around an incident window
A file opened or saved from a Downloads, Temp, or email-attachment staging folder shortly before other execution or persistence evidence appears
The "*" list and a specific extension subkey disagreeing on ordering or contents for the same time period, suggesting selective tampering
Entries for files that no longer exist anywhere on disk with no legitimate explanation for their absence
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Because this key is populated by the shared Windows common-dialog control rather than by individual applications, clearing it removes evidence of file interaction across many programs at once rather than just one - a single deletion event with broad evidentiary impact. Entries survive deletion of the underlying file, making this a durable record of files that once existed even after they and any Recycle Bin trace are gone.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: The "*" key is a cross-extension MRU capturing only the single most recent files regardless of type, while the per-extension .??? subkeys retain a longer, type-specific history that can still hold an entry the "*" list has since rolled off. Reviewing both levels together, rather than just the "*" key, is necessary to recover the full file-interaction history for a specific extension of interest. Capacity: the "*" key holds the 20 most recently accessed files of any extension, and each per-extension subkey separately holds its own 20 most recent entries for that extension.

File and Folder Opening.name: Recent Files
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Records documents and folders recently opened through File Explorer / common Open-Save dialogs, organized both as one flat MRU list and as per-file-extension subkeys, plus a dedicated Folder subkey for recently opened folders.
key_fields: RecentDocs (root) - numbered binary values holding the filename plus associated .lnk shortcut data, ordered by the root MRUListEx
RecentDocs\.<ext> subkeys - one per file extension (e.g. .docx, .pdf, .xlsx) with their own numbered values and MRUListEx, recording only files of that extension
RecentDocs\Folder subkey - recently opened folders, with its own MRUListEx
MRUListEx - binary DWORD-array value giving access order (most recent first) at each level
Key LastWrite time - approximates when the most recently listed item was opened
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Extension subkeys matching the applications the user regularly works with (Office documents, PDFs, images), with entries for files stored in expected user-profile locations.
anomalies: Extension subkeys appearing for file types the user does not normally work with (e.g. .zip, .rar, .7z, .ps1, .vbs, .hta) around the time of an incident
Entries referencing files in Temp, Downloads, or AppData paths rather than typical document locations
Filenames referencing sensitive data categories (finance, HR, credentials) opened by an account with no business reason to access them
RecentDocs entries with no corresponding file present in the file system and no plausible legitimate deletion, especially paired with other exfiltration-staging evidence
The root RecentDocs MRUListEx/order inconsistent with the per-extension subkeys' order, suggesting one was edited without the other
parsing_tools: KAPE: e.g. kape.exe --msource source-volume --mdest output-folder --module RECmd_UserActivity --mef csv
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Entries persist after the referenced file is deleted, so RecentDocs commonly outlives the evidence it points to and is a good source for reconstructing what files existed even after cleanup. The key's LastWrite time only reflects the most recent addition across the whole key structure, so establishing a precise timeline for older entries requires the MRUListEx ordering rather than timestamps alone.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: Capacity: the root RecentDocs key retains the 150 most recently opened files/folders overall; each per-extension subkey retains its own 20 most recent entries (30 for the Folder subkey, or files without an extension). A file can still show up in its extension subkey after it has aged out of the root 150-item list, so check both levels rather than the root alone.

File and Folder Opening.name: Shell Bags
File and Folder Opening.location: Windows XP: NTUSER.DAT: Software\Microsoft\Windows\ShellNoRoam\BagMRU and \Bags. Windows Vista and later: NTUSER.DAT: Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU and \Bags, plus UsrClass.dat: Software\Classes\Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU and \Bags
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Stores Windows Explorer's per-folder view preferences (icon size, view mode, window position). As a side effect of tracking which folder each preference belongs to, it preserves a record of every folder a user has browsed in Explorer, including folders on removable media, network shares, and mounted volumes that no longer exist on the system.
key_fields: BagMRU - a tree of numbered subkeys mirroring the folder hierarchy the user navigated (each numbered key = a path segment), with binary shell item ID list data encoding the folder name and, for many item types, timestamps
MRUListEx (in each BagMRU node) - binary value giving the access order of child folders at that level
NodeSlot - value inside a BagMRU node linking it to its corresponding view-settings entry under Bags
Bags\{slot}\Shell - view mode, icon size, sort column, and window position/size for the referenced folder
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: A tree reflecting the user's ordinary folder navigation habits: profile folders, Documents/Downloads/Desktop, commonly used application data folders, and drive letters the user routinely opens.
anomalies: Shellbag entries referencing removable drives, mounted encrypted volumes, or network shares that are no longer present on the system and have no corresponding entry in current MountPoints2/USBSTOR-if the volume genuinely never existed on this host, this points to remnants worth cross-referencing
Folder paths referencing staging directories, archive tool output, or exfiltration-style naming shortly before a data-loss event, even though the folder itself has since been deleted
Shellbag entries for folders on a device that was connected only briefly or outside expected business hours

A gap in shellbag timestamps/structure inconsistent with the account's normal usage pattern, suggesting selective deletion of BagMRU/Bags entries (uncommon since most cleanup tools do not target these keys)
Folder access evidence in shellbags with no corresponding Prefetch, RecentDocs, or Jump List activity, indicating the folder was browsed but its contents were not opened through the expected channels
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Shellbags are not commonly targeted by mainstream privacy-cleaner tools, so they frequently retain folder-access history well after the corresponding files, folders, or removable/network volumes are gone-making them one of the more resilient sources of historical folder-browsing evidence. They exist in two hive locations (NTUSER.DAT and UsrClass.dat on Vista+), so an incomplete acquisition that only captures one hive will miss part of the picture.

File and Folder Opening.name: Shortcut (LNK) Files
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Auto-created shortcuts to recently opened files/folders, encoding target path, volume serial, and MAC timestamps of the target at time of access.
key_fields: Target full path
Volume serial number
TrackerDataBlock (machine ID / MAC address)
Target MAC timestamps embedded at creation
Explorer's Recent folder UI shows roughly the ~149 most recent LNK files to the user, though many more may actually exist in the folder and are accessible via the command line or forensic tools
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Shortcuts correspond to documents/programs the user has opened, consistent with normal work patterns.
anomalies: LNK pointing to a target on removable media matching an unauthorized USBSTOR entry
LNK referencing a file staged in a temp/exfil directory
parsing_tools: LECmd (Eric Zimmerman): e.g. LECmd.exe -d "%AppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent" --csv output-folder --csvf LNK.csv
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Persists after the target file is deleted, preserving path and volume evidence; the TrackerDataBlock MAC address can help attribute the originating machine when a file was moved across systems.
File and Folder Opening.interpretation: A LNK file is created whenever a file or folder is created or opened, and Windows also creates LNK files for the parent and grandparent folders in the same operation, so the mere existence of a LNK file does not by itself prove the target file was actually opened, nor whether its contents were modified. Always interpret alongside other artifacts (Jump Lists, MRU keys) rather than in isolation.

File and Folder Opening.name: Clipboard History
File and Folder Opening.os_min: Windows 10 version 1809 (October 2018 Update) for local Clipboard History (Win+V); Windows 10 version 1803+ for clipboard activity logged into ActivitiesCache.db; Cloud Clipboard sync uses the same infrastructure and requires a Microsoft account
File and Folder Opening.location: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Clipboard\HistoryData\<GUID>\ and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Clipboard\Pinned\<GUID>\ (per-entry Locale/Text/Bitmap payload files, DPAPI-NG protected); %LOCALAPPDATA%\ConnectedDevicesPlatform\<user>\ActivitiesCache.db (Windows Timeline database, also records clipboard sync activity); HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Clipboard (EnableClipboardHistory, EnableCloudClipboard DWORD values); HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System (AllowClipboardHistory policy DWORD)
File and Folder Opening.purpose: Retains multiple past clipboard entries (text, HTML, and small bitmaps) beyond the single most-recent item accessible via Win+V, and can sync entries to other signed-in devices through Cloud Clipboard, extending how long and how widely copied data remains exposed.
key_fields: EnableClipboardHistory (HKCU DWORD)
EnableCloudClipboard (HKCU DWORD)
AllowClipboardHistory (HKLM policy DWORD)
HistoryData/<GUID> and Pinned/<GUID> subfolders
Locale/Text/Bitmap base64-named payload files per entry
StartTime / ExpirationTime (ActivitiesCache.db)
ClipboardPayload (base64-encoded content, ActivitiesCache.db)
Payload (source application of the copy, ActivitiesCache.db)
ActivityType (10 = resides in clipboard, 16 = copy/paste, ActivitiesCache.db)
File and Folder Opening.normal_baseline: Feature is off by default. When enabled, up to 25 items are retained (text under 4 MB per entry, small bitmaps and HTML); unpinned items age out as new ones are copied, pinned items persist until manually unpinned, and cloud-synced items expire from the remote cache after roughly 12 hours.
anomalies: EnableClipboardHistory or EnableCloudClipboard toggled on shortly before sensitive data is copied and off again afterward
Clipboard History enabled on a server or kiosk-type endpoint with no legitimate multi-device workflow
HistoryData/Pinned folders contain data while the registry shows history currently disabled, indicating recent use followed by disabling
Bulk ClipboardPayload rows in ActivitiesCache.db correlating with credential, key, or financial-data copy events
History folders emptied while other artifacts on the same account show an active session (manual anti-forensic wipe)
parsing_tools: Nirsoft DataProtectionDecryptor (legacy DPAPI only; does not decrypt DPAPI-NG-protected history)
File and Folder Opening.anti_forensic_notes: Unpinning an item deletes its folder outright with no tombstone or Recycle Bin entry, so unpin timing cannot be reconstructed from the file system alone. Disabling Clipboard History after the fact does not purge previously written HistoryData/Pinned files, but toggling EnableClipboardHistory off before a sensitive copy prevents any entry from ever being written. Content is protected with DPAPI-NG, so offline decryption generally requires the user's credentials or domain key material.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: $LogFile (NTFS Transaction Log)
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: Implements NTFS's write-ahead logging for metadata operations, recording redo/undo records for filesystem transactions (creates, renames, deletes, attribute and index changes) so the volume can be rolled forward or back to a consistent state after a crash. Forensically it is a short-lived but very high-fidelity record of the most recent filesystem activity.
key_fields: Log Sequence Number (LSN) - identifies and orders each transaction record
Redo/Undo operation pairs - describe the specific metadata change being journaled (e.g., an attribute update or an index entry add/delete)
Transaction records referencing MFT record numbers and the specific attribute types affected (e.g., $STANDARD_INFORMATION, $FILE_NAME, $INDEX_ALLOCATION)
RCRD page headers containing the NTFS restart/log-area structures
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: A relatively small, constantly-recycled ring buffer of the most recent metadata transactions; on an active system it typically covers only minutes to a few hours of activity before being overwritten, so its normal state is mostly recent, routine metadata churn.
anomalies: Recovered $LogFile records showing a file create, rename, and delete sequence for the same object within a very short window - consistent with a dropper or wiper cleaning up after itself

A $LogFile transaction record referencing an MFT entry/attribute change with no corresponding entry left in the live MFT, indicating the live artifact was altered or the underlying record removed after the fact
Redo records showing repeated $FILE_NAME or $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute rewrites clustering around a known intrusion timeframe, corroborating a timestomping finding surfaced in the MFT
Index-related transaction records showing the same directory entry added and removed in rapid succession, consistent with an attempt to hide a file by briefly moving it in and out of a directory
parsing_tools: MFTECmd (Eric Zimmerman, $LogFile support via the -f option)
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: $LogFile is a small, actively recycled ring buffer, so its window of coverage is short and normal system activity naturally overwrites older transactions - the absence of an expected transaction is not by itself proof of tampering. Because it records transactions independently of the MFT and USN Journal, it can corroborate or contradict those artifacts after they have been altered, but only if the volume is imaged quickly, before routine churn recycles the relevant log pages.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: Master File Table ($MFT)
Filesystem Artifacts.location: \$MFT (root of every NTFS volume; not directly accessible via normal file APIs while the volume is mounted)
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: The MFT is the core NTFS structure holding one (or more) records per file and directory on the volume, including its attributes, timestamps, size, and data location. It is the primary source for filesystem timeline reconstruction and for detecting timestomping.
key_fields: $STANDARD_INFORMATION ($10) attribute - MACB timestamps (Modified, Accessed, Created, MFT-entry-modified); settable by any user-mode process via Win32 APIs like SetFileTime

$FILE_NAME ($30) attribute - a second, independent set of MACB timestamps plus the parent directory reference; written only by the kernel and not reachable through standard Win32 timestamp-modification APIs
MFT record header - record number, sequence number, and an in-use flag distinguishing allocated from deleted records
$DATA attribute - resident (small files stored inline in the MFT record) or non-resident (data runs pointing to clusters) file content
Allocated size vs. real (actual) size fields
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: $SI and $FN timestamps for the same file are close together and consistent with when the file entered its current directory (they are written together at creation), and timestamp deltas track plausible install, build, or download times for that path.
anomalies: $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps earlier than the corresponding $FILE_NAME timestamps on the same file - the classic timestomping signature, since most timestomping tools and the SetFileTime API only reach $SI

$FILE_NAME timestamps that also look forged (e.g., matching an unusually round or historical date), indicating 'double timestomping' where both attributes were rewritten to defeat a simple $SI/$FN comparison
MFT record flagged not-in-use (deleted) with attribute data still resident and recoverable, especially when it correlates with a USN Journal delete-reason record at a matching time
Create time for a security-relevant executable inconsistent with the OS build/install baseline expected for that path (e.g., a System32 binary 'created' years after the OS was installed)

Nanosecond component of $SI timestamps reading exactly zero across many otherwise unrelated files - a weak, heuristic indicator of automated timestamp-setting tooling, prone to false positives and not conclusive on its own
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: Standard timestomping tools and the Win32 SetFileTime API only reach $STANDARD_INFORMATION, so comparing $SI against $FN exposes most cases - but 'double timestomping' that also rewrites $FILE_NAME defeats this comparison, and if a timestomped file is later moved or renamed, Windows copies the (already-forged) $SI times into a freshly written $FN attribute, erasing the discrepancy entirely. Deleted-file MFT records are frequently overwritten as the volume reuses space, so the window to recover a deleted entry's full attribute set shrinks over time, making correlation with the USN Journal and $LogFile necessary once the live MFT record itself has been reused.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: Zone.Identifier ADS (Mark of the Web)
Filesystem Artifacts.os_min: Introduced with Internet Explorer; ADS format standardized further by Windows 10
Filesystem Artifacts.location: Alternate Data Stream on the downloaded file: <filename>:Zone.Identifier:$DATA
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: Marks files originating from the internet (or other untrusted zones) so Windows/Office apply extra security prompts (Protected View, SmartScreen).
key_fields: ZoneId (0=Local Machine, 1=Intranet, 2=Trusted Sites, 3=Internet, 4=Untrusted)
ReferrerUrl
HostUrl
HostIpAddress (Windows 10+)
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: Downloaded files carry ZoneId=3 with a HostUrl matching a known, expected source.
anomalies: Executable or script with ZoneId=3 and a HostUrl pointing to a known malicious-tool distribution or paste site
MOTW-bearing file with the Unblock checkbox cleared shortly before execution, indicating deliberate bypass
parsing_tools: dir /r (legacy) or forensic ADS-aware tools (FTK Imager, X-Ways)
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: Transferring a file to/from a non-NTFS filesystem (FAT32, network transfer that doesn't preserve ADS, or extraction from certain archive formats) strips the ADS and the mark along with it, so its absence does not prove local origin.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: NTFS $STANDARD_INFORMATION Timestamp Behavior Rules
Filesystem Artifacts.os_min: Behavior documented for Windows 10 v1903 and Windows 11 v22H2 (SANS FOR500 poster testing). Varies by OS version and action combination on other builds
Filesystem Artifacts.location: Not a location itself: this is a reference matrix describing how the $MFT's $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute (Modified/Access/Creation/Metadata-change, i.e. MACE) changes under common file operations. See the `mft` artifact for where this data physically lives.
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: Documents exactly which of the four $STANDARD_INFORMATION timestamps (Modified, Access, Creation, Metadata/MFT-entry-change) update, stay unchanged, or get inherited from the source file for each common file operation (creation, access, modification, rename, local move, volume move via CLI, volume move via cut/paste, copy, deletion). The single most load-bearing reference for timeline reconstruction and timestomping detection.
key_fields: File Creation: Creation/Metadata/Modified all set to time of creation; Access set to time of creation (Win11 access time may differ by a few seconds from actual activity)

File Access: only Access updates (to time of access); on Windows 11 with the system volume over 128 GiB, Access may show No Change at all due to the last-access-update throttling introduced in that build
File Modification: Modified and Metadata update to time of data modification; Creation stays unchanged
File Rename: only Metadata updates (to time of rename); Modified/Creation/Access unchanged
Local File Move (same volume, Explorer or CLI): only Metadata updates (to time of move); Modified/Creation/Access unchanged
Volume File Move via CLI (cross-volume, command line): Creation, Access, and Metadata all update to the time of the move; Modified is inherited from the original
Volume File Move via cut/paste in Explorer (cross-volume): Access and Metadata update to time of cut/paste; Modified and Creation are inherited from the original
File Copy (new file created): Access, Creation, and Metadata all set to time of copy; Modified is inherited from the original file
File Deletion (Shift+Delete): no $STANDARD_INFORMATION change at all on the now-deleted MFT record. Modified/Access/Creation/Metadata remain exactly as they were before deletion
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: Timestamp deltas across an evidence file's MACE values are internally consistent with one of the operation patterns above. E.g. a file with Creation and Modified times that differ, and a Metadata time matching neither, is consistent with an ordinary copy rather than tampering.
anomalies: $STANDARD_INFORMATION Creation time later than the $FILE_NAME attribute's creation time for the same MFT record. The classic timestomping signature, since common timestomp tools rewrite $SI but not $FN
A timestamp pattern that matches none of the known operation signatures above for the OS in use (e.g. Modified predating Creation with no corresponding move/copy/rename context)
Batch of files sharing suspiciously identical MACE values inconsistent with individual creation/access history, suggesting a scripted timestamp-setting tool rather than organic use
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: This behavior is highly version- and action-specific (the SANS poster itself documents meaningful differences between Windows 10 v1903 and Windows 11 v22H2 for the same operations), so rules here are heuristics for common actions, not guarantees. Always validate against the specific OS build and exact action sequence when the finding is load-bearing for a case. Attackers who timestomp $SI but leave $FN untouched are still caught by comparing the two attributes.
Filesystem Artifacts.interpretation: Read as: given an observed MACE pattern on a file, work backward to the most likely operation that produced it, then check whether that operation is consistent with the rest of the case timeline. Windows 11 introduces two specific quirks worth remembering: (1) Access time updates can be fully suppressed if the system volume exceeds 128 GiB, so a static-looking Access time on Win11 does not by itself prove the file was never accessed; (2) some Access-time updates on Win11 (e.g. after data modification or rename) were observed to differ from the true activity time by up to a few seconds, so treat Win11 Access times as approximate, not exact, when timing precision matters. Cross-reference the `mft` artifact for the $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME structural distinction that makes timestomp detection possible in the first place.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: USN Journal ($UsnJrnl)
Filesystem Artifacts.os_min: Windows 2000 (present but not enabled by default until Windows Vista, which enables it by default on NTFS volumes)
Filesystem Artifacts.location: \$Extend\$UsnJrnl (root of the NTFS volume, inside the $Extend system directory); change records live in the alternate data stream $UsnJrnl:$J, with sizing/config metadata in $UsnJrnl:$Max
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: A per-volume, append-only log of file and directory create, delete, rename, and modification-type changes, recorded independently of the MFT. It provides a durable, sequential record of filesystem activity that often survives after the underlying file or its MFT entry is gone.
key_fields: USN (Update Sequence Number) - the byte offset of the record within the $J stream, monotonically increasing

Reason - bitmask of change-reason flags, e.g. USN_REASON_FILE_CREATE (0x100), USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE (0x200), USN_REASON_DATA_OVERWRITE (0x1), USN_REASON_RENAME_OLD_NAME (0x1000), USN_REASON_RENAME_NEW_NAME (0x2000), USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE (timestamp/attribute change)
FileReferenceNumber / ParentFileReferenceNumber - link the record to its MFT entry and parent directory, used to reconstruct full paths
Timestamp - the time the change was recorded
FileName - the name of the file/directory at the time of that specific record; a rename appears as an old-name record immediately followed by a new-name record
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: A high-volume, continuously scrolling record of routine file activity (temp file churn, application writes, OS updates) consistent with expected user and system behavior. Because it is a fixed-size, effectively circular log, older entries are overwritten as new ones are written.
anomalies: A USN_REASON_FILE_DELETE record for a file with no corresponding live or freed-but-intact MFT entry and no matching Recycle Bin $I/$R pair - consistent with a non-Explorer deletion path (e.g., Shift+Delete or a direct deletion API call)

A cluster of USN_REASON_BASIC_INFO_CHANGE records with no accompanying data-write reason, correlating in time with an $SI/$FN timestamp mismatch found in the MFT - two independent sources converging on a timestomping event
RENAME_OLD_NAME/RENAME_NEW_NAME pairs moving an executable from a staging or Temp path into a persistence location (Startup folder, System32) shortly before other execution evidence
A gap in USN sequence numbers larger than the volume's typical churn rate would explain, suggesting the journal was deleted and recreated (fsutil usn deletejournal) to break continuity
A file create immediately followed by a delete for the same name within a very short window, consistent with a dropper writing and then removing a payload
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: An attacker with administrative access can delete and recreate the journal via `fsutil usn deletejournal <volume>`, wiping all prior change history for that volume in one step; because this resets the journal's starting USN, an unexplained discontinuity in the sequence numbers is itself the anti-forensic indicator to look for. The journal's fixed size also means it naturally overwrites its own oldest entries during normal system use, so the absence of activity from further back than the volume's typical churn rate cannot be assumed to be suspicious on its own.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: Volume Shadow Copies (VSS)
Filesystem Artifacts.os_min: Windows XP / Server 2003 (Volume Shadow Copy Service and vssadmin); the Explorer 'Previous Versions' / System Protection restore-point workflow used since Windows Vista
Filesystem Artifacts.location: Mounted via device paths such as \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy<N>; the change-block storage for a volume's shadow copies is kept in the hidden System Volume Information\ directory on that same volume
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: A Windows service that creates point-in-time snapshots of a volume, used by System Restore, backup software, and Explorer's 'Previous Versions' feature. Forensically, a mounted shadow copy lets an investigator browse a volume's file system and registry hives exactly as they existed at an earlier point in time, recovering files and hive states since deleted or modified on the live volume.
key_fields: Shadow copy set ID and creation timestamp, from `vssadmin list shadows`
Originating volume and the resulting shadow copy device path
Full file-system tree captured inside each snapshot, including files since deleted, modified, or overwritten on the live volume
Prior versions of registry hives (SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, NTUSER.DAT) captured inside each snapshot
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: A small number of shadow copies per volume on systems with System Restore/System Protection enabled, created periodically or before driver/OS updates. On many hardened enterprise builds and some consumer configurations, System Restore is disabled entirely and no shadow copies exist at all, which is itself unremarkable.
anomalies: All shadow copies for a volume deleted immediately prior to or during a suspected ransomware or destructive-attack timeframe
Command-line or process telemetry showing `vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet`, `wmic shadowcopy delete`, or a PowerShell `Get-CimInstance Win32_ShadowCopy | Remove-CimInstance` invocation
Shadow copy storage association resized to an unusually small maximum via `vssadmin resize shadowstorage`, causing older snapshots to be silently pruned

diskshadow.exe (a legitimate, Microsoft-signed backup utility) invoked interactively or via script outside of any known backup job - a common technique used to delete shadow copies while evading vssadmin-specific detection rules
A shadow-copy-capable volume showing zero shadow copies on a host where organizational baseline/policy expects System Protection to be enabled
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting the VSS catalog via vssadmin, WMI, or diskshadow removes the enumerable shadow copy set, but the underlying change-block data in System Volume Information is not necessarily zeroed and may still be recoverable through raw carving until overwritten by subsequent disk activity. Because VSS deletion is a near-universal precursor to ransomware detonation, its presence is high-signal - but a system where System Restore was already disabled will show no shadow copies for entirely benign reasons, so absence alone should not be conflated with an attacker's deletion without corroborating command-line or event evidence.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: NTFS $Extend Metadata Files
Filesystem Artifacts.location: \$Extend\$ObjId (hidden NTFS metadata file, volume root); \$Extend\$Quota (hidden NTFS metadata file, volume root)
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: Two of the metadata files inside NTFS's hidden $Extend system directory: $ObjId maintains a distributed link-tracking object-ID index so files/directories can be located after being moved or renamed, and $Quota records per-user disk quota usage/limits; both can support user-activity reconstruction independent of the $MFT.
key_fields: $ObjId: Object ID (GUID) per file, Birth Volume ID, Birth Object ID, Birth Domain ID (via the $O index attribute)
$Quota: SID of quota owner, quota used, quota threshold/limit
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: $ObjId entries exist for files/folders touched by Distributed Link Tracking-aware applications (e.g., Office documents, shell shortcuts) or reparse-point operations; $Quota is typically empty/unused unless disk quotas were explicitly enabled by an administrator.
anomalies: $ObjId entry for a file that no longer exists on the volume, or whose current MFT record shows a different object ID, indicating it was moved/renamed/deleted after being tracked
Object ID entries matching known malicious file names/paths despite the file itself being absent from disk
Unexpected population of $Quota on a system where quotas were never administratively configured
parsing_tools: The Sleuth Kit (istat, fls) to locate/dump the $Extend directory's MFT records
MFTECmd (Eric Zimmerman) to parse the containing $MFT records
hex/binary editor for manual $O index attribute analysis
