Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: Because $ObjId tracks object identity independently of file name/path, it can retain a record of a file's prior identity even after an attacker renames or relocates it to evade filename-based detection; deleting the $Extend files themselves requires raw disk access and is not a normal user-level operation.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS)
Filesystem Artifacts.location: Any NTFS file or directory, addressed via filename:streamname syntax (e.g., dir /r, PowerShell Get-Item -Path file.txt -Stream *); enumerable through the $MFT's $DATA attribute entries carrying a named stream identifier
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: General mechanism for attaching arbitrary named data streams to an NTFS file beyond its default unnamed data stream; used by adversaries to hide executable payloads, scripts, or other data from casual directory listings and to execute code directly from a stream.
key_fields: Parent file path
Stream name
Stream size
Stream data/content
Associated $MFT record's $DATA attribute list
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: Legitimate ADS usage is common and mostly benign, e.g. Zone.Identifier streams added by browsers/Outlook to downloaded files, or bookkeeping streams added by some applications; most files carry only the default stream plus at most a MOTW zone marker.
anomalies: Non-Zone.Identifier named streams containing a PE executable header (MZ) or script content (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript)
Streams attached to files in Temp/Downloads/user-profile paths that are significantly larger than a typical MOTW marker
Process creation where the image path includes a colon-delimited stream name, indicating direct execution from an ADS
Sysmon Event ID 15 (FileCreateStreamHash) entries generated by non-browser, non-installer processes
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: ADS content is invisible in Windows Explorer and standard directory listings without stream-aware tools; copying a file to a non-NTFS volume (FAT32, most removable media, many cloud-sync clients) silently strips all alternate streams, which attackers can exploit to both hide payloads and later destroy evidence of them.

Filesystem Artifacts.name: WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) Artifacts
Filesystem Artifacts.os_min: Windows 10 version 1607 (Anniversary Update) for WSL1 in beta, generally available at version 1709 (Fall Creators Update); WSL2 requires Windows 10 version 1903 build 18362.1049 or later (ARM64 requires version 2004 build 19041 or later)
Filesystem Artifacts.location: WSL2 per-distro virtual disk: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<PackageFamilyName>\LocalState\ext4.vhdx for classic Microsoft Store-installed distros (newer Store-model distros, e.g. Ubuntu 24.04+, have their VHDX managed internally by the WSL service and abstracted from a fixed AppData path); WSL1 root filesystem: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<PackageFamilyName>\LocalState\rootfs\ (plain NTFS folder tree, no VHDX); Registry: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Lxss\<DistroGUID> (BasePath, DistributionName, Version, State, DefaultUid, Flags); live mounted view: \\wsl$\<DistroName>\ or \\wsl.localhost\<DistroName>\
Filesystem Artifacts.purpose: Identifies where WSL stores each Linux distribution's virtual disk/root filesystem and configuration, which matters because WSL is an increasingly used staging and execution surface for evading Windows-native EDR/AV — Linux-side files, processes, and network activity inside the ext4.vhdx or rootfs run largely outside the visibility of host-based Windows security tooling.
key_fields: BasePath (registry, path to the distro's VHDX or root)
DistributionName (registry, e.g. Ubuntu-22.04)
Version (registry, 1 = WSL1, 2 = WSL2)
State (registry, install status)
DefaultUid, Flags (registry, per-distro config)
PackageFamilyName (Store package identifying the distro app)
ext4.vhdx (WSL2 virtual disk holding the full Linux filesystem)
Filesystem Artifacts.normal_baseline: One Lxss subkey and one corresponding ext4.vhdx (WSL2) or rootfs folder (WSL1) per installed distro on a developer or admin workstation; the VHDX grows over time up to its configured maximum and is not typically present on standard end-user machines that never installed WSL.
anomalies: Lxss registry key and/or ext4.vhdx/rootfs present on a system with no documented developer or administrative need for Linux tooling
Recently created or modified ext4.vhdx with no matching software-install history or change ticket
Distro BasePath pointing outside the normal Packages directory (e.g., a user-writable temp folder or non-standard drive), suggesting a manually imported distro used to avoid Store telemetry
Outbound network connections or process activity attributable to the host with no corresponding Windows-native process, consistent with activity occurring inside the WSL VM
wsl.exe or bash.exe invoked to launch scripts/binaries as an indirect execution path around application control
parsing_tools: TSK/Autopsy or a Linux-capable forensic boot environment (ext4 filesystem parsing)
Registry Explorer (Eric Zimmerman) for the Lxss registry structure
wsl.exe --list --verbose / wsl.exe --export (live triage of installed distros and version)
Filesystem Artifacts.anti_forensic_notes: Because ext4.vhdx is opaque to native Windows filesystem drivers, standard Windows-side triage (MFT parsing, native indexing, most EDR file-scanning) does not see inside it without mounting the VHDX and parsing ext4 directly. Uninstalling a distro removes its Lxss subkey and, depending on method, may leave the VHDX orphaned on disk (recoverable) or delete it outright; either way the registry key's own timestamps can outlive or contradict the VHDX's internal filesystem timestamps.

Memory Forensics.name: Injected Code / Process Hollowing Detection (Malfind)
Memory Forensics.os_min: N/A (RAM capture, any Windows version supported by the analysis tool)
Memory Forensics.location: Not a disk location - identified within a RAM acquisition using Volatility 3's malfind plugin (windows.malfind; renamed to windows.malware.malfind as the malware-related plugins were consolidated under the windows.malware namespace, with the old windows.malfind name deprecated).
Memory Forensics.purpose: Walks each process's Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) tree looking for memory regions whose protection and backing are consistent with injected code - executable-and-writable private memory not backed by any file on disk - and dumps a hex/disassembly preview of the region so an analyst can confirm shellcode, a reflectively-loaded PE, or a hollowed-out legitimate process.
key_fields: Process / PID - the process whose VAD tree contained the suspicious region
Start VPN / End VPN - virtual address range of the flagged VAD
Tag - the VAD's internal tag; VadS or VadF indicates a private allocation with no mapped file (e.g. VirtualAlloc'd memory), as opposed to a normal image-backed Vad/VadImageMap

Protection - the region's memory protection constant; malfind flags EXECUTE+WRITE combinations such as PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, which is abnormal for a legitimately loaded module (normal module code pages are typically PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY or PAGE_EXECUTE_READ)
Hexdump / Disassembly preview - the plugin's rendered preview of the first bytes of the flagged region, used to spot a PE header (MZ), shellcode patterns, or an unpacking stub

Empty-VAD filtering - malfind checks whether a candidate region is entirely paged-out or all-zero and suppresses it, to avoid reporting VADs that match the protection/tag criteria but hold no actual injected content
Memory Forensics.normal_baseline: On a clean system, malfind returns few or no hits; a small number of false positives can occur from legitimate just-in-time compilation (.NET CLR, JVM, browser JS engines) which intentionally allocate executable-writable private memory - these should map to a known JIT-using process and be corroborated before being treated as suspicious.
anomalies: A VAD with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE protection and a VadS/VadF (private, non-image) tag inside a process with no legitimate reason to JIT-compile code - the canonical injected-shellcode or reflective-DLL signature

A flagged region whose hexdump/disassembly preview begins with an MZ/PE header sitting in private (non-image-backed) memory, consistent with a manually-mapped or reflectively-loaded executable rather than one loaded through the normal Windows loader

The main executable's own VAD region (normally image-backed) showing content inconsistent with the on-disk file, or a mismatch between the process's reported image path and the actual code present at its base address - consistent with process hollowing, where a legitimate process is started suspended and its original image is unmapped and replaced

Cross-referencing a malfind hit's PID against windows.pslist/windows.psscan to find the process is otherwise unremarkable (normal parent, normal path) but carries this one anomalous VAD - typical of injection into an existing benign process rather than a wholly malicious one
Multiple unrelated processes each carrying a similarly-shaped injected VAD (same size, same protection pattern), suggesting a single injection tool or loader was used against several targets
parsing_tools: Volatility 3 - windows.vadinfo / windows.vadyarascan for follow-up VAD inspection and YARA scanning of flagged regions
Memory Forensics.anti_forensic_notes: malfind's detection logic depends on a specific, known-abusable protection/tag combination; malware authors aware of this commonly allocate memory as PAGE_READWRITE, write their payload, then call VirtualProtect to flip it to PAGE_EXECUTE_READ or PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY before execution, which removes the EXECUTE+WRITE combination malfind screens for and causes a false negative - a clean malfind result therefore does not rule out injection and should be paired with manual VAD review (windows.vadinfo) and cross-process handle/thread analysis (windows.handles, windows.threads) rather than trusted alone.

Memory Forensics.name: Command-Line History via Process-Creation Auditing (4688 / Sysmon EID 1)
Memory Forensics.os_min: N/A - Event ID 4688 command-line logging requires Windows Vista/Server 2008 or later plus the specific audit policy below enabled; Sysmon requires separate installation on any supported Windows version.
Memory Forensics.location: Security.evtx (Event ID 4688, Process Command Line field) and/or Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx (Event ID 1, CommandLine field).
Memory Forensics.purpose: This entry documents the mechanism that must be in place for command-line arguments to be captured at process-creation time at all - it is not the general Security or Sysmon event log entry, but specifically what has to be configured (or not) for the Process Command Line / CommandLine field to be populated, and how analysts use that field to reconstruct exactly what an attacker typed or a script executed.
key_fields: 4688 requires two separate settings to show a command line: (1) Audit Process Creation itself, under Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Detailed Tracking - without this, no 4688 events are generated at all; (2) the separate policy 'Include command line in process creation events', under Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > System > Audit Process Creation - without this second setting, 4688 events fire but the Process Command Line field is blank

Registry equivalent of the second setting: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit\ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled (DWORD 1 = enabled); both settings default to Not Configured / disabled out of the box
4688 Process Command Line - the full command line of the newly created process, logged in plain text once both policies above are enabled
4688 New Process Name / Creator Process Name - full image paths of the child and parent processes, correlating via Process ID and Logon ID

Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create) CommandLine and ParentCommandLine fields - captured by default as part of the event schema the moment Sysmon is installed and its configuration does not explicitly filter out Event ID 1; unlike 4688, there is no separate 'include command line' toggle to enable - if Sysmon logs a Process Create event at all, the full command line is in it

Sysmon Event ID 1 also carries ProcessGuid, Hashes (SHA1 by default, or MD5/SHA256/IMPHASH depending on config), and integrity level alongside the command line, giving more built-in context than 4688 for the same event
Memory Forensics.normal_baseline: On a host where both 4688 audit settings are enabled, or where Sysmon is deployed with a config that does not suppress Event ID 1, process-creation events accumulate continuously with plausible command lines matching normal software behavior (installers, browser helper processes, scheduled maintenance scripts) and legible arguments; on a host where only 'Audit Process Creation' is enabled without the command-line addendum, 4688 events exist but every Process Command Line field is empty - a very common and easily overlooked misconfiguration that silently blinds command-line reconstruction while giving the false impression that process auditing is fully enabled.
anomalies: 4688 events present but every Process Command Line field is blank across the board - indicates the 'Include command line in process creation events' policy was never enabled, meaning command-line reconstruction from this host is not possible from 4688 alone regardless of the time period examined
A command line containing encoded/obfuscated content (e.g. powershell.exe -EncodedCommand, base64 blobs, excessive character escaping) used specifically to defeat casual review of the logged text
A command line invoking a living-off-the-land binary (certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, bitsadmin) with arguments inconsistent with that binary's normal administrative use

A gap in 4688 or Sysmon Event ID 1 volume that does not align with any other logged activity stopping - Sysmon or the audit policy may have been reconfigured/tampered with rather than the host simply going idle

Sysmon Event ID 1 present with populated CommandLine while the Security log's 4688 events for the same time window show blank Process Command Line fields - confirms the audit-policy gap above and that Sysmon is the only reliable source of command-line data on that host

A parent-child command-line pair showing a script interpreter (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe) spawned from an Office application, browser, or PDF reader with an unexpected command line - the standard initial-access-to-execution pivot point analysts search for first
Memory Forensics.anti_forensic_notes: An attacker who disables or stops the EventLog service, clears the Security log (which itself generates a 4688-independent 1102 event), or reconfigures/uninstalls Sysmon removes future command-line visibility going forward, but cannot retroactively populate command lines that were never captured because the audit policy addendum was off in the first place - the absence of command-line data on a host is therefore ambiguous between 'never configured' and 'deliberately tampered with' and must be checked against the actual policy/registry state and against whether other event types from the same source continued logging normally.

Memory Forensics.name: Network Connections at Capture Time (Memory Forensics)
Memory Forensics.os_min: N/A (RAM capture, any Windows version supported by the analysis tool)
Memory Forensics.location: Not a disk location - reconstructed from a RAM acquisition using Volatility 3's windows.netscan and windows.netstat plugins.
Memory Forensics.purpose: Recovers TCP/UDP endpoints and TCP listeners that existed in memory at the moment of capture, including connections a live netstat could no longer show because the process had already exited or the socket had closed - giving an analyst a network snapshot tied to the exact moment of acquisition rather than to whenever the host was later examined live.
key_fields: windows.netscan - scans the entire memory image pool allocations (via Volatility's poolscanner) for network object structures, independent of any kernel list; recovers both currently active and recently-closed/terminated connections still resident in memory

windows.netstat - parses the kernel's live TcpPortPool/UdpPortPool (or, on newer builds, TcpCompartmentSet/UdpCompartmentSet) structures the same way the real netstat.exe does; faster but reports only endpoints still tracked by those live structures
Offset - virtual address of the recovered network object structure
Proto - transport protocol (TCPv4, TCPv6, UDPv4, UDPv6)
Local Address / Local Port and Foreign Address / Foreign Port
State - TCP connection state (e.g. LISTENING, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT)
PID and Owner - the owning process ID and its image name, letting a suspicious connection be pivoted directly to the process-list/DLL/handle findings for that PID
Created - the timestamp the connection/listener was created, when recoverable from the structure
Memory Forensics.normal_baseline: Listeners and established connections map cleanly to known services and applications (browser processes with ESTABLISHED connections to expected destination ports, svchost.exe instances LISTENING on expected service ports), with owning PIDs matching the process list produced by pslist/psscan for the same image.
anomalies: An endpoint or listener recovered by windows.netscan that windows.netstat does not report, because netstat only walks the live port-pool structures - the discrepancy itself can indicate a connection whose owning process has since exited or that used a technique bypassing the standard pool tracking

A connection owned by a PID that does not appear at all in windows.pslist/windows.psscan for that same image, indicating the owning process itself was hidden or has since exited, but its network footprint persisted in memory

A well-known process name (svchost.exe, explorer.exe, rundll32.exe) shown as the Owner of an ESTABLISHED connection to an unexpected external address/port, especially over ports not typical for that binary
A LISTENING state on an unexpected local port bound by a process with no legitimate reason to accept inbound connections (backdoor / reverse-shell listener)

Connections whose Owner is blank/unresolvable in netscan output - the underlying object was found by pool signature but its owning EPROCESS pointer could not be resolved, which itself is unusual and worth flagging
Foreign address matching a known C2 IP/CIDR range or a raw IP with no corresponding DNS cache entry elsewhere in the same memory image
Memory Forensics.anti_forensic_notes: Because windows.netscan finds network objects by scanning memory for pool signatures rather than by following any kernel list, it will still surface a connection object even after the owning process exits or a rootkit unlinks the process elsewhere - making memory acquisition timing (as close as possible to the suspected activity) the main lever an analyst has, since a connection's pool allocation can eventually be overwritten/reused by later memory activity and become unrecoverable. windows.netstat, by only walking the live port-pool structures, will show nothing for a connection whose structure has already been torn down, so relying on netstat alone can silently miss activity that netscan would still catch - always run both and diff the results rather than treating either as complete on its own.

Memory Forensics.name: Process List, Handles & Loaded DLLs (Memory Forensics)
Memory Forensics.os_min: N/A (RAM capture, any Windows version supported by the analysis tool)
Memory Forensics.location: Not a disk location - reconstructed from a RAM acquisition (raw memory image, hibernation file, or crash dump) using Volatility 3's windows.pslist, windows.pstree, windows.psscan, windows.dlllist, and windows.handles plugins.
Memory Forensics.purpose: Reconstructs which processes were running at the moment of memory capture, their parent-child relationships, loaded modules, and open handles, by parsing EPROCESS/ETHREAD kernel structures and the process PEB directly out of the memory image. Because several of these plugins locate processes by different mechanisms, comparing their output is the primary way to catch a process a rootkit tried to hide.
key_fields: windows.pslist - walks the kernel's doubly-linked PsActiveProcessHead list (via each EPROCESS's ActiveProcessLinks) to enumerate PID, PPID, process name, thread count, handle count, and create/exit time
windows.pstree - same enumeration as pslist, rendered as a parent-child tree using the recorded PPID/creation-time relationships

windows.psscan - does not trust the active-process list; scans the entire memory image for pool allocations matching the EPROCESS pool tag/structure signature, so it also surfaces unlinked and recently terminated processes
windows.dlllist - per process, walks the PEB's InLoadOrderModuleList (a list of _LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY structures) to list loaded module path, base address, and size

windows.handles - per process, enumerates the open handle table and reports handle type (Process, Thread, Key, Event, Mutant, Token, File, Section, etc.), the target object, and access rights; filterable by object type
PID / PPID - process and parent process ID (both are simply reused numbers in Windows and can be spoofed by an attacker's chosen parent)
Offset (virtual) - the EPROCESS structure's memory address, useful for direct correlation between plugin outputs and for volshell follow-up
Memory Forensics.normal_baseline: pslist, pstree, and psscan agree on the same set of processes and PIDs; every process has a plausible parent (e.g. explorer.exe under a userinit/logon chain, svchost.exe under services.exe), loaded DLLs match what the executable and its known dependencies would load, and handle counts are unremarkable for the process type.
anomalies: A process visible in windows.psscan's raw pool scan but absent from windows.pslist's linked-list walk - the classic signature of a rootkit that used Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) to unlink the EPROCESS from PsActiveProcessHead while the process's threads kept running

A process name mimicking a legitimate system binary but running from an unexpected path (e.g. svchost.exe outside %SystemRoot%\System32) or with an implausible parent (e.g. lsass.exe or services.exe not spawned by wininit.exe)
windows.dlllist showing a module loaded from a suspicious or non-standard path (temp directory, user profile) inside an otherwise legitimate process, consistent with DLL injection

A process with very few or zero entries in windows.dlllist despite being a normal Windows executable that should have a substantial import list - can indicate manual PEB/module-list unlinking to hide an injected or reflectively-loaded module

windows.handles showing a process holding a handle to lsass.exe with access rights consistent with memory-reading (credential dumping), or holding handles to another unrelated process with PROCESS_VM_WRITE/PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD rights (injection primitives)

PPID mismatch such as a PID reused by an unrelated later process (PPID spoofing), or a shell/office-application process tree where a document viewer or browser is the direct parent of cmd.exe or powershell.exe

psscan surfacing a process that has already exited (terminated) but whose EPROCESS pool allocation has not yet been reused - itself not anomalous, but the executable path, command line, and DLL list of that terminated process can still be extracted and are worth checking against other indicators
parsing_tools: Volatility 3 (Volatility Foundation) - windows.pslist, windows.pstree, windows.psscan, windows.dlllist, windows.handles
volshell (Volatility 3 interactive shell) for manual EPROCESS/PEB inspection
Memory Forensics.anti_forensic_notes: Volatility 3 does not ship a direct equivalent of Volatility 2's psxview cross-view plugin; the cross-view check that psxview automated must be performed manually by diffing the PID sets returned by windows.pslist (linked-list walk) against windows.psscan (raw pool scan) - a PID present in the latter but missing from the former is the strongest single indicator of DKOM-based process hiding. Because psscan finds EPROCESS structures by pool signature rather than by following any list, an attacker who fully unlinks a process from every kernel list Volatility can walk still cannot prevent that process's memory pool footprint from being found by psscan, short of also zeroing/overwriting the EPROCESS pool tag itself, which would typically crash the running process's scheduling.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: ARP Cache
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows XP (caching mechanism changed significantly starting Windows Vista)
Network Activity and Physical Location.location: In-memory neighbor/ARP table maintained by the TCP/IP stack; not written to a file or registry hive. Viewed live via `arp -a` or PowerShell `Get-NetNeighbor` / `netsh interface ipv4 show neighbors`.
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Maps IPv4 addresses on the local subnet to their resolved MAC (link-layer) addresses so the host doesn't re-broadcast an ARP request for every packet; shows which local hosts a machine has actually exchanged Layer 2 traffic with recently.
key_fields: Internet Address (IPv4)
Physical Address (MAC)
Type (dynamic / static / invalid)
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: A short list of entries for the default gateway, local DNS/DHCP server, and any recently-contacted LAN hosts. Under Vista-and-later's RFC 4861-based Neighbor Discovery, entries cycle between Reachable and Stale states rather than aging on a fixed timer.
anomalies: The default gateway's IP resolving to an unexpected MAC address (classic ARP spoofing / on-path attacker indicator)
Unexplained static (permanent) entries added via arp -s that don't correspond to known network hardware
One MAC address mapped to multiple IPs at once, or duplicate/conflicting entries for the same IP
Entries for hosts the asset owner denies contacting, captured during live triage of a suspected lateral-movement incident
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: Purely volatile: the whole table is lost on reboot, and Windows Vista and later moves an unused entry from Reachable to Stale after roughly 15-45 seconds (BaseReachableTime defaults to 30000 ms, randomized per RFC 4861) unless it is re-referenced, so it must be captured live per the RFC 3227 order-of-volatility guidance or the evidence is gone. Windows XP/Server 2003 exposed ArpCacheLife and ArpCacheMinReferencedLife registry values to tune this timing, but Microsoft documents that these values no longer apply from Windows Vista onward, which instead uses Neighbor Unreachability Detection tunable via netsh interface ipv4 set interface ... basereachable=.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Browser URL Parameters
Network Activity and Physical Location.location: Embedded within ordinary browser history URL records (see chrome-edge-browser-artifacts / firefox-browser-artifacts) - not a dedicated artifact store of its own.
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Captures geolocation and network-identification clues leaked within otherwise-ordinary browser history URL parameters - for example, captive-portal sign-in redirects or a Google Maps URL containing geocode/daddr parameters revealing a searched address - that can identify connected networks and approximate physical locations.
key_fields: Mapping-service URL query parameters such as geocode=, daddr=, saddr=, ll=, q= found in History.urls-equivalent tables
Captive-portal redirect URLs recorded in ordinary browsing history, sometimes referencing an AP/SSID identifier
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: Mapping/navigation URLs reflecting the user's genuine, expected routine locations (home, office, known travel); captive-portal redirects only for networks the user is expected to have used.
anomalies: Mapping-service URL parameters resolving to a location inconsistent with the user's claimed whereabouts at the relevant time
A captive-portal redirect URL referencing a network inconsistent with the organization's or user's known network history
Geolocation-revealing URLs clustering around a time window relevant to an investigation, such as immediately before or after a suspected physical security incident
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: This is not a dedicated artifact store - it is a byproduct signal inside otherwise-normal browsing history. Clearing browser history removes it identically to any other history entry (see chrome-edge-browser-artifacts / firefox-browser-artifacts anti-forensic notes), and there is no separate registry- or log-based backup of these URL parameters.
Network Activity and Physical Location.interpretation: Treat this as a byproduct signal inside otherwise-normal browsing history, not a dedicated artifact store of its own - review URL query strings within existing browser history data (mapping services, captive-portal redirects, etc.) for geolocation and network-identification clues rather than expecting a purpose-built artifact location.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: DNS Client (Resolver) Cache
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows 2000 (DNS Client / Dnscache service); Get-DnsClientCache cmdlet requires Windows 8 / Server 2012+
Network Activity and Physical Location.location: In-memory cache maintained by the DNS Client (Dnscache) service; not persisted to disk. Related configuration lives at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache\Parameters (e.g. MaxCacheTtl). Viewed live via `ipconfig /displaydns` or PowerShell `Get-DnsClientCache`.
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Speeds up repeat name resolution by caching successfully resolved DNS answers and negative (failed) lookups, and preloads static mappings from the local Hosts file; records which domain names a host recently attempted or succeeded in resolving.
key_fields: Record Name
Record Type (A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, SRV, etc.)
Time To Live (remaining TTL, seconds)
Data (resolved value)
Status (Success / NotExist / NoRecords)
Section (Answer / Authority / Additional)
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: Entries reflecting the browsing, telemetry, and update domains for applications actually running on the host, each with a TTL counting down from the value the authoritative DNS server supplied; Hosts file entries also appear here as preloaded records.
anomalies: Resolved entries for known C2/malicious domains or high-entropy, DGA-style hostnames
A legitimate domain resolving to an unexpected, attacker-controlled IP (upstream DNS hijack or cache poisoning)
Cache found empty during incident response with no corresponding reboot, suggesting ipconfig /flushdns or Clear-DnsClientCache was run to cover tracks
An unusually large number of distinct subdomains under one parent domain, consistent with DNS-based C2/tunneling
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: Entirely volatile, like the ARP cache: it lives only in the Dnscache service's memory and is wiped on reboot or by ipconfig /flushdns / Clear-DnsClientCache, so it must be collected during live response. A cache that is suspiciously empty on a system clearly used for recent browsing is itself a possible indicator that it was deliberately flushed.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Hosts File
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows 2000 (path has remained stable through current Windows releases)
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Plain-text, manually-maintained IP-to-hostname mapping table that the DNS Client consults before querying any DNS server; lets an administrator, or an attacker, override name resolution for specific domains without touching DNS infrastructure.
key_fields: IP address
Hostname(s) mapped to that address
Optional # comment lines
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: Ships with only commented example lines and, on many systems, a single localhost mapping (127.0.0.1 localhost / ::1 localhost); no active third-party entries.
anomalies: Entries redirecting security-vendor, Windows Update, or telemetry domains to 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 (defense/update crippling)
Entries redirecting a legitimate domain (bank, SSO/MFA provider) to an attacker-controlled IP for credential harvesting, or to localhost specifically to break MFA callback traffic
File modification timestamp falling outside any known admin change window, or the file made hidden/read-only to resist casual edits

Unexpected growth into a long list of redirect entries, which can indicate either malicious blocking/redirection or a legitimate ad-blocking hosts file. Intent must be judged by the specific target domains
parsing_tools: diff against a known-good baseline hosts file
File-integrity monitoring or EDR alerting on writes to the etc\hosts path
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: A plain text file with no built-in audit trail of its own; NTFS timestamp metadata and any file-write telemetry (e.g. Sysmon Event ID 11) are the only artifacts of when it changed, and both can be altered by an attacker with sufficient privilege. Its contents are also preloaded into the volatile DNS client cache, so a redirect may still be visible in ipconfig /displaydns even after the hosts file itself has been reverted.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Network History
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows Vista (NetworkList keys); Interfaces/NetworkCards present since Windows XP
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Identifies networks the computer has connected to, including domain/intranet name, SSID, first and last connection times, and the network gateway's MAC address; covers wired, wireless, and VPN connections.
key_fields: Interfaces\{adapter-GUID}\DhcpDomain - correlates an interface to its network domain
NetworkList\Profiles\{ProfileGUID}\ProfileName, DateCreated, DateLastConnected, NameType
NetworkList\Signatures\Managed|Unmanaged\{signature}\DefaultGatewayMac, ProfileGuid
NetworkList\Nla\Cache entries - cached network location-awareness data
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: A small, stable set of known/expected networks (home, office, approved VPN) with DateLastConnected timestamps consistent with routine use.
anomalies: A Profile/Signature entry for an unfamiliar SSID or gateway MAC appearing around a suspected compromise window
A VPN-type (NameType 0x17) profile the user or organization does not recognize, consistent with attacker-established persistence or a tunnel out of the environment
A gateway MAC address associated with a known public or otherwise unexpected location inconsistent with the user's claimed whereabouts at the time
DateCreated/DateLastConnected values inconsistent with the surrounding activity timeline, suggesting manipulation
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: These keys are populated by the OS only at connection time and hold no lower-level backup - deleting a Profile or Signature subkey removes that network's history entirely. A wired-only host still generates a Profiles/Signatures entry for its wired connection, so the absence of any wireless-type entries here is not by itself conclusive that Wi-Fi was never used; corroborate against wifi-profiles and the WLAN event log.
Network Activity and Physical Location.interpretation: These keys correlate with each other: Interfaces links to NetworkCards/Signatures via the DhcpDomain value, while Signatures and Profiles link to each other via the ProfileGUID value, together building a richer picture of network activity including VPN connections. The MAC address of the gateway for an SSID can assist with device geolocation. NetworkList Profile NameType values: 6 (0x06) = Wired, 23 (0x17) = VPN, 71 (0x47) = Wireless, 243 (0xF3) = Mobile Broadband.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Network Interfaces
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Lists the network interfaces (physical and virtual adapters) available on the system and their last known configuration, including IP addressing, DHCP, and domain information.
key_fields: Interfaces\{adapter-GUID}\IPAddress / DhcpIPAddress / DhcpServer / DhcpDomain / DhcpSubnetMask / Domain
NetworkCards\{index}\Description - the adapter's friendly/descriptive name
NetworkCards\{index}\ServiceName - the interface GUID, mapping this entry back to its Interfaces subkey
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: A stable, expected set of adapter GUIDs (the built-in NIC plus any known VPN/virtual adapters) with IP/DHCP configuration consistent with the organization's known subnets.
anomalies: An unexpected virtual adapter appearing (VPN client, virtualization/tunneling software, or an attacker-installed network proxy tool) shortly before or during suspicious activity
An interface's DhcpDomain/Domain value not matching the organization's expected Active Directory domain, consistent with the host having connected to an untrusted or rogue network
A NetworkCards entry with no corresponding Interfaces GUID subkey, or vice versa, indicating adapter removal or registry inconsistency
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: These keys retain each interface's last-known configuration and subkeys may hold some prior DHCP-lease data depending on how the adapter has been reconfigured over time, but this is not a guaranteed complete history - a removed or re-enumerated (new GUID) adapter's earlier configuration can be lost entirely.
Network Activity and Physical Location.interpretation: The Interfaces key includes the last known IP address plus DHCP and domain information for both physical and virtual adapters, and its subkeys may hold some historical network data. The NetworkCards key provides more descriptive detail on each adapter's availability. The two keys are mapped to each other via the interface GUID value. This is unlikely to represent a fully complete view of every network the host has ever connected to.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Timezone
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Identifies the system's currently configured time zone, needed to correctly interpret event log and other artifact timestamps recorded in local time; System.evtx can supplement this with historical time zone change information.
key_fields: ActiveTimeBias / Bias - offset from UTC in minutes
StandardName / DaylightName - the configured time zone's display names
TimeZoneKeyName - the named time zone (e.g., "Eastern Standard Time")
DynamicDaylightTimeDisabled - whether automatic DST adjustment is disabled
System.evtx Event ID 6013 - logged when the time zone setting changes
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: TimeZoneKeyName matches the system's expected physical location or the organization's standard imaging configuration, and remains stable over the system's operational life.
anomalies: A time zone change shortly before or after suspicious activity, which can be used to confuse timeline analysis or make locally recorded timestamps appear to originate from a different region
TimeZoneKeyName inconsistent with the host's known physical location or the organization's standard build
Repeated Event ID 6013 entries in System.evtx indicating multiple time zone changes within a short period
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: TimeZoneInformation reflects only the currently configured time zone, not a history of prior changes - that history, when it exists, comes solely from System.evtx Event ID 6013 entries, which are subject to the same log-retention and clearing limits as any other event log.
Network Activity and Physical Location.interpretation: Some log files and artifact timestamps can only be correctly interpreted by knowing the system's time zone. Event ID 6013 in System.evtx can provide additional information on historical time zone settings, supplementing the single current-state value stored in the registry.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: WiFi (WLAN) Profiles
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows Vista (Native Wifi / WLAN AutoConfig service and WLAN_profile XML schema)
Network Activity and Physical Location.location: XML files under %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces\{interface-GUID}\{profile-GUID}.xml, one file per saved network per wireless adapter; also queryable live via `netsh wlan show profiles` and `netsh wlan show profile name="SSID" key=clear`.
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Stores every wireless network (SSID) a machine has been configured to connect to, including its authentication/encryption settings and, unless cleared, its pre-shared key. Providing SSID connection history and potential credential recovery.
key_fields: name (SSID / profile name)
connectionMode (auto / manual)
authEncryption (authentication and encryption type)
sharedKey/keyMaterial (the passphrase/key)
sharedKey/protected (true = keyMaterial is DPAPI-encrypted hex; false = keyMaterial is stored as cleartext, as seen in some GPO-deployed profiles)
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: One profile per network the user has genuinely joined (home, workplace, known public hotspots); sharedKey/protected is normally "true", meaning keyMaterial is DPAPI-encrypted and unreadable outside the machine/user context that saved it.
anomalies: A profile for an SSID the user denies ever connecting to (rogue AP / evil-twin association, or a profile silently added by a script or malware)
sharedKey/protected set to "false" with the passphrase stored in cleartext, outside of an expected GPO-managed wireless deployment
A burst of new profile files created in a short time window, consistent with a Wi-Fi credential-harvesting tool run rather than normal user connection behavior
Execution of `netsh wlan show profile ... key=clear` or a wireless key-recovery tool shortly before data staging/exfiltration
parsing_tools: netsh wlan show profiles / netsh wlan show profile name=X key=clear (built-in)
Direct XML review of the Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces path
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: keyMaterial is DPAPI-protected by default (protected="true"), tying decryption to the machine/user context that saved it, which is why recovery is normally done through `netsh ... key=clear` (or an equivalent DPAPI unwrap) run in that same context rather than by reading the XML key material directly. Deleting a saved network removes its XML profile file, and with it the SSID history, leaving only whatever MFT/file-deletion metadata the filesystem retains.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: Windows Firewall Log
Network Activity and Physical Location.os_min: Windows XP (legacy pfirewall.log); Windows Vista+ for the Windows Firewall with Advanced Security event log channel
Network Activity and Physical Location.location: Legacy text log, must be manually enabled and is off by default: %windir%\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log. Rule-change/administrative history: Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Windows Firewall With Advanced Security\Firewall (.evtx).
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Records network traffic Windows Firewall evaluated (dropped and/or allowed connections, once logging is enabled) and, separately in the WFAS event channel, administrative changes to firewall rules and profile state. Used to reconstruct blocked/allowed connection attempts and to detect firewall tampering.
key_fields: date, time
action (ALLOW / DROP)
protocol, src-ip, dst-ip, src-port, dst-port, size
tcpflags, tcpsyn, tcpack, tcpwin, icmptype, icmpcode, info, path (W3C extended log fields in pfirewall.log)
Event ID 2004 (rule added) / 2005 (rule modified) / 2006 (rule deleted) in the WFAS Firewall event channel
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: On a default installation pfirewall.log does not exist at all, because both dropped-packet and successful-connection logging are disabled by default on every profile (Domain/Private/Public). When enabled, entries reflect routine blocked broadcast/scan noise from the local segment plus a low, steady trickle of rule-change events tied to application installs.
anomalies: pfirewall.log present with DROP entries for outbound traffic to known-bad IPs/ports, or unexplained inbound ALLOW entries
A burst of Event ID 2004/2005/2006 entries around the time of an intrusion, especially rules opening high ports or allowing a specific unsigned binary
Firewall log file missing or truncated on a system where logging was known (via GPO) to be enabled, suggesting tampering
Log rolling off at its default 4096 KB cap during a long-dwell intrusion, losing early entries
parsing_tools: PowerShell Import-Csv / text viewer against pfirewall.log
SIEM ingestion (e.g. Microsoft Sentinel Windows Firewall connector)
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: Legacy pfirewall.log logging is off by default for both dropped and successful connections and must be explicitly enabled per network profile; an adversary with admin rights can disable logging, delete the file, or add/remove rules via netsh advfirewall, and the log itself is capped at a small rolling size (default 4096 KB / max 32767 KB, oldest entries deleted first), so its absence proves nothing about whether logging was ever on. The WFAS event log channel records rule-change events (2004/2005/2006) independently of whether text logging is enabled, though clearing that event log is itself recorded as a log-cleared event.

Network Activity and Physical Location.name: WLAN Event Log
Network Activity and Physical Location.purpose: Provides a historical, event-based record of wireless network association attempts and outcomes, complementing the current-state wifi-profiles XML files and the correlatable network-history registry keys.
key_fields: Event ID 11000 - wireless network association started
Event ID 8001 - successful wireless connection
Event ID 8002 - failed wireless connection
Event ID 8003 - wireless disconnect
System.evtx Event ID 6100 - network diagnostics
Network Activity and Physical Location.normal_baseline: Association/connect/disconnect events limited to known, previously approved SSIDs matching the wifi-profiles inventory, with disconnects aligning with expected mobility (leaving the office, device sleep, etc.).
anomalies: 11000/8001 success events for an SSID with no corresponding wifi-profiles XML or network-history Profile entry, suggesting the resulting profile was subsequently deleted
A burst of 8002 failed-connection events against an unfamiliar SSID, consistent with automated or repeated association attempts against a rogue access point or evil-twin network
8001 success events for an SSID matching a known rogue-AP naming pattern that impersonates a legitimate network (e.g., a subtle variation on the organization's SSID)
Association events implying a geographic location inconsistent with the user's claimed whereabouts at that time
Network Activity and Physical Location.anti_forensic_notes: This is a separate, event-log-based record from the wifi-profiles XML files and NetworkList registry keys - deleting a saved Wi-Fi profile or a NetworkList entry does not retroactively remove the association/connect events already written here, making this log a durable cross-check even after profile-level cleanup. Conversely, clearing this operational log removes the association timeline while leaving the current-state profile artifacts intact.
Network Activity and Physical Location.interpretation: Provides a historical record of wireless network connections. The SSID recorded here can be used to correlate against and retrieve additional network information from the Network History registry keys.

Persistence.name: Image File Execution Options / AppInit_DLLs
Persistence.os_min: Windows Vista (IFEO Debugger abuse formalized); AppInit_DLLs from Windows NT
Persistence.location: HKLM\SOFTWARE{\Wow6432Node}\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<executable>\Debugger; AppInit_DLLs at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows
Persistence.purpose: IFEO Debugger value causes a specified debugger/program to launch in place of (or before) the target executable; AppInit_DLLs forces a DLL to load into every process that loads user32.dll.
key_fields: Debugger value under an executable's IFEO key
SilentProcessExit\MonitorProcess value
AppInit_DLLs value list
Persistence.normal_baseline: IFEO keys typically empty or used only by legitimate debugging/compatibility tooling; AppInit_DLLs typically empty on modern systems (deprecated with secure boot).
anomalies: Debugger value attached to an accessibility or security-tool binary (e.g. utilman.exe, taskmgr.exe)
AppInit_DLLs pointing to an unsigned DLL in a user-writable path
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: IFEO abuse can double as defense evasion by attaching an invalid or crashing debugger to security tools, silently disabling them.

Persistence.name: Run / RunOnce Registry Keys
Persistence.purpose: Machine-wide or per-user autostart mechanism executing listed commands at logon/boot.
key_fields: Value name
Command/executable path
Key (machine vs. user)
Persistence.normal_baseline: Entries match known startup agents (AV, cloud sync clients, drivers).
anomalies: Entry pointing to a script interpreter with an encoded argument
New entry in a user-writable path added outside a software install event
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Trivially removed by deleting the value; correlate against SOFTWARE/NTUSER.DAT hive backups (RegBack) to detect since-deleted entries.

Persistence.name: Scheduled Tasks
Persistence.os_min: Windows Vista (XML tasks); legacy .job on XP
Persistence.location: C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\<TaskName> (XML); registry mirror at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tree and \Tasks
Persistence.purpose: Defines actions executed on a schedule or trigger (logon, event, time); a common legitimate and malicious persistence mechanism.
key_fields: Action command/arguments
Trigger definition
Author/principal (execution context)
Task creation/last-run time
Persistence.normal_baseline: Tasks correspond to installed software's update/maintenance routines and OS-native scheduled maintenance.
anomalies: Action node pointing to Temp/AppData with base64-encoded PowerShell arguments
Suspicious repetition interval (e.g. every few minutes)
Task registered without a corresponding Security 4698 event, suggesting log gaps or non-standard creation (e.g. direct XML drop)
parsing_tools: TaskScheduler view + PECmd/Registry Explorer for TaskCache
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: TaskCache registry entries can persist under \Tasks\{GUID} even after the XML file is deleted, useful for timeline reconstruction. Event IDs 4698/4699 require Object Access auditing to be enabled, which many environments lack by default.

Persistence.name: Windows Services (Persistence)
Persistence.purpose: Services configured with Start=2 (auto) or 3 (demand) launch at boot or on demand, commonly abused for SYSTEM-level persistence.
key_fields: ImagePath
Start type
ServiceDll (for svchost-hosted services)
ObjectName (run-as account)
Persistence.normal_baseline: Services correspond to installed hardware drivers and legitimate software.
anomalies: ImagePath pointing to a non-standard directory
svchost-hosted service with an unrecognized ServiceDll
Service created shortly before/after other IOC timestamps
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Services can be created/deleted quickly with sc.exe; correlate with Security event 4697/7045 (System log) for creation evidence when auditing is enabled.

Persistence.name: Startup Folders
Persistence.purpose: Any shortcut or executable placed here launches automatically at user logon.
key_fields: File/shortcut name
Target path (if LNK)
Creation/modification timestamp of the item
Persistence.normal_baseline: Contains only shortcuts placed by legitimate software installers.
anomalies: Unrecognized script or executable dropped directly into the folder
LNK target pointing to a scripting interpreter with suspicious arguments
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Trivially removed by deleting the file; file-system timestamps on the item itself (not just its LNK target) can help date when persistence was planted.

Persistence.name: WMI Permanent Event Subscription
Persistence.os_min: Windows XP (WMI infrastructure); technique common from Windows 7+
Persistence.purpose: Lets code execute automatically when a defined WMI event occurs (e.g. process start, time, logon), providing fileless, reboot-surviving persistence.
key_fields: __EventFilter (Query, QueryLanguage - WQL)
__EventConsumer (CommandLineTemplate or ScriptText)
__FilterToConsumerBinding (links filter to consumer)
Persistence.normal_baseline: Subscriptions correspond to known monitoring/management software (SCCM, AV agents); a subscription is only active when filter, consumer, and binding all exist.
anomalies: CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer with an unrecognized command or obfuscated script
wmic.exe or mofcomp.exe process creating filter/consumer objects
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Leaves no on-disk executable if using a script consumer, making it a favored fileless technique; corroborate with Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational Event ID 5861 and Sysmon Event IDs 19/20/21 for a live-log view of when it was installed or fired.

Persistence.name: BITS Jobs
Persistence.location: %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\qmgr.db (ESE format, Windows 10+); qmgr0.dat / qmgr1.dat (legacy custom format, pre-Windows 10); Event log: Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client/Operational
Persistence.purpose: Stores the queue-manager state of Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) jobs used for asynchronous, throttled file transfers; abused by malware to stage downloads and to gain persistence via a command executed on job completion or error.
key_fields: Job ID (GUID)
Job name
Job owner SID
Job type (download/upload)
Remote URL
Local file path
Job state
NotifyCmdLine (command executed on job completion/error)
Job creation/modification timestamps
Transferred byte counts
Persistence.normal_baseline: Jobs created by Windows Update, Microsoft Store, OneDrive, and other legitimate updaters; short-lived, low in number, pointing to Microsoft or known vendor URLs.
anomalies: NotifyCmdLine pointing to cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or another non-standard binary
Job downloading from a non-Microsoft, newly-registered, or suspicious domain
Long-lived job approaching the 90-day default lifetime with no legitimate owning application
Job created via bitsadmin.exe or PowerShell BITS cmdlets outside normal update windows
Unusually high job volume tied to a single non-standard process
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Job records are removed from the database on completion or cancellation but may persist recoverably in unallocated ESE database pages for a time afterward; bitsadmin /reset or a BITS service restart clears active jobs, and the Bits-Client/Operational event log can be cleared or size-limited to roll evidence out of view.

Persistence.name: COM Hijacking
Persistence.purpose: Registry-based technique that overrides references to a Component Object Model (CLSID) object so a malicious DLL or script loads in place of, or ahead of, the legitimate component when a trusted process instantiates that COM object.
key_fields: CLSID (GUID)
InprocServer32 default value (DLL path)
LocalServer32 default value (EXE path)
ThreadingModel
TreatAs value
ProgID mapping
Key last-write timestamp
Owning hive (HKCU vs HKLM)
Persistence.normal_baseline: CLSID entries under HKLM point to legitimate, digitally signed DLLs/EXEs in %SystemRoot%\System32 or Program Files; HKCU rarely contains CLSID overrides for well-known system CLSIDs.
anomalies: InprocServer32/LocalServer32 pointing to a file in %AppData%, %Temp%, or another user-writable path
HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID entry duplicating a well-known system CLSID normally only defined in HKLM
Unsigned or newly-created DLL referenced by a CLSID belonging to a frequently-invoked shell/COM object
TreatAs key redirecting one CLSID to an unrelated CLSID
Registry key last-write time inconsistent with any known software install
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: HKCU-based hijacks require no administrative privileges and never touch HKLM, leaving no elevated-access trail; the override can be written and deleted around a single execution, and Autoruns does not surface generic COM hijacks, making registry key last-write time and HKCU-vs-HKLM hive comparison the primary detection lever.

Persistence.name: Sticky Keys Backdoor
Persistence.location: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\sethc.exe (also \utilman.exe, \osk.exe, \Magnify.exe, \Narrator.exe, \DisplaySwitch.exe, \AtBroker.exe) — Debugger value
Persistence.purpose: Abuses the Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Debugger value for Windows accessibility binaries, which are launchable pre-authentication at the logon screen (locally or over RDP), so that cmd.exe or another program runs as SYSTEM instead of the legitimate accessibility tool.
key_fields: Debugger (REG_SZ path to the substituted binary, e.g. cmd.exe)
Target accessibility executable (sethc.exe/utilman.exe/osk.exe/Magnify.exe/Narrator.exe/DisplaySwitch.exe/AtBroker.exe)
Key last-write timestamp
GlobalFlag value (if FLG_USE_DEBUGGER is set)
Persistence.normal_baseline: No Debugger value exists under Image File Execution Options for any accessibility-tool executable on a clean system; these binaries run directly with no IFEO entry.
anomalies: Debugger value present under IFEO for any accessibility-tool executable
Debugger value pointing to cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or another non-standard binary
Accessibility binary itself replaced or renamed on disk rather than redirected via IFEO (the older variant of the same technique)
IFEO key present in HKLM (system-wide, pre-auth) with no corresponding legitimate software install
Unexpected SYSTEM-level cmd.exe spawned from winlogon.exe or from the logon screen
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: The modification lives in HKLM\SOFTWARE, so it survives reboot and logoff, but a single add/delete of the Debugger value around the point of use leaves only the key's last-write timestamp as a marker unless Security-log object-access auditing (SACL, Event ID 4657) is enabled on the IFEO key; attackers commonly delete the Debugger value immediately after use to restore the key's normal appearance.

Persistence.name: Application Compatibility Shim Database
Persistence.os_min: Windows XP+ (Application Compatibility Infrastructure); sdbinst.exe and custom shim support remain present through current Windows 10/11
Persistence.location: C:\Windows\AppPatch\Custom\*.sdb (32-bit custom shim databases); C:\Windows\AppPatch\Custom\Custom64\*.sdb (64-bit custom shim databases); registry: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\AppCompatFlags\Custom and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\AppCompatFlags\InstalledSDB
Persistence.purpose: Holds custom Application Compatibility Database (.sdb) files installed via sdbinst.exe, each defining one or more 'shims' that intercept and patch a target executable's behavior at launch — a legitimate backward-compatibility mechanism that can be abused to redirect execution, inject DLLs, or disable protections for persistence.
key_fields: Registry subkey name under Custom/InstalledSDB (SDB GUID, matches the installed .sdb filename)
DatabasePath value (full path to the installed .sdb file on disk)
DatabaseDescription / DatabaseType values
Internal .sdb records: target EXE matching criteria (name/size/checksum) and attached shim/fix names (e.g., InjectDLL, RedirectEXE, DisableNX, DisableSEH)
Persistence.normal_baseline: A small number of vendor- or IT-deployed custom .sdb files registered through sdbinst.exe during legacy line-of-business software installs or OEM/Microsoft compatibility updates; each InstalledSDB/Custom registry entry corresponds 1:1 with a file present on disk.
anomalies: sdbinst.exe execution with no corresponding legitimate installer activity in Prefetch/Amcache
New .sdb file appearing in AppPatch\Custom (or Custom64) without a matching software deployment record
Shim entries referencing InjectDLL, RedirectEXE, DisableNX, or DisableSEH targeted at security tooling or common LOLBins
Registry Custom/InstalledSDB entries with no corresponding file on disk, or vice versa (partial cleanup)
A shim targeting a core system process such as services.exe (documented FIN7/CARBANAK pattern)
parsing_tools: Microsoft Application Compatibility Toolkit / Compatibility Administrator (the GUI counterpart to sdbinst.exe)
Manual binary/hex inspection of the proprietary .sdb format
Persistence.anti_forensic_notes: Running sdbinst.exe /u <GUID> cleanly removes both the on-disk .sdb file and its registry keys, leaving process-execution artifacts (Amcache, Prefetch) as the main residual evidence that sdbinst.exe ever ran; an attacker can also write the AppCompatFlags\Custom/InstalledSDB registry keys and copy the .sdb file directly, bypassing sdbinst.exe entirely and evading process-creation-based detections for the installer itself.

Registry Hives.name: NTUSER.DAT (User Registry Hive)
Registry Hives.os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
Registry Hives.location: Mounted as HKEY_CURRENT_USER while the user is logged on; also reachable as HKEY_USERS\<SID> for a non-interactive profile. File: %UserProfile%\NTUSER.DAT (e.g. C:\Users\<username>\NTUSER.DAT)
Registry Hives.purpose: Root of a single user's registry: mounted as HKEY_CURRENT_USER for the duration of that user's session. Holds per-user application settings and UI preferences and, forensically, a per-user Run/RunOnce autostart location. User-activity artifacts that also live in this hive. UserAssist, RunMRU, TypedPaths, RecentDocs. Are documented as separate artifacts; this entry covers the hive's general role and its own persistence keys.
key_fields: Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and \RunOnce: per-user autostart entries, executed only when that specific user logs on
Software\Classes: per-user COM/file-association overrides layered on top of HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes (the underlying per-user Classes data itself is stored in the separate UsrClass.dat hive)
Volatile Environment: session-specific environment variables (e.g. USERNAME, USERDOMAIN, logon server) recreated at each logon
Hive last-write time and the paired NTUSER.DAT.LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: Per-user Run entries correspond to user-installed, signed applications (chat clients, cloud-sync apps); the hive's last-write time tracks with the account's actual last logoff or sync cycle.
anomalies: A per-user Run/RunOnce entry pointing to a script or binary the profile owner denies installing, especially one staged in %AppData%\Roaming or %AppData%\Local.

NTUSER.DAT's last-write time falling outside any interactive logon recorded for that account in the Security event log, suggesting the hive was modified offline or via a remote/administrative technique rather than by the user themselves.

An NTUSER.DAT file present under a user-profile folder with no corresponding account in the SAM (or SECURITY domain-cache). An orphaned profile from a deleted account, or vice versa, a profile folder with no NTUSER.DAT.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: NTUSER.DAT is fully flushed to disk at logoff or periodic sync; a copy acquired live from a still-logged-on session can miss the most recent writes still held in the in-memory hive unless the .LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs are also collected and replayed. Deleting a user profile removes NTUSER.DAT from its normal location, but Windows.old, Volume Shadow Copies, or backup/roaming-profile stores can retain earlier copies.

Registry Hives.name: SAM (Security Account Manager) Hive
Registry Hives.os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
Registry Hives.purpose: Stores local user account definitions for the machine. RIDs, group memberships, and encrypted password hashes. Plus per-account login metadata. It is unreadable in place even by local Administrator while Windows is running; access requires SYSTEM privileges or an offline copy.
key_fields: SAM\Domains\Account\Users\<RID in 8-digit hex>: one subkey per local account (e.g. 000001F4 = RID 500)
V value: username, full name, comment, and the encrypted LM/NT hash blob
F value: account flags and timestamps: last logon, password last set, account expires, failed-logon count
SAM\Domains\Account\Users\Names: maps account name to RID
SAM\Domains\Builtin\Aliases: builtin group (e.g. Administrators, RID 544) membership
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: RID 500 is the built-in Administrator (often renamed and/or disabled per hardening baselines); RID 501 is the built-in Guest (disabled by default); real user accounts start at RID 1000 and increment sequentially as created. F-value timestamps track plausibly with the account's known usage and the org's password-rotation policy.
anomalies: RID hijacking: the F value of a low-privilege or disabled account (commonly Guest, RID 501) is patched so the account authenticates with the Administrator's RID (500) SID, granting admin rights while `net user`/account-listing tools still show it as Guest.
The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is enabled when the environment's baseline/GPO expects it disabled.
A new local account's RID or last-write time doesn't fit the expected sequential/temporal pattern for how accounts are normally provisioned on that host.
An account newly added to a privileged builtin alias (e.g. Administrators) shortly before or during suspicious activity.
F-value 'last logon' or 'password last set' timestamps inconsistent with the account's known usage window.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: Password hashes in the SAM are encrypted with a boot key derived from the paired SYSTEM hive; a SAM hive collected without its matching SYSTEM hive cannot be decrypted. Attackers with SYSTEM-level access can dump SAM via `reg save`, Volume Shadow Copies (bypassing the live file lock), or in-memory extraction (e.g. Mimikatz lsadump::sam), leaving little or no on-disk trace beyond the access itself. RID hijacking abuses the F-value structure directly, so it will not show up in standard account-enumeration output and requires binary inspection of the F value to detect.

Registry Hives.name: SECURITY Hive
Registry Hives.os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
Registry Hives.location: HKLM\SECURITY (file: %SystemRoot%\System32\config\SECURITY): not readable in place even by local Administrator; requires SYSTEM privileges
Registry Hives.purpose: Stores the Local Security Authority's policy database: the effective local audit policy, LSA secrets (service-account passwords, autologon password, machine account secret), and cached domain-logon credentials used when a domain controller cannot be reached.
key_fields: Policy\Secrets\<name>: encrypted LSA secrets (service-account credentials, machine account secret, autologon password)
Policy\PolSecretEncryptionKey: LSA key material, combined with the SYSTEM hive's boot key to decrypt Secrets
Policy\PolAdtEv: binary-encoded effective audit policy that LSASS consumes
Cache\NL$1 through NL$10: DCC2/MSCache v2 cached domain-credential hashes (Windows Vista and later)
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: Cache slots (NL$x) are populated only on domain-joined systems that log on while off-network; Policy\Secrets contains only entries tied to known, installed services or scheduled-task run-as accounts; the audit policy reflected in PolAdtEv matches the organization's GPO baseline.
anomalies: PolAdtEv reflects fewer audit categories enabled than the organization's GPO baseline defines. E.g. process-creation or logon auditing disabled locally shortly before other suspicious activity, blinding downstream logging.
New or unexpected entries under Policy\Secrets that aren't tied to any known installed service (possible credential staging/harvesting).
Cache entries present on a system that isn't supposed to be domain-joined.
A Cache slot's last-write time with no corresponding logon event in the Security event log.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: The SECURITY hive has no SACL configured by default, so routine access to LSA Secrets (e.g. via Mimikatz lsadump::secrets) generates no Security event log entries unless an analyst has proactively set an audit SACL on the key beforehand (which then generates Event ID 4656/4663 on access). MSCache v2 (DCC2) hashes cannot be used in pass-the-hash attacks and only yield a plaintext password via offline cracking, so their mere presence indicates exposure risk rather than confirmed compromise.

Registry Hives.name: SOFTWARE Hive
Registry Hives.os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
Registry Hives.purpose: Stores machine-wide installed-application data, OS version/build identity, and system-wide autostart (Run/RunOnce) persistence locations that apply to every user of the machine.
key_fields: Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and \RunOnce: machine-wide autostart command lines (REG_SZ/REG_EXPAND_SZ), run at every user logon
Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\<AppGUID or Name>: DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallDate, UninstallString, InstallLocation
Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion: ProductName, CurrentBuildNumber, InstallDate, RegisteredOwner
Wow6432Node mirror of the above Run/Uninstall keys, holding 32-bit software entries on 64-bit Windows
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: Run/RunOnce entries correspond to known, digitally-signed vendor software (AV agents, GPU tray utilities, cloud-sync clients) launched from Program Files. Uninstall entries match software the organization actually deployed, with plausible InstallDate and Publisher values.
anomalies: A Run or RunOnce value pointing to an executable or script in a user-writable path (%Temp%, %AppData%, Downloads) instead of Program Files.
A Run key value invoking powershell.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe, or rundll32.exe with an encoded or heavily obfuscated argument string. A common Registry Run Key persistence pattern.

An Uninstall key entry with no corresponding installed files on disk, or an InstallDate immediately followed by execution of its own UninstallString. Suggesting a dropper that installs, runs, and removes its own uninstall metadata to reduce visibility.
An Uninstall entry's Publisher/DisplayName spoofing a well-known, trusted vendor.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: RunOnce values are deleted by Windows automatically once the referenced command has executed, so a RunOnce-based dropper leaves nothing behind in this key after it fires. Its absence is expected behavior, not evidence of tampering, and must be correlated with Prefetch or event-log data instead. An attacker may also manually delete a Run value once a longer-term persistence mechanism (e.g. a scheduled task or service) has taken over, leaving only the key's last-write time as a narrow window of evidence.

Registry Hives.name: SYSTEM Hive
Registry Hives.os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
Registry Hives.purpose: Stores machine-wide configuration needed to boot and run Windows, kept as multiple redundant ControlSets. This entry focuses on services/drivers, network configuration, and hardware (USB) enumeration data; BAM and Shimcache also live under this hive but are documented as separate artifacts.
key_fields: Select\Current: index of which ControlSetNNN is the active configuration this boot
CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>\Start, Type, ErrorControl, ImagePath, DisplayName. Per-service/driver configuration
CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters\Interfaces\<GUID>: DhcpIPAddress, IPAddress, DhcpServer, DhcpDomain (historical network config per interface)

CurrentControlSet\Enum\USBSTOR\<Device Class>\<Serial Number>: USB mass-storage device instance keys, with a first-connect timestamp implicit in key creation and a last-write time on the device subkey
CurrentControlSet\Control\ComputerName\ComputerName: hostname
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: Select\Current typically points to the ControlSet the system last booted successfully with (which ControlSet number that is varies by machine and isn't itself meaningful). Installed services' Start/Type values match their documented purpose and vendor; ImagePath values point into Program Files or System32; USBSTOR entries correspond to devices the user/organization recognizes.
anomalies: A service key with ImagePath pointing to a binary in a user-writable location (%AppData%, %Temp%, C:\Windows\Temp) rather than Program Files or System32.
Start value changed to 0x2 (Automatic) on a service that should be Manual (0x3) or Disabled (0x4), so it now persists across reboots.
ImagePath referencing rundll32.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe, or powershell.exe with an encoded or unusually long argument string. Classic service-based LOLBin persistence.
ImagePath on an existing, previously legitimate service silently changed (service hijacking), especially where DisplayName/Description no longer match what the binary actually is.
A USBSTOR device's connect/last-write timestamp falling immediately before a mass file-copy, deletion, or exfiltration event of interest.
Select\Current pointing to a different ControlSet than Select\Default/LastKnownGood around the time of an incident, indicating the system booted into an alternate/recovery configuration.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: Deleting a malicious service key removes it from the active ControlSet's live view, but a non-active ControlSet, registry transaction logs, or unallocated hive slack space can still retain remnants until the hive is compacted. USBSTOR entries are not automatically cleared when a device is removed and persist indefinitely. Their absence for a device an organization or witness says was used is itself suspicious and suggests deliberate key deletion.

Registry Hives.name: UsrClass.dat (User Classes Hive)
Registry Hives.location: Mounted as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes (a per-user view of HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT) while the user is logged on. File: %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\UsrClass.dat (Vista and later; Windows XP path was %UserProfile%\Local Settings\Application Data\Microsoft\Windows\UsrClass.dat)
Registry Hives.purpose: A separate per-user hive, distinct from NTUSER.DAT, that holds the user-specific portion of the Classes registry: per-user COM class registrations and shell-extension data that override or supplement the machine-wide HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes. It is also one of the two locations where Shellbags data is stored (the other being NTUSER.DAT on pre-Vista systems).
key_fields: Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU: folder paths/names visited in Explorer, tracked as a most-recently-used tree
Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Bags: per-folder view settings (window size, position, view mode) referenced by BagMRU entries
CLSID\<GUID> subkeys: per-user COM class registrations (e.g. shell extension handlers, context-menu/property-sheet handlers)
Wow6432Node mirror for 32-bit COM registrations on 64-bit Windows
Registry Hives.normal_baseline: COM/CLSID entries correspond to installed, legitimate applications' shell-extension components (e.g. archive managers, cloud-sync icon overlays); BagMRU/Bags entries reflect folders the user is known to have browsed, including removable and network paths no longer present on the system.
anomalies: A CLSID entry registering a shell extension (context-menu handler, icon handler, property-sheet handler) whose InprocServer32 path points to a binary in a user-writable or unusual location rather than a normal application install directory. A known technique for gaining persistence that loads automatically whenever Explorer touches a file/folder.

BagMRU/Bags entries referencing paths on removable or network volumes that align with known data-staging or exfiltration locations, present even though the volume itself is no longer attached to the system. Proving the folder was browsed at some point regardless of current volume presence.
Shellbags entries showing folder access to a sensitive directory that the account has no legitimate business reason to browse.
Registry Hives.anti_forensic_notes: Shellbags entries in this hive are not tied to a file's own metadata and are not cleared when the referenced folder or volume is deleted or removed, so they can outlive the evidence they point to. An analyst can prove a folder was accessed even after the folder, and the drive it was on, are both gone. Because the hive loads only for its owning user, correlating it correctly requires matching the hive to the right SID/profile.

System Information.name: Computer Name
System Information.purpose: Stores the hostname of the system in the ComputerName value, used to identify the machine on a network and correlate its identity across logs and other artifacts.
key_fields: ComputerName value - the configured hostname, effective from the next reboot
ComputerName\ActiveComputerName\ComputerName - the hostname actually in effect for the current boot session
System Information.normal_baseline: Hostname matches the organization's naming convention and asset inventory, and remains stable for the operational life of the system; ComputerName and ActiveComputerName values agree.
anomalies: Hostname changed shortly before or after other incident indicators, consistent with renaming a compromised host to evade endpoint-name-based detections, blocklists, or analyst attention
Hostname not matching the organization's naming convention, DNS record, or asset inventory for that machine
ComputerName and ActiveComputerName values differing at time of acquisition, indicating a rename was staged but had not yet taken effect (pending reboot) when the system was imaged
Mismatch between the ComputerName registry value and the hostname recorded in logs collected from the same system, indicating the value was changed after those logs were generated
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: A rename only fully takes effect after reboot; comparing ComputerName\ComputerName (pending/current) against ComputerName\ActiveComputerName (in effect for the current session) can reveal a rename made but not yet completed at the time of acquisition, which is otherwise easy to miss if only one of the two subkeys is checked.
System Information.interpretation: Hostname can facilitate correlation of log data and other artifacts that reference the machine by name. Because the value only changes fully after a reboot, compare ActiveComputerName (current session) against ComputerName (pending/next-boot) to detect an in-progress or recent rename.

System Information.name: Operating System Version
System Information.os_min: Windows XP (Source OS historical-update subkeys present on Windows 10+)
System Information.purpose: Determines the operating system type, edition, version, and build number, plus installation date(s) for both the currently installed build and any prior builds the system was updated from.
