key_fields: ProductName / EditionID - the OS type and edition
DisplayVersion / ReleaseId / CurrentBuildNumber - version and build information
InstallTime - installation time of the current build (64-bit FILETIME, Windows 10+)
InstallDate - installation time of the current build (32-bit Unix epoch)
SYSTEM\Setup\Source OS\<subkey> - one subkey created per historical OS update, holding the same style of ProductName/version/install-time fields for that prior build
System Information.normal_baseline: InstallTime/InstallDate consistent with the organization's known imaging or deployment date; ProductName/EditionID matching the licensed SKU on record; Source OS history showing an orderly, expected progression of prior feature updates.
anomalies: InstallTime far more recent than expected for a host believed to be long-lived, consistent with a re-image used to cover tracks or a fresh OS drop tied to an incident
ProductName/EditionID inconsistent with the asset inventory record for that host
Missing or truncated Source OS history where the patch-management record shows multiple feature updates should have occurred
CurrentBuildNumber indicating an outdated/end-of-life build inconsistent with the org's patch-compliance records
InstallTime and InstallDate values that don't correspond to the same moment when converted, suggesting one of the two was altered
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: InstallTime reflects the installation time of the CURRENT build only - it is refreshed by feature updates - and does not represent the system's original installation date; the Source OS subkeys must be reviewed together to reconstruct the true build lineage. Timestamps embedded in the Source OS subkey names themselves are extraneous and should not be relied on.
System Information.interpretation: CurrentVersion stores ProductName/EditionID (OS type), DisplayVersion/ReleaseId/CurrentBuildNumber (version info), and InstallTime (installation time of the current build, not the original installation). Source OS subkeys are created for each historical OS update and store the same style of information for each prior build. InstallTime is 64-bit FILETIME format (Windows 10+); InstallDate is 32-bit Unix epoch format - both should represent the same moment and can be cross-checked against each other.

System Information.name: System Boot & Autostart Programs
System Information.purpose: Lists of programs that will run automatically on system boot or at user login, spanning both the user-level and machine-level Run/RunOnce keys and the Services key's Start value.
key_fields: HKCU/HKLM Run and RunOnce value names and their command/executable paths
SOFTWARE\...\Policies\Explorer\Run (GPO-pushed autostart entries)
SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services Start value: 0x02 means the service starts at boot (0x00 for drivers)
System Information.normal_baseline: Entries correspond to known startup agents: antivirus/EDR, cloud-sync clients, and vendor-installed utilities consistent with the machine's software inventory.
anomalies: A Run/RunOnce entry pointing to a script interpreter (wscript, powershell, mshta) with an encoded or obfuscated argument
A new autostart entry added in a user-writable path with no corresponding software installation event
A driver or service Start value flipped to boot-start (0x00/0x02) shortly before or during a suspected compromise
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: This is not an exhaustive list of autorun locations. Dozens of other registry and file-system locations can achieve autostart (see the dedicated `run-runonce-keys`, `services-persistence`, `startup-folders`, `ifeo-appinit`, and `wmi-event-subscription` artifacts for the more specific mechanisms this overview summarizes).
System Information.interpretation: Treat this as the summary/checklist view the SANS poster uses under its 'System Information' category; for the actual per-mechanism detail (exact registry paths, anomaly patterns, and anti-forensic notes specific to each autostart technique), use the dedicated artifacts it points to rather than treating this entry as complete on its own.

System Information.name: System Last Shutdown Time
System Information.os_min: Windows XP (ShutdownCount value is Windows XP only)
System Information.location: SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Windows (ShutdownTime value) ; SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Watchdog\Display (ShutdownCount value, Windows XP only)
System Information.purpose: Records the last time the system was shut down; on Windows XP, also records a running count of the total number of shutdowns.
key_fields: ShutdownTime - 64-bit Windows FILETIME value for the most recent shutdown
ShutdownCount - running shutdown counter (Windows XP only)
System Information.normal_baseline: ShutdownTime consistent with routine business-hours shutdown/reboot patterns or a known scheduled-maintenance window for that host.
anomalies: ShutdownTime immediately preceding or following other incident indicators, consistent with an attacker-forced reboot to complete malware/driver installation or to disrupt live-response collection of volatile evidence
ShutdownTime inconsistent with other timeline artifacts for uptime/boot activity, suggesting the value or the system clock was manipulated

A ShutdownTime value present despite other evidence indicating the system was never gracefully shut down (e.g., crash/power-loss indicators), suggesting the value was set through an unexpected process rather than a genuine shutdown
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: ShutdownTime is a single value overwritten on every shutdown, so it only ever reflects the MOST RECENT shutdown - no history of prior shutdowns is retained here. Cross-reference System.evtx (e.g., Event ID 1074/6006 style shutdown/service-stop records) for a fuller shutdown/reboot history than this single registry value can provide on its own.
System Information.interpretation: Determining the last shutdown time can help detect user behavior and system anomalies. The value is stored in 64-bit Windows FILETIME format.

System Information.name: Windows Update History
System Information.os_min: Windows 8.1+ (ETW-based windowsupdate.log); DataStore.edb present since earlier Windows Update client versions
System Information.location: C:\Windows\Logs\WindowsUpdate\*.etl (raw ETW trace files, Windows 8.1+; merged into readable form via Get-WindowsUpdateLog); legacy %WINDIR%\WindowsUpdate.log (pre-8.1); %WINDIR%\SoftwareDistribution\DataStore\DataStore.edb (ESE update history database); %WINDIR%\SoftwareDistribution\ReportingEvents.log
System Information.purpose: Records Windows Update scan, download, and installation activity so an investigator can build a patch-level timeline for the host and determine whether a specific update/CVE was already installed at the time of an incident.
key_fields: Timestamp
Component name (e.g., ProtocolTalker, DownloadManager, Handler, DataStore)
Update ID (GUID) and revision number
Revision ID
Local ID
Installation result/error code
System Information.normal_baseline: Periodic scan/download/install entries aligned with Patch Tuesday and scheduled maintenance windows, with consistent component sequences (AU, COMAPI, Handler) and no unexplained gaps.
anomalies: Gaps in update history around the incident timeframe suggesting Windows Update service was disabled or logs tampered with
A known-exploited CVE's update missing or showing repeated failed installation despite otherwise current patch history
DataStore.edb modification time inconsistent with the surrounding update timeline
wuauserv stop/start events immediately bracketing suspicious activity
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: Update history in DataStore.edb can be wiped by stopping wuauserv and deleting the SoftwareDistribution folder; raw ETL trace files are rotated and not retained indefinitely, so delayed triage can lose ETW-level detail even after a WindowsUpdate.log snapshot exists.

System Information.name: Group Policy Application Logs
System Information.os_min: Windows Vista+ / Windows Server 2008+ (Microsoft-Windows-GroupPolicy/Operational evtx channel)
System Information.location: Event log channel Microsoft-Windows-GroupPolicy/Operational (Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > GroupPolicy > Operational); System.evtx (Group Policy service events, e.g. Event IDs 1002, 1006, 1030, 1053, 1058, 1097, 1129, 4016, 5016); gpresult /r or /h output (RSoP report); %WINDIR%\debug\usermode\gpsvc.log (verbose debug log, enabled via HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Diagnostics\GPSvcDebugLevel)
System Information.purpose: Documents each instance of Group Policy processing (start, client-side extension processing, success, failure) on a host, enabling reconstruction of which GPOs applied and when, or detection of GPO-based tampering.
key_fields: ActivityID (correlates all events for one processing instance)
Event ID
GPO name/GUID
Client-side extension (CSE) name
User vs. computer processing context
Error code/description
System Information.normal_baseline: Regular start/success event pairs at logon, logoff, and background refresh intervals for each linked GPO, consistent ActivityID correlation, and no recurring failure events (1002/1006/1030/1053/1058/1097/1129).
anomalies: Unfamiliar GPO names/GUIDs applying outside normal change-management windows
Repeated Group Policy processing failures coinciding with suspicious activity, suggesting deliberate disruption of policy-based controls
A Scheduled Task or logon/logoff script CSE entry pushed via GPO shortly before malicious execution
GroupPolicy.evtx or gpsvc.log cleared/rotated near the incident window
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: An attacker with domain rights can modify or delete a GPO directly in Active Directory/SYSVOL, leaving little endpoint-side trace beyond the next re-application event; clearing the local Microsoft-Windows-GroupPolicy/Operational log (wevtutil cl) removes the endpoint's processing history.

System Information.name: BitLocker Artifacts
System Information.location: Event log channels Microsoft-Windows-BitLocker-API/Management and Microsoft-Windows-BitLocker-API/Operational; registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\FVE (BitLocker Group Policy configuration, including LogVerboseLevel); Active Directory msFVE-RecoveryInformation object (msFVE-RecoveryPassword attribute) on the computer object, viewable via the BitLocker Recovery Password Viewer RSAT snap-in; Entra ID (Azure AD) device BitLocker key escrow
System Information.purpose: Establishes whether a volume was BitLocker-protected and when protection was enabled, suspended, or removed, and where its recovery key was escrowed, relevant both for data recovery and for confirming whether encryption was abused as an anti-forensic or ransomware mechanism.
key_fields: Event ID and channel (Management vs. Operational)
Volume/protector GUID
Protector type (TPM, PIN, password, recovery key, network unlock)
Encryption/decryption state and percentage
Recovery key backup destination (AD DS, Entra ID, printed, saved to file)
FVE registry policy values (e.g., LogVerboseLevel, encryption method)
System Information.normal_baseline: BitLocker enabled once at deployment/imaging with a corresponding recovery-key backup event to AD/Entra ID logged shortly after; suspend/resume events correlating with routine firmware or OS updates; no unexpected full-volume decrypt or protector-removal events.
anomalies: BitLocker suspended (manage-bde -protectors -disable) immediately before other suspicious activity, removing the authentication requirement on next boot
Volume encryption started outside imaging/patch windows or on a system that shouldn't be encrypted, consistent with BitLocker/ShrinkLocker-style ransomware abuse
Recovery password change/protector removal with no matching AD/Entra escrow record
FVE policy registry keys modified shortly before an incident
parsing_tools: BitLocker Recovery Password Viewer (RSAT AD Users and Computers extension)
Event Viewer / wevtutil for BitLocker-API log export
System Information.anti_forensic_notes: ShrinkLocker and similar malware abuse the legitimate BitLocker feature to encrypt volumes for extortion while deleting or rotating the local recovery key so it cannot be recovered from the endpoint, sometimes shrinking the partition to install its own boot components; suspending protection or disabling TPM-based unlock removes evidence of the intended recovery path.
